articles.description:
A new open-core project called ARES is giving red teams a way to run planned, controlled attack tests against Active Directory and cloud systems. A developer who goes by Mafifrizi released the tool on GitHub. It ships with 66 active modules, with 70 cataloged in total, covering more than 60 techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. […]

The post ARES AI Red Team Platform Automates 66 Attack Modules for Active Directory and Cloud Security Testing appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new open-core project called ARES is giving red teams a way to run planned, controlled attack tests against Active Directory and cloud systems. A developer who goes by Mafifrizi released the tool on GitHub.

It ships with 66 active modules, with 70 cataloged in total, covering more than 60 techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. It is aimed at enterprise red teams, managed security providers (MSSPs), and security operations centers.

Mafifrizi publishes the project as an open-core platform, which means the base tool is free to read and test while a sponsorship page supports ongoing work.

The project page lists the repository under the handle “mafifrizi/ares” and describes it as an autonomous red-team engagement platform with MITRE ATT&CK module orchestration, attack-path solving, and reporting. The README does not give a real name, company, or team behind the code, so readers should treat it as an independent project for now.

The author’s pitch is simple. Traditional penetration tests cost a lot, happen rarely, and only show one moment in time, so new misconfigurations can sit unseen for months.

Vulnerability scanners add to the problem by listing thousands of possible CVEs without proving that any of them can be used. ARES tries to fill that gap by running real test steps and showing which ones lead to the most valuable systems, such as domain admin accounts.

The part of ARES that stands out most is how hard it tries to keep tests inside approved limits. Before a module runs, a check called ScopeGuard confirms the target is in scope.

A second layer, the Scope Firewall and Egress Filter, then blocks traffic at two levels. One level uses the operating system firewall, which is Windows Defender Firewall or Linux Netfilter when the tool runs with elevated rights. The other watches network calls inside Python itself. The goal is a “fail-closed” design, where the tool stops instead of sending traffic to an address nobody approved.

The tool also profiles how noisy each action is, so operators can pick quieter steps when they want to test whether the blue team notices. This matters because a careless test can knock over a production server. For the same reason, security teams are shifting toward tools that put a person in charge of each decision.

Active Directory Attack Paths

For Active Directory, ARES can load BloodHound collections or map live domain sessions. Its built-in graph engine then works out the shortest route to Domain Admin, points out chokepoints, and checks whether a sideways move is possible.

BloodHound uses the same graph idea, where a small group membership can open a path that is many steps long. Cyber Security News has explained how BloodHound Community Edition maps these paths across Active Directory and Azure.

Operators can set a goal such as domain_admin, full_compromise, or cloud_audit. The planning engine then builds a multi-step plan from graph rules. It can also use AI agents such as Claude, OpenAI, or a local Ollama model, but only after the operator gives clear permission.

The same planning engine covers cloud checks, and the cloud_audit goal is one of the built-in options. Letting a language model suggest next steps is now common in offensive tools. Cyber Security News recently reported on Decepticon, an open-source agent with 16 specialist roles. ARES keeps the AI optional, which many teams will prefer.

Defenders have a reason to watch this space. Criminals are using similar tools. Cyber Security News covered how hackers used the ARTEX AI agents to map Windows networks, steal service account passwords, and try to spread inside the network. A platform like ARES lets defenders test the same steps first, on their own terms.

Because ARES stores sensitive material, the author added several protections. Sessions live in the database, access tokens are short-lived and kept in memory, and refresh tokens are rotated. ARES stores harvested hashes and client evidence in a local vault protected with AES-256-GCM and PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 rounds.

When a test ends, ARES can produce branded reports in PDF, HTML, Markdown, and JSON. The PDF step runs through a headless browser, so it needs no extra GTK libraries on Windows or Linux. For teams that want a deeper guide to the Active Directory side, the Active Directory attack checklist on Cyber Security News is a useful companion.

Only run ARES on systems you own or have written permission to test. Start in a lab, check that the scope rules block out-of-range addresses, and review the code before using it on real networks. Fix any path the tool finds to a domain admin account, then run it again to confirm the fix.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Adobe Commerce Zero-Day to Deploy PSK Agent RAT and Remotely Control Servers
articles.description:
Attackers are abusing a serious flaw in Adobe Commerce and Magento to install a hidden remote access tool called PSK Agent on online store servers. Once it is running, they can run commands, route traffic through the server, and keep access even after a restart. The flaw, named StyleSmuggler and tracked as CVE-2026-75650, was first […]

The post Hackers Exploit Adobe Commerce Zero-Day to Deploy PSK Agent RAT and Remotely Control Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are abusing a serious flaw in Adobe Commerce and Magento to install a hidden remote access tool called PSK Agent on online store servers.

Once it is running, they can run commands, route traffic through the server, and keep access even after a restart. The flaw, named StyleSmuggler and tracked as CVE-2026-75650, was first revealed as a zero-day in early September.

Sansec said it let anyone run code on a store without logging in, and it affected every current version, including 2.4.9. Within days, more than one group was using it to drop different malware.

Researchers at Imperva noted the PSK Agent activity after tracking a coordinated campaign between September 9 and September 13, 2026.

They saw it hit stores in Western Europe, North America and the Asia-Pacific region. The malware had a 0% detection rate on VirusTotal at the time of analysis, so basic file scanning would likely have missed it.

Hackers Exploit Adobe Commerce Zero-Day

The attackers went after one endpoint, /paypal/transparent/response/, which matches the first step of StyleSmuggler. In that step, the attacker places PHP code in the request’s query string.

Magento then logs the error and writes that code into a report file under var/report/. A second request to /graphql uses attacker-controlled styles values to load the poisoned file and run the code.

Imperva tracked five attack clusters coming from a small set of IP addresses. The near-identical payloads point to automated tools that scan for weak stores at scale.

The download link for the first script, psk_agent.sh, showed up 96 times across 12 payload variants, which suggests the attackers kept using one stable delivery path.

The PHP payload tries the shell_exec, system and exec functions in turn. If one is blocked, it quietly moves to the next. It then runs a curl command that pipes the script straight into bash, so the first command never touches the disk.

The 3,313-byte script looks for a folder that is both writable and executable, such as /tmp or /dev/shm. It then downloads the next stage with curl, wget or Python and starts it in the background.

That stage is chi_down, a heavily obfuscated 10.5 MB Go program. It can run shell commands, collect host details and proxy traffic through SOCKS5.

It also talks to its operators over HTTP, HTTPS and encrypted channels. Its launch arguments, -checkagent=false -maintain=true, suggest it is meant to survive restarts.

DNS Beacons, Webshells and Signs of a Chinese-Speaking Operator

Some payloads also told the attackers when an attack worked. The code put the victim’s hostname into a unique subdomain under 0f851bdc9d.ddns.1433.eu.org and then made both an HTTP and a DNS request.

The attackers controlled the DNS servers, so the lookup alone proved success, even if the web request failed. That gave them a quiet, running list of hacked servers.

In some cases, the operators added a second way back in. They downloaded t4.php and saved it as zer4.php in public folders such as pub/media/.

This 910-line file manager and PHP web shells like it let attackers edit files, upload or download data, and run system commands. It uses PHP’s Foreign Function Interface to call libc directly, which can still work when common PHP functions are turned off.

The same hardcoded AES-256-CBC key appeared in every sample, which hints at one operator or a shared toolkit. Imperva found Chinese-language comments in the script, with names such as chinow and chi_down in the infrastructure.

The researchers rate a Chinese-speaking operator as likely, with moderate confidence. They warn that language clues can be planted or copied, and they do not name a specific group.

They also stress that this applies only to PSK Agent, since other attackers have used the same flaw to drop a Rust backdoor and different PHP droppers.

Store owners should apply Adobe’s VULN-39341 hotfix. That only closes the entry point, though. It does not remove a RAT, webshell or stolen credentials that were planted earlier.

A server with any of these signs should be treated as fully compromised. Check for psk_agent.sh, chi_down, zer4.php and fake process names like kworker, fc-cache and chronyd.

Rotate the Magento encryption key, database logins, admin credentials, API tokens and SSH keys. Watch for DNS lookups to the beacon domain and for web servers making unexpected outbound connections.

Zscaler also saw some of the same download infrastructure in Citrix NetScaler attacks, but that overlap is only a lead and does not prove the same actor is behind both.

Magento stores have long been a favorite target. A past campaign showed how fast things can spread, when the CosmicSting flaw hit thousands of stores.

Patching quickly and checking for earlier compromise remain the best defenses. The full technical breakdown is in Imperva’s research blog.

File Hashes

Network Indicators

articles.description:

AI-assisted research helped identify the vulnerabilities and develop working exploits […]

The post Cogent Security Makes the Fortune Cyber 60 for a Second Year, With a Plan to Run Cyber Defense Like a Factory appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
San Francisco, CA, November 3rd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Cogent Security, an applied AI cybersecurity company, reported that the PHP2Shell vulnerability exposed significant gaps in enterprise vulnerability response.

Disclosed on October 21, PHP2Shell involved two critical flaws that had remained in PHP for more than a decade.

AI-assisted research helped identify the vulnerabilities and develop working exploits in approximately one week, with attacks beginning before a patch was available. Cloudflare recorded millions of exploitation attempts that day.

According to Cogent Security’s research, by 5 p.m. Pacific, the average Fortune 500 company had patched fewer than 1% of its 2,266 affected assets.

That gap between how fast attackers move and how fast large companies respond is the problem Cogent was built to close.

The company, an applied AI lab focused on cybersecurity, has been named to the Fortune Cyber 60 for the second consecutive year.

The list, developed by Fortune with Lightspeed Venture Partners and AWS, recognizes 60 of the most important venture-backed cybersecurity startups that have yet to go public, be acquired, or reach another significant exit, grouped by stage.

Selection weighs financial performance, growth, business operations, and cybersecurity market research, and Fortune validates the final list. 

“Attackers already run like a factory. AI is finding the bugs and writing the exploits, and in some cases it’s running most of the attack,” said Vineet Edupuganti, Cogent’s co-founder and CEO.

“Most enterprises are still defending by hand, one ticket and one handoff at a time. Making this list two years in a row tells us security leaders are ready to change how that work gets done.”

The attackers built their factories first

Edupuganti borrows an analogy from manufacturing. Factories replaced the lone skilled worker with a production line, and the most advanced plants now run largely on their own while people design the line and handle the exceptions.

Offense, he argues, has already made that shift.

The data points the same way. Google’s M-Trends 2026 report estimates the mean time to exploit at negative seven days, which means exploitation now routinely begins before a fix exists.

Researchers have shown AI producing working exploits for newly published vulnerabilities in about 15 minutes, at roughly a dollar apiece. In a state-sponsored campaign that Anthropic disrupted, AI agents carried out 80 to 90% of the tactical work.

Enterprise defense still moves at the pace of its slowest handoff. When PHP2Shell landed, security teams had to find every asset running PHP, including base images and forgotten servers, then work out which were internet-facing and which the business depended on.

After that came owners, tickets, change windows, and a rescan to confirm each fix held, with every step falling to a skilled person with a tool.

Building the Defender’s Production Line

Cogent’s answer is what it calls the Cyber Defense Factory, an operating model in which AI agents take over the work that now moves by hand between security tools, while people set the policies those agents follow.

The company sells an enterprise platform for autonomous cyber defense, and its first product applies the model to vulnerability management.

The line starts with an inventory. Agents build one deduplicated record of every asset across cloud, on-premises and endpoint environments, inferring each one’s owner and business importance from systems the company already keeps.

Findings flow in from the scanners and security tools customers already run, and Cogent matches newly published vulnerabilities against its live software inventory so exposure surfaces before scanners catch up.

Agents then check whether the vulnerable software is running and reachable, and they write out the reasoning behind every priority.

Cogent groups remediation work by fix, so one patch can resolve a vulnerability across dozens of servers. Inside the autonomy zones each customer defines, agents carry out supported fixes on their own.

On managed endpoints, for instance, they write the remediation script, push it through the company’s existing endpoint management platform, and read back the results.

Changes outside those zones go to a single owner as a ticket and wait for a person’s approval, and Cogent closes the work only after the next scan confirms the fix held.

The company says the goal is for enterprises to transform their cybersecurity functions with a factory model to do 100 times more work, 100 times faster.

Most customers start with agents in an assistive role and widen their authority as the results earn trust, an approach Cogent calls progressive autonomy.

PHP2Shell gave the model a live test. Cogent’s Zero Day Response processed the advisory and mapped vulnerable assets across customer environments in an average of five minutes, days before scanner signatures were available.

Applied to the average Fortune 500 environment in Cogent’s research, the analysis cut 2,266 affected assets down to 16 that had PHP loaded at runtime, faced the internet, and supported critical business functions.

That shortlist was waiting for security teams when they sat down to start work.

A Lab With Its Own Models

Cogent describes itself as an applied AI lab that just happens to focus on defensive cybersecurity, and the label reflects how the company is built.

It is the only cybersecurity company that trains and deploys its own frontier reasoning models for security use cases.

Its domain-specific model, VR-1, has topped cybersecurity benchmarks, outperforming general-purpose frontier models on security tasks.

The model works alongside Cogent’s Context Engine, which ties each vulnerability to the assets, identities, applications, owners, and dependencies around it.

That context usually sits scattered across asset databases, ticket histories and architecture documents, and pulling it together is what lets agents judge which changes are safe to make.

“A general-purpose AI model knows a little about everything,” Edupuganti said. “When an AI agent is deciding whether a patch is safe to push to a few thousand production servers, it needs a model that has learned how vulnerabilities, exploits and enterprise systems behave, plus deep context on the company it’s protecting. Put those together and you can give agents real responsibility.”

Racing the Exploit Clock

For security leaders, Edupuganti argues, the number that matters now is the time between a vulnerability’s disclosure and a verified fix, and that window has to be shorter than the time an attacker needs to build and launch an exploit.

Cogent is betting that closing it takes a different operating model, one where security work grows with the production line rather than with headcount.

The company’s second straight appearance on the Cyber 60 suggests buyers are warming to that bet, though Edupuganti expects people to stay at the center of it.

“The most advanced factories still have people in them. They decide what the line builds and the standard it holds,” he said. “Security teams are moving into that role. They set the policy and make the judgment calls, and the agents do the work at machine speed.”

About Cogent

Cogent Security is an applied AI lab building the enterprise platform for autonomous cyber defense. Its AI agents find and fix vulnerabilities at machine speed so every enterprise can run its own Cyber Defense Factory.

Starting with autonomous vulnerability management, Cogent carries vulnerabilities from disclosure to a verified fix across cloud, on-premises, and endpoint environments, identifying exposure within minutes and confirming what attackers can reach along the way.

Customers set the policies the agents follow and decide which fixes run autonomously and which wait for approval.

Fortune 500 security teams using Cogent have reduced the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97 percent.

Built by researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal Security, and Coinbase, Cogent is backed by Greylock Partners and Bain Capital Ventures. Learn more at cogent.com.

Contact

Ignacio Ramirez

press@cogent.com

The post Cogent Security Makes the Fortune Cyber 60 for a Second Year, With a Plan to Run Cyber Defense Like a Factory appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Hackers Hijacked Linux Hosting Server Security Tool cPGuard and Used It as a Backdoor
articles.description:
An unidentified attacker compromised the update channel for cPGuard, a security tool used on Linux hosting servers, to distribute a malicious script that installed a backdoor and collected sensitive files. OPSSHIELD confirmed that the attacker retrieved some stolen data and urged administrators to install version 5.88.25 or later immediately. According to OPSSHIELD’s security advisory, the […]

The post Hackers Hijacked Linux Hosting Server Security Tool cPGuard and Used It as a Backdoor appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An unidentified attacker compromised the update channel for cPGuard, a security tool used on Linux hosting servers, to distribute a malicious script that installed a backdoor and collected sensitive files. OPSSHIELD confirmed that the attacker retrieved some stolen data and urged administrators to install version 5.88.25 or later immediately.

According to OPSSHIELD’s security advisory, the breach began on November 2, 2026, at 02:06 UTC. The attacker used compromised credentials to access the company’s update distribution infrastructure, or CDN. How those credentials were obtained remains under investigation.

cPGuard Supply Chain Attack

The attacker distributed the script through cPGuard versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19. OPSSHIELD detected the attack within 12 hours of the affected updates becoming available, secured the compromised account, cleared infrastructure credentials, and stopped further distribution. Because servers check for updates at intervals, some may not have executed the malicious script.

The attack turned a trusted security update into a route for malware delivery. Related Cybersecuritynews coverage of compromised Terraform workflows shows another way attackers have used trusted software processes to deliver backdoors. The cPGuard incident specifically involved stolen access to the vendor’s distribution infrastructure.

The malicious script collected Linux account files, including /etc/shadow and /etc/passwd, root MariaDB or MySQL configuration, root shell history, and root SSH authorization and known-hosts files. OPSSHIELD has not established that every listed file was collected from every affected server.

Collected data went to OPSSHIELD’s own licensing server under a compromised account, where the attacker could retrieve it later. In a November 3 update, the company estimated that the attacker retrieved 32 collected files, each corresponding to one customer server. That preliminary figure measures confirmed retrieval, not the total number of potentially affected servers.

Linux passwords in /etc/shadow are stored as hashes rather than readable passwords. Attackers can test password guesses against stolen hashes offline, making weak or reused passwords particularly risky. Database configuration and shell history may contain other secrets without that protection.

The wider concern is credential reuse beyond the original server. Cybersecuritynews previously covered QLNX credential theft targeting Linux developers, another case highlighting the value of SSH keys and cloud credentials to attackers. No connection between these incidents has been established.

Administrators should review update history with grep 'Successfully updated' /opt/cpguard/logs/install_log. Entries showing versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 confirm installation of an affected update, but do not prove script execution or data transfer. Missing or incomplete logs also cannot establish that a server escaped compromise.

Known indicators include the script cpguard-v58812-i91511.sh, backdoor shell /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh, collection directory /var/tmp/.cpg91511, and staged archive /var/tmp/.cpg91511/loot.tgz. Their absence after cleanup does not rule out earlier execution.

OPSSHIELD instructs every customer to run cpgcli update --start, then check cpgcli --version to confirm version 5.88.25 or later. Administrators whose updates fail should contact OPSSHIELD Support. The corrective update removes the known backdoor and staged files, but cannot invalidate credentials already copied.

Potentially compromised servers require password resets for root and other password-enabled local accounts from a trusted recovery environment. Administrators should rotate affected database passwords, S3 keys, DigitalOcean tokens, and exposed shell-history secrets. They should replace private keys under /root/.ssh and remove corresponding old public keys wherever trusted.

OPSSHIELD is also releasing an update to remove previously added support-access keys. It does not currently recommend routine server rebuilds, but that guidance remains provisional. Additional compromise signs or uncertain server integrity may justify rebuilding after an individual assessment.

The expanded alliance focuses on a practical problem: identifying […]

The post CrowdStrike and Deloitte Expand AI Security Partnership to Transform How Enterprises Detect Cyber Threats appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CrowdStrike and Deloitte have expanded their cybersecurity partnership to connect business risk decisions with threat detection and response. Announced on November 2, 2026, at Fal.Con Europe in Barcelona, the agreement brings Falcon IQ into Deloitte Spain’s advisory services, linking security planning with implementation and managed operations.

The expanded alliance focuses on a practical problem: identifying security weaknesses does not automatically lead to fixing them. CrowdStrike supplies its Falcon platform and AI tools, while Deloitte turns findings into investment plans, technology changes, and ongoing security work.

“Finding risk is only half the battle. What matters is how quickly you can act on it and evolve strategy for the future,” said Daniel Bernard, CrowdStrike’s chief business officer.

Falcon IQ Connects Risk Findings

At the center of the expansion is Falcon IQ, which gives Deloitte a measurable view of exploitable risk. Deloitte will use those findings alongside executive Innovation Workshops to build security plans covering immediate fixes, medium-term improvements, and longer-term goals tied to business needs and regulatory priorities.

CrowdStrike introduced Falcon IQ on August 31, 2026, to automate assessment and repair workflows under Project QuiltWorks. The platform combines customer security data, CrowdStrike threat intelligence, and findings from Falcon OverWatch threat hunters to help partners understand exposure and recommend action.

Built on Falcon Foundry and Charlotte AI AgentWorks, Falcon IQ uses more than 50 AI agents across assessment, prioritization, and remediation tasks. NVIDIA’s open Nemotron models power its agent engine. Partners can also map findings to their own services, producing action plans and tracking progress through a customer dashboard.

This work sits alongside broader concerns about AI systems. Cyber Security News previously covered CrowdStrike’s research into prompt injection techniques, showing how malicious instructions can target agents that browse websites, access data, and execute commands.

The implementation stage includes moving customers to Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. SIEM, short for security information and event management, brings security data together for analysis. CrowdStrike’s platform combines that data with AI-based detection, investigation tools, threat intelligence, and automated response workflows.

For analysts, the intended benefit is clearer context across connected systems rather than isolated alerts. Falcon Next-Gen SIEM supports third-party security and IT data, while licensed Falcon modules can contribute endpoint, identity, and cloud activity without additional ingestion charges.

Data handling is also part of this shift. Cyber Security News previously reported on CrowdStrike’s planned acquisition of Onum, whose technology filters and routes security data before analysis. Falcon’s current SIEM offering includes Onum data pipelines.

The operational stage builds on Deloitte’s November 2025 integration of Falcon Next-Gen SIEM into its Managed Extended Detection and Response service, known as MXDR. That service combines continuous monitoring with human investigation, threat intelligence, and response support.

Deloitte’s EMEA Cybersphere Center in Madrid will support delivery under the expanded agreement. Edward James Moore, cybersecurity partner at Deloitte Spain, said the collaboration helps clients connect risk insights with security investments and carry those priorities into implementation and daily operations.

The announcement sets out a service model, not measured customer results. It provides no deployment timelines, pricing, or evidence showing how much the expanded arrangement improves detection or response times.

articles.title: Attackers Started Scanning in the Wild for Linux Kernel RCE Flaw, Ubuntu Releases Fixes
articles.description:
Ubuntu has put early kernel fixes for CVE-2026-98432 in its -proposed pocket for 22.04 LTS and newer releases. The bug is a serious Linux kernel flaw that can let a remote user run commands as root without a login or any user action. The patches are still in testing, so many servers stay open for […]

The post Attackers Started Scanning in the Wild for Linux Kernel RCE Flaw, Ubuntu Releases Fixes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ubuntu has put early kernel fixes for CVE-2026-98432 in its -proposed pocket for 22.04 LTS and newer releases. The bug is a serious Linux kernel flaw that can let a remote user run commands as root without a login or any user action. The patches are still in testing, so many servers stay open for now.

Canonical’s security team says the flaw sits in how the Linux kernel sets up IPv4 TCP connections, and it affects kernel versions 4.4 and later. The fixed builds are 5.15.0-203.213 for Jammy (22.04), 6.8.0-149.149 for Noble (24.04), and 7.0.0-43.43 for Resolute (26.04). Stonking (26.10) is already fixed in 7.3.0-10.10, and Trusty (14.04) is not affected. Fixes for Xenial, Bionic and Focal are still pending.

Canonical runs tests on more than 2,000 certified servers and devices before it moves a kernel to the updates pocket. Teams that run their own acceptance tests can install the early builds today, as described in Canonical’s new SRU strategy for faster CVE fixes.

Ubuntu’s CVE-2026-98432 tracker rates the bug 9.8, which is Critical. Its own blog post calls the same score “High,” so readers may see both labels. The record was published on October 15, 2026.

The bug is a use-after-free. In plain terms, the kernel keeps using a piece of memory after it has already let go of it. One CPU frees the IP options of a new connection. Another CPU, handling a repeated SYN packet, still reads them while building a reply. The upstream fix delays that free with kfree_rcu(), so readers finish first.

Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team shared its research on October 27, 2026. It says an unreleased Claude model wrote a working exploit after one first prompt. The exploit targets Linux servers with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener.

It works in two stages. First, it makes the kernel send back extra bytes that may hold a kernel pointer, which defeats KASLR, a defense that hides where kernel code sits. Second, it overwrites a callback pointer so the kernel runs a payload and ends in a shell command as root.

A lost race only fails the handshake and does not crash the machine, so the attacker can retry. In the test, the leak took 48 minutes, and the shell took five more.

Cyber Security News covered this in Claude AI Exploits Linux Kernel Flaw to Execute Root Commands Without User Interaction. Our earlier report on Claude building Chrome and Linux exploit chains shows how this fits a wider pattern. Anthropic’s exploit has not been released. It also says this was a lab test and not a real-world incident.

Signs of Scanning in the Wild

Researcher Marcus Hutchins says his team has seen what looks like threat actors scanning the whole internet for affected systems. In a post on X, he reports that residential proxies and Russia-based VPN servers began probing port 443 with MPTCP connections as of November 2.

Normal scanners do not use MPTCP by default, so he strongly suspects this activity targets CVE-2026-98432. His scan on October 30 found about 2,102,043 servers reachable over MPTCP on port 443.

A deeper TLS scan found about 762,774. He says a valid HTTP request is not needed, so the true exposure is likely closer to 2.1 million. These counts show exposure only and do not prove the kernels are unpatched.

There is no public remote code execution exploit yet. Several denial-of-service proofs-of-concept do exist, and they give attackers a starting point.

Some people assumed MPTCP listeners were rare. Hutchins points out that Debian and several other kernels enable MPTCP by default. Go 1.24 and later also bind MPTCP sockets when the kernel allows it, so tools built on Go, such as Caddy, create the needed listener.

Ubuntu emphasizes that the flaw itself is not tied to MPTCP, and the MPTCP link comes only from the Anthropic exploit. Ubuntu’s security team says updates are the only proper fix. Hutchins adds that setting net.mptcp.enabled=0 does not close sockets that are already open, so those apps must restart. You can list MPTCP listeners with sudo ss -Mlnp.

For Admins

Run uname -r and compare the result with the fixed versions above. Ubuntu’s guide to enabling the -proposed pocket explains how to pull in the new kernel, and a reboot is needed afterward. Packages in -proposed are not chosen for upgrade by default, so you must name the pocket when you install.

For hosts that cannot update yet, Ubuntu’s tracker lists an nftables rule that drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. It reduces risk but does not fully prevent exploitation, and it breaks any connection that relies on IP options.

Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and older need Ubuntu Pro. Focal and Bionic fall under Expanded Security Maintenance, while Xenial and Trusty need the Legacy add-on. Ubuntu Pro is free for up to five machines.

It also compromised a high-profile person in Israel who works in the security sector. The campaign ran from August to October 2026 and was still […]

The post Iran-Linked DarkBlinders Hackers Breach Government Cloud Systems and Steal Over 1GB of Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An Iran-linked hacking group called DarkBlinders has broken into a government cloud system in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. The group stole at least 1 GB of data from it.

It also compromised a high-profile person in Israel who works in the security sector. The campaign ran from August to October 2026 and was still active when it was reported.

The same actor is behind Blinder Tunnel, a campaign that used a Dubai Airports coding test lure to target Iraqi infrastructure. Unit 42 documented that earlier work. This new wave shows the group is still active and keeps changing its tools.

Researchers at Dream noted the malware while tracking the group’s new activity. They reverse-engineered it and gained read-only access to the attacker’s command servers. That gave them a rare look at what the operators were doing to victims.

Iran-Linked DarkBlinders Hackers Breach Government Cloud Systems

The group began with fake login pages and fake downloads. Some copied Outlook Web App pages and posed as the Kuwait Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Gulf Cooperation Council Secretariat General.

These pages only collected usernames and passwords. A stolen login can open email, contacts, shared files and linked cloud services without setting off a malware alert. This is similar to the Iran-linked password spray campaign that hit Microsoft 365 tenants earlier this year.

Other lures copied Google Drive sharing links on domains themed around the Kurdistan Regional Government. The page said a ZIP file could not be previewed and told the victim to download it.

A fake video-meeting app named StarkMeet was the second delivery route. It showed a normal setup wizard and a working-looking meeting screen, but the Join button always failed.

While the decoy ran, hidden files were installed in a separate folder. They kept running even if the user removed StarkMeet. The malware sent details about the infected computer to a GitHub repository, and the operator reviewed them first.

Only chosen victims received the key needed to unlock the second-stage backdoor. About ten systems checked in, but only two victims showed up in the tasking channel.

The backdoor ran PowerShell commands inside its own process, so it never started powershell.exe. It could also upload and download files.

Recovered commands showed credential theft and the removal of at least 1 GB of data from the Iraqi government cloud. If GitHub shut down the account, the malware could read a hidden comment in the public Microsoft vscode repository to find new settings.

Who Is Behind DarkBlinders and How to Respond

Dream links DarkBlinders to UNC5795 and Dust Specter with medium-to-high confidence. It says, with medium confidence, that this cluster and UNC5187 may be related subclusters of APT34.

The evidence includes shared servers, matching malware and a similar focus on Iraqi government targets. The signs of an Iranian link are real but limited.

The first host to check in was a virtual machine with a Persian keyboard layout, and one decoy domain used ParsVDS name servers.

Dream says neither fact proves the operator’s identity on its own. Other Iran-linked groups work in similar ways. One example is the Seedworm signed binaries campaign, which hid behind trusted software.

Defenders should watch for fake meeting tools and for GitHub traffic that does not match normal developer work. They should also look for PowerShell running in unusual places and for login pages that imitate regional institutions.

Because GitHub and Cloudflare are shared platforms, block only the exact accounts and paths listed below, not the whole services. Quiet access like this often fits a wider pattern of Iranian hackers building access before they use it.

articles.title: Hackers Use Malicious VHDX Files and WebDAV Links to Infect Windows Devices With PapRAT Malware
articles.description:
A suspected espionage group is sending fake meeting letters and event invitations to organizations in South Asia. The files look harmless, but they quietly install a custom remote access trojan called PapRAT on Windows computers. The campaign uses Windows disk images, shortcut files, and remote web folders to avoid easy detection. The activity points to […]

The post Hackers Use Malicious VHDX Files and WebDAV Links to Infect Windows Devices With PapRAT Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A suspected espionage group is sending fake meeting letters and event invitations to organizations in South Asia. The files look harmless, but they quietly install a custom remote access trojan called PapRAT on Windows computers.

The campaign uses Windows disk images, shortcut files, and remote web folders to avoid easy detection. The activity points to BITTER, a group believed to be based in South Asia and active since at least 2013.

It has a history of targeting government, energy, and engineering organizations. Readers who follow the Bitter group’s custom-developed tools will see that PapRAT is another sign of steady investment in its malware toolkit.

Researchers from Fortinet’s FortiGuard Labs identified the malware while tracking the campaign for several months.

They linked it to BITTER with high confidence based on lure file names, command-and-control (C2) traffic patterns, file details, and malware analysis. They found three separate infection chains, and two of them rely on VHDX files and WebDAV links.

Hackers Use Malicious VHDX Files and WebDAV Links

The second infection chain starts with a VHDX file, which is a virtual hard disk image that Windows can mount like a USB drive. In one case, the file was named “Letter from the Ambassador – 11th Belt and Road Summit.”

Once opened, it shows a single visible shortcut (LNK) file. Two hidden files sit beside it: a decoy spreadsheet called “Attachment-2.xls” and an installer called “Visa_Details.msi”.

When the victim clicks the shortcut, it runs a command that starts the installer in the background and opens the spreadsheet at the same time.

The victim sees a normal document and has no reason to be suspicious. This trick is not unique to BITTER. Earlier, APT-C-60 weaponized VHDX files in a similar way against recruiters in Japan.

The third chain uses WebDAV, a Windows feature that lets a computer open files on a remote web server as if they were local. It begins with an archive named “Official Invitation Majilis 2026 Gala Dinner.rar.”

Inside is a URL shortcut that connects to a remote server and pulls down a shortcut file and a script. That script creates a scheduled task, contacts the attacker’s server, and then installs a second MSI file called “Imp_Details.msi”.

Attackers like WebDAV because the remote folder looks like a normal local folder. Cofense researchers have reported that this connection skips the usual browser warnings, which is why abuse of Windows File Explorer has become a growing delivery method for remote access trojans.

The first chain is the quietest. A shortcut file abuses the built-in Windows ftp.exe tool to run a hidden script. It then sets up scheduled tasks with names such as “MicrosoftUpdates” and uses curl to reach the attacker’s server.

A fake pop-up tells the victim that Explorer could not open the file. No traditional malware file is dropped at this stage, so security tools that look only for executables may miss it.

What PapRAT Can Do and How It Is Changing

Inside the MSI installer, the only real action is a custom step that drops PapRAT onto the machine. The file pretends to be a Microsoft component named “bruzsvc.exe” with the product name “Microsoft redistributables.”

Once running, it contacts a hardcoded C2 server over plain HTTP every 10 seconds. The server address is hidden with XOR encoding using the key 0x50. It identifies each victim by joining the username and computer name with an underscore.

The first version of PapRAT is written in C++ and understands eight commands. These let the attacker run shell commands, list folders, delete files, run programs, list drives, take screenshots, and upload or download files.

In the third chain, PapRAT used its download command to fetch a second tool, “vnces.exe,” which is WmRAT. WmRAT is another remote access trojan that BITTER uses for system information, screenshots, and command execution.

Fortinet also found a newer version written in Rust. The name PapRAT comes from this build, which contains the file name “requpap.pdb” and the product name “papsolutions.”

The Rust version uses HTTPS, waits 42 seconds before starting, and then checks in every 5 seconds. It hides its constants with reversed text and a ROT-3 shift. It also adds three commands for PowerShell execution, sleeping, and exiting, which raises the total to eleven.

Defenders should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, especially when they arrive in unsolicited messages.

Fortinet advises watching scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity instead of relying only on file signatures.

Teams can also learn from the Russian RedFlick phishing campaigns, where researchers advised linking archive extraction, VHDX mounting, LNK execution, and WebDAV activity in one view.

articles.title: BYDFi’s Up to 8,100 USDT Welcome Rewards: A Security-First Guide for New Users
articles.description:
BYDFi’s September 2026 platform upgrade, BYDFi Revamp, brings campaigns, tasks, and reward claims together in a single Rewards Hub, where new users can explore crypto welcome rewards for new users of up to 8,100 USDT. From a security perspective, a welcome offer is also an onboarding window in which an account goes from empty to […]

The post BYDFi’s Up to 8,100 USDT Welcome Rewards: A Security-First Guide for New Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
BYDFi’s September 2026 platform upgrade, BYDFi Revamp, brings campaigns, tasks, and reward claims together in a single Rewards Hub, where new users can explore crypto welcome rewards for new users of up to 8,100 USDT. From a security perspective, a welcome offer is also an onboarding window in which an account goes from empty to funded while its owner is still learning the interface, the official domains, and what a legitimate notification looks like. That window is exactly what credential phishers, SIM swappers, and wallet-drainer operators plan their campaigns around. This guide treats the BYDFi offer as a threat model as well as a promotion: what attackers target at each step, which controls BYDFi exposes to block them, and how to configure those controls before any USDT is at risk. 

How to get started securely

  1. Register through the official page. Type the address yourself or use a bookmark; never follow a link from a message or search ad. Sign up using an email address, phone number, or Google, Apple, or Telegram account. A dedicated email address used only for crypto limits the blast radius if another account is ever breached.
  2. Harden the account before you fund it. Set up passkey sign-in with Face ID or Touch ID. Passkeys are bound to the real BYDFi domain, so a cloned login page cannot use them; Cyber Security News explains how this biometric authentication model works. Then enable Google Authenticator, create an anti-phishing code, and turn on the withdrawal whitelist. With the whitelist restriction on, newly added addresses must wait 24 hours before they can receive funds, which gives you a window to catch and reverse an unauthorized change.
  3. Complete identity verification. BYDFi offers Primary KYC and Advanced KYC. Completing verification early unlocks tasks that require it and makes account recovery far easier if you are ever locked out. Submit documents only inside the BYDFi app or website, never to a “verification agent” who messages you.
  4. Visit the Rewards Hub. Review the available tasks, their requirements, and deadlines. Your progress and claim buttons are also shown there. If a reward is real, it is visible here after you log in; anything that exists only in an email or chat should be treated as suspect.
  5. Choose how you want to explore BYDFi. Crypto deposits are free. If you buy crypto with a card, the minimum purchase is the equivalent of 50 USD. Only deposit and trade amounts that fit your own plans and risk tolerance.
  6. Try the available tools. If you are new to futures, practise first in Demo Trading, which requires a BYDFi login. You can also explore spot trading, Convert, Copy Trading (from 30 USDT), and trading bots such as Futures Grid (from 10 USDT).

Explore the 8,100 USDT Welcome Reward Package

The BYDFi welcome reward package gives new users several ways to get more from their first steps on the platform.  If you are weighing up crypto welcome rewards for new users, the structure here is simple: eligible tasks are organized around four milestones: Sign Up, KYC, Deposit, and Trade. Depending on the campaign and your eligibility, rewards include a BTCUSDT Position Airdrop, USDT Futures Bonus, and USDT Vouchers.

These rewards can help you explore different BYDFi features. Futures Bonuses can be used for USDT-M futures trading. Vouchers may provide benefits such as token rewards, fee offsets, or an APR boost for a specified Earn product. Check each reward’s terms in the Rewards Hub to see how it can be used. Every claim happens inside your logged-in account; BYDFi never asks you to “unlock” a reward by sending funds or sharing a code.

Explore more campaigns in the Event Center

The Event Center is separate from the Rewards Hub and features limited-time promotions across futures, spot, referrals, fiat, and selected regions. For example, BYDFi’s past 0-Fee Fest offered 0% maker and taker fees on selected futures pairs for a limited time.

Event requirements and payout schedules vary. Some events are first come, first served, while others may take up to 7 business days after the event ends to pay out. Check each event’s terms for its eligibility requirements and reward timeline. From a security standpoint, the payout delay matters: scammers often exploit the waiting period by impersonating support and offering to “speed up” a payout for a fee or a login code. Legitimate payouts arrive in your account without any action on your part.

What to know about Futures Bonuses

A Futures Bonus is trial credit for USDT-M futures. You can withdraw profits earned using the bonus, while the bonus amount itself cannot be withdrawn.

Futures use leverage, which can magnify both gains and losses, and positions can be liquidated. BYDFi lists limited-time leverage of up to 500x for BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT, with lower caps on other contracts, for example up to 300x on DOGEUSDT and up to 100x on SOLUSDT. Available leverage decreases as position size increases. Review the contract details carefully before trading.

Check eligibility and current terms

BYDFi serves users in more than 190 countries and regions, but product and promotion availability varies by location. Most rewards require identity verification, and each task may have its own eligibility rules and deadline. If you are unsure what applies in your country, contact BYDFi’s 24/7 support team at cs@bydfi.com. The Help Center also lists common reasons users may be unable to join events or claim rewards.

The advertised 8,100 USDT is the maximum available across eligible tasks, rather than an amount automatically credited at registration. The rewards you can access depend on your account’s eligibility and completion of the applicable tasks within their deadlines. Check the live Rewards Hub for the offers currently available to you, since third-party blogs and coupon pages may display outdated figures. Inflated or “guaranteed” bonus claims on third-party sites are also a common lure for phishing pages, so treat any number that does not match the Rewards Hub as a red flag rather than a better deal.

Protect your account

Popular offers can attract impersonators. Fake websites and social accounts may copy exchange branding and ask for passwords or verification codes. Use BYDFi Verify at bydfi.com/official-verify to check whether an email address, phone number, website, Telegram handle, or X account belongs to BYDFi. Genuine BYDFi emails also include the anti-phishing code you set. BYDFi support will not ask for your password or a one-time code.

Operational habits that close the remaining gaps

  • Open BYDFi from a bookmark you created yourself, never from search results, ads, or messages.
  • Before confirming any deposit or withdrawal, compare the first and last six characters of the address shown in-app against the destination. Clipboard-swapping malware relies on you not checking.
  • Never type a seed phrase, private key, or one-time code into anything that is not the official app or site, including a “verification bot.”

If you suspect compromise

  1. From a clean device, change your password and re-enroll 2FA, revoking the old authenticator.
  2. Review and terminate all active sessions and devices.
  3. Delete every API key and re-create only what you need.
  4. Check the withdrawal whitelist for addresses you did not add, and remove them.
  5. Contact cs@bydfi.com from the email address on the account, and report any impersonating site or handle through BYDFi Verify.
  6. Run a malware scan and rotate the password on the email account tied to BYDFi, since that mailbox is the recovery path.

Awareness is the one layer attackers cannot patch around. Cyber Security News’ guide to social engineering tactics is a useful primer on the pressure techniques (urgency, authority, fear of missing out) that nearly every crypto scam relies on.

Frequently asked questions

Does every new user receive 8,100 USDT? 8,100 USDT is the maximum available across eligible tasks. The rewards you receive depend on your eligibility and the tasks you complete before their deadlines.

Is KYC required? Most rewards require identity verification. Check the requirements shown for each task.

Can I withdraw the Futures Bonus? The bonus itself cannot be withdrawn, but profits earned using it can be.

How soon do rewards arrive? It depends on the reward. Some event payouts may take up to 7 business days after the event ends.

Is the offer available in every country? Availability varies by region. Contact BYDFi support if you are unsure about your eligibility.

The bottom line

BYDFi brings spot and perpetual futures, USDT-margined futures on US stocks, gold and crude oil, Copy Trading, and automated bots together under one account, and the Rewards Hub gives eligible new users a clear place to explore available tasks and track their progress. The security takeaway is simple: the controls that defeat the attacks in this guide (passkeys, TOTP, the anti-phishing code, the withdrawal whitelist, and BYDFi Verify) are all available on day one and take about ten minutes to configure. Switch them on before the first deposit, verify every channel before you trust it, and treat the Rewards Hub as the only authoritative source for what you have earned. A welcome reward is only worth what you can keep.

The post BYDFi’s Up to 8,100 USDT Welcome Rewards: A Security-First Guide for New Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: OpenAI Launches New Security Sprint to Hunt Vulnerabilities and Strengthen Defenses
articles.description:
OpenAI is preparing a new internal security sprint that will bring outside researchers together with its own teams to find vulnerabilities, test fixes, and strengthen its platforms using AI. Announced on November 2, the effort includes a partnership with Cathedral Systems and higher bug bounty rewards to encourage independent researchers to report serious security flaws. […]

The post OpenAI Launches New Security Sprint to Hunt Vulnerabilities and Strengthen Defenses appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI is preparing a new internal security sprint that will bring outside researchers together with its own teams to find vulnerabilities, test fixes, and strengthen its platforms using AI.

Announced on November 2, the effort includes a partnership with Cathedral Systems and higher bug bounty rewards to encourage independent researchers to report serious security flaws.

The security sprint announcement describes a broader push toward continuous defense, where finding weaknesses and checking repairs becomes ongoing work rather than a one-time assessment.

Cathedral researchers will use OpenAI models alongside company staff to challenge existing protections and bring fresh approaches to testing its systems.

Cathedral Partnership Expands Security Testing

Gavin Kliger, CEO and co-founder of Cathedral Systems, said the collaboration would combine his team’s research with OpenAI’s models and security expertise to find weaknesses, test fixes, and improve continuous defense. The announcement outlines the planned collaboration but does not provide a start date, target list, or vulnerability findings from the upcoming sprint.

The effort builds on an earlier sprint in which OpenAI assigned 25% of its product engineers to security work. Engineers used Codex to investigate reports, reproduce vulnerabilities in isolated environments, and prepare patches for review. This approach ties AI-assisted vulnerability discovery to practical checks before proposed changes reach production systems.

OpenAI’s published Defense Factory architecture explains how that process works. Agents map systems, investigate possible flaws, confirm whether issues can be reproduced, identify responsible teams, and prepare tested fixes. Isolated environments provide the code, services, and settings needed to test a suspected vulnerability without running experiments directly against live systems.

The company also describes lessons from early testing. Duplicate findings slowed review, severity ratings needed clearer instructions, and missing dependencies made some tests difficult to run. OpenAI says follow-up checks exposed another important gap: a merged patch did not always mean the fix had reached every deployed system. Human review and independent checks therefore remain part of the workflow.

This builds on the capabilities covered in Cybersecurity News’ report on OpenAI Codex Security, which examined the agent’s role in discovering, validating, and fixing software vulnerabilities. The new sprint applies that model-assisted approach to OpenAI’s own defenses with added outside research support.

Higher Bug Bounties

Alongside the sprint, OpenAI has increased Security Bug Bounty rewards. Critical vulnerabilities in core products, including ChatGPT, Codex, and the API Platform, can now earn up to $30,000.

Exceptional critical findings remain eligible for a $100,000 base award, with bonuses bringing potential payouts to about $172,000. Report quality, researcher loyalty, and priority campaigns affect the final amount.

These changes extend the program previously covered in OpenAI’s $100,000 bug bounty expansion. Researchers should distinguish normal critical rewards from exceptional awards rather than treat the highest advertised payout as standard.

OpenAI is also connecting this work to Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, its $1 billion commitment to subsidized access, training, support, and partnerships over six months. The initiative targets essential services and organizations with limited security resources.

Its stated goal mirrors the internal sprint: help defenders turn confirmed weaknesses into tested fixes, while keeping people responsible for consequential decisions.

articles.description:
Anthropic has introduced a beta integration that lets businesses run endpoint detection and response sensors inside Claude Cowork’s local virtual machine. The feature addresses a monitoring gap: security software installed on a computer cannot see the shell commands and code Cowork runs inside its isolated environment. Teams can now send that activity to their existing […]

The post Anthropic Enables EDR Monitoring in Claude Cowork to Detect Hidden AI Agent Activity appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic has introduced a beta integration that lets businesses run endpoint detection and response sensors inside Claude Cowork’s local virtual machine.

The feature addresses a monitoring gap: security software installed on a computer cannot see the shell commands and code Cowork runs inside its isolated environment. Teams can now send that activity to their existing security console.

The EDR integration supports Team and Enterprise plans on macOS and Windows. It also works with Claude Desktop connected to Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry. Anthropic’s setup guidance makes one limit clear: coverage applies only to the local VM, not Cowork sessions hosted on Anthropic’s servers.

Anthropic Enables EDR Monitoring

Cowork uses a virtual machine to separate code execution from the user’s computer. That boundary also prevents the host computer’s EDR sensor from inspecting activity inside the guest environment. Installing a sensor within the VM gives security teams visibility into work that otherwise sits beyond their existing endpoint monitoring.

The change matters as AI tools gain more freedom to act. Cybersecurity News previously covered Claude’s background computer use, which lets the assistant interact with desktop applications. That capability is distinct from sandboxed code execution, but both raise questions about how organizations monitor automated actions.

Earlier reporting on a Claude Cowork sandbox vulnerability also showed why activity inside these environments deserves attention. That research described a Windows attack chain leading to root access within the Linux sandbox. The new monitoring feature should not be confused with a fix for that reported flaw.

Each time the Cowork VM starts, Claude Desktop copies the configured sensor package into it. Desktop then checks the package’s signature against the approved key for the selected vendor. If validation succeeds, Claude runs the vendor’s installation script, at most once per VM startup. Without the setting, nothing is installed.

Approved vendors are CrowdStrike, Evoke Security, Neo, Palo Alto Networks, Pluto Security, SentinelOne, and Tanium. The installed sensor connects to its vendor’s cloud and reports activity. Its telemetry can leave the VM outside Cowork’s network allowlist, an important detail for teams reviewing outbound data flows.

Administrators need Claude Desktop version 4.4212.0 or later. Windows deployments require the MSIX build, Windows 10 or 11, hardware virtualization, and Virtual Machine Platform enabled.

Configuration uses mobile device management on macOS or registry policies on Windows, including Group Policy or Intune. Vendors provide their own packages and instructions.

The sensor can access prompts, files, Claude responses, and other content inside the VM. That data goes to the EDR vendor, not Anthropic. Organizations therefore need to review vendor data handling alongside detection coverage.

Anthropic also requires customers to test the software before deployment and after Claude or sensor updates. Removing management settings does not uninstall an existing sensor. It stops package execution at later VM starts. Package signatures expire within two years and do not cover updates downloaded afterward.

Anthropic charges nothing extra during beta, although vendors may charge. For defenders, the benefit is clearer local visibility, not complete coverage of every Cowork session.

The company detected the incident on October 30, 2026, and published a security bulletin on November 2. Its investigation identified an AI-assisted offensive security framework used to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts. Founder and CEO Michael […]

The post Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Breach WorkOS and Access Customer Slack Conversations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WorkOS has confirmed unauthorized access to an internal sales application, exposing customer contact information and records of business conversations. The company detected the incident on October 30, 2026, and published a security bulletin on November 2. Its investigation identified an AI-assisted offensive security framework used to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.

Founder and CEO Michael Grinich said the attack involved ARTEX, an AI-powered framework that automates offensive security tasks. His statement on X adds detail to the company’s security bulletin, which describes an AI-assisted framework that automates reconnaissance and exploitation attempts without naming the tool.

The affected application provided access to names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, and company affiliations stored in customer relationship management systems. It also contained customer account histories and sales relationship information.

Customer communications included summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations. Operational metadata covered customers’ use of WorkOS products, including product usage and connection or directory health.

WorkOS Confirms Data Breach

These categories describe information available through the application, not a confirmed record-by-record account of everything accessed.

WorkOS is reviewing affected records to determine the impact on individual organizations. The statement supplied with the disclosure says there is no evidence that WorkOS application data or production services were accessed or impacted. The investigation currently points to CRM and customer support information.

The incident comes amid growing abuse of automated security-testing tools. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant describe ARTEX as a multi-agent platform that turns broad attacker goals into commands. Its agents can test permissions, map networks, adjust failed commands, and continue through several attack stages with limited human input.

Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of ARTEX agents explains how attackers have used the framework for Active Directory discovery, credential attacks, and lateral movement. These are observations from separate investigations, not confirmed steps in the WorkOS breach.

Wiz research also documented agents downloading application files, discovering internal API routes, and testing authentication controls. Related coverage of ARTEX targeting Microsoft 365 shows how stolen application credentials can support attacks across customer environments. Neither report establishes attribution for WorkOS.

WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application, began reviewing access controls across internal tools, and retained an independent digital forensics and incident response firm. It will contact affected customers directly as findings are verified.

Exposed conversation details could make phishing messages more convincing. WorkOS advises customers to verify unexpected requests before sharing sensitive information or taking action, even when messages reference real colleagues or support discussions.

The post Google Dismantles 1.3 Million Device XCPE Botnet, Bans Android TV Maker Over Preinstalled Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google and industry partners have dismantled the XCPE botnet, which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes through preinstalled malware. In a November 2 report, Google linked the operation with high confidence to Videostrong Technology, accusing the Android device maker of deliberately building and running the backdoor for profit.

According to Google’s technical investigation, Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates that installed advertising fraud tools, proxy software, and further malware.

Google banned the company, including future subsidiaries and affiliates, from producing certified Android devices or supplying software to certified vendors.

1.3 Million Device XCPE Botnet Dismantled

The backdoor, named x.cpe or com.oemservice, was built into device firmware and ran with Android system privileges. Removing its installed package did not clear the infection because it could reinstall from the /oem/ partition after a reboot. Google said hidden code loaded after first boot helped bypass security checks.

Its three-stage design separated remote control from malware execution. The backdoor passed instructions to com.abc.nexus, a loader that configured affiliate modules.

Those modules turned devices into proxy exit points, generated fake advertising views, or installed more backdoors. This separation also helped keep malicious activity harder to detect.

Control traffic used MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol. Google identified mqtt.szbboys[.]com on ports 3885–3887. Operators could silently install apps, execute shell commands, capture screens, and inspect networks.

Researchers also observed stolen account details and system logs, injected keystrokes, and commands that opened remote shell access. The malware could disable Google Play Protect verification.

Disruption Reaches Beyond XCPE

Google worked with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI. Legal action targeted XCPE servers and control domains serving more than a dozen affiliate malware families.

Google estimates these wider takedowns will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, separate from XCPE’s 1.3 million boxes.

The findings follow earlier Google legal action against BadBox 2.0, which affected over 10 million uncertified Android devices. Earlier BADBOX infections involving 190,000 Android devices also exposed the risks of compromised connected hardware. These earlier counts should not be combined with XCPE’s total.

Most XCPE infections involved Android TV boxes, but researchers also found affected telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signs. Google has changed its device review process and is improving firmware integrity checks following the discovery.

The takedown disrupts control infrastructure, rather than proving every device is clean. Google urges buyers to choose reputable manufacturers, consult its certified partner list, use trusted app stores, and keep Play Protect enabled. It also warns against apps offering payment for sharing unused bandwidth.

The post Mercado Bitcoin Suffers Cyberattack as Researchers Flag $40 Million in Suspicious Crypto Transfers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Brazilian cryptocurrency exchange Mercado Bitcoin suspended deposits and withdrawals on November 2, 2026, after detecting a security incident in one of its systems.

Blockchain security firm Hypernative flagged more than $40 million in suspicious transfers across at least 10 blockchains, raising questions about the scope of the breach. The exchange has not confirmed that amount as its actual loss.

In its official statement, Mercado Bitcoin said it quickly contained the incident early Monday morning. The company said customers suffered no harm and no data leaked. It described the service suspension as a protective measure while its teams investigate, trace assets, and work with authorities.

According to reports, Opsek founder Pablo Sabbatella shared findings describing transfers from wallets linked to Mercado Bitcoin into fresh addresses. The affected networks included Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Tron, Polygon, Arbitrum, Avalanche, BNB Chain and Stellar. Researchers said the activity covered at least 10 chains in total.

Mercado Bitcoin Suffers Cyberattack

Most of the reported outflows occurred between 06:19 and 06:53 UTC, a 34-minute window. Earlier Bitcoin activity reportedly began around 02:15 UTC, when funds from deposit addresses started moving to addresses linked to the suspected attacker.

The preliminary count included approximately 2,852 ETH, 106 BTC, 10,700 SOL and 6.7 million XLM, alongside more than 200 other tokens. These figures remain researcher estimates rather than amounts verified publicly by Mercado Bitcoin.

Researchers described the movements as ordinary transfers rather than a smart contract exploit. That distinction puts attention on how the transactions received valid signatures. However, the available findings do not establish how the attacker obtained signing access or which internal system was compromised.

The incident follows other exchange wallet breaches covered by Cybersecurity News, including the Bitget hot wallet hack. That case involved unauthorized transfers affecting hot and warm wallet infrastructure. It offers industry context, but does not establish a shared attack method or attacker in the Mercado Bitcoin incident.

Mercado Bitcoin later published destination addresses covering Ethereum-compatible networks, Bitcoin, Solana, Stellar and Tron. The exchange said it released them to help identify and track funds on public blockchains. Such tracking also featured in the Bitfinex hack investigation, which documented how investigators followed stolen cryptocurrency through laundering activity.

As Bitcoin Magazine reported, Mercado Bitcoin had not announced a reopening time or disclosed the affected system. The unresolved issue remains the gap between suspicious wallet movements and confirmed losses. Its statement that customers were unharmed should not be read as confirmation that no exchange assets were taken.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Miami, United States, November 2nd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Prisma Browser for Business joins Guardz to connect browser protection with email, identity and endpoint security, helping security teams investigate and respond to threats across the workspace

Guardz, the Agentic Workspace Security platform built for managed service providers (MSPs), today announced the integration of Prisma Browser for Business from Palo Alto Networks.

The integration connects browser protection with email, identity, endpoint, data and user risk, helping small businesses prevent threats and giving security experts the platform to streamline autonomous unified detection, investigation, and response to incidents across the workspace.

Employees rely on browsers to access business applications, handle company information and use AI tools.

But attacks often cross these environments: a phishing email can direct an employee to a fake login page, exposing credentials and putting connected accounts at risk. 

With Prisma Browser for Business built into Guardz, MSPs and the Guardz 24/7 managed detection and response (MDR) team can investigate related activity as a unified incident.

If an employee clicks a phishing link, Prisma Browser for Business can block the malicious page, while Guardz correlates the browser event with the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity, and endpoint telemetry to support investigation and response for a single identity.

“Identity is the new center of gravity in cybersecurity, and the browser has become the primary gateway to the modern workspace. Traditional security tools operate in silos, leaving critical gaps in visibility and response,” said Dor Eisner, CEO and Co-Founder of Guardz.

“Together with Palo Alto Networks, we’re advancing a new era of identity-centric security operations, connecting signals across identity, browser, email, endpoint, and data into a unified security fabric that is powered by agents. Guardz enables MSPs to autonomously investigate, correlate, and respond to threats across the entire workspace, while giving small businesses the freedom to embrace AI securely and thrive. This is the future of cybersecurity: identity-centric, unified data fabric, and built for autonomous defense at scale,” Eisner added.

Browser Protection Across the Workspace

Powered by Prisma Browser for Business, the integration brings Palo Alto Networks’ browser security technology into the wider security service MSPs manage through Guardz. Capabilities include:

  • Phishing and session-theft protection: Inline machine-learning phishing detection and Advanced URL Filtering help block malicious pages, including fake login pages and attacks designed to steal live session tokens.
  • Malware and extension security: WildFire file analysis helps detect malicious files, while browser security scans uploads and downloads and identifies risky extensions.
  • Connected investigation and response: Browser events are linked with email, identity and endpoint signals to support incident investigations through Guardz’s 24/7 MDR service.
  • Simplified deployment: Guardz streamlines provisioning, setup and default configuration so MSPs can deploy browser protection within minutes.

The streamlined deployment has also impressed early-access MSPs. “The rollout through our RMM was super smooth.

Within minutes, the Prisma Browser for Business extension was on every Chrome and Edge profile, and it was quick and easy to configure and deploy,” said Kevin Kehoe of Datawise Networks.

“For most small businesses, the browser is now the office. Working with Guardz brings Prisma Browser for Business into the security these organizations receive from the providers they already trust.

It connects our browser protection with the wider coverage and support their MSP delivers, helping safeguard the applications and information employees use every day,” said Shivam Srivastava, VP Product at Palo Alto Networks.

AI Usage and Control

As employees increasingly use browser-based generative AI tools, small businesses need practical ways to manage which services are permitted and how company information is shared.

Guardz AI Usage and Control capabilities let technicians apply client-specific policies, including restrictions on copying, pasting, uploading and downloading files by website or category.

Complementing these controls, Guardz has introduced an AI usage report that gives MSPs a per-client view of AI tool usage based on all signals. The controls help enforce usage policies, while the report provides visibility into adoption.

About Guardz

Guardz delivers Agentic Workspace Security, helping MSPs protect the small businesses they serve.

The platform unifies protection across identities, email, endpoints and browsers, alongside adaptive security awareness and user risk, connecting signals around each identity to give security teams the context to act.

The Guardz 24/7 agentic MDR provides triage and response at machine speed, supported by an elite research and threat hunting team. Learn more at guardz.com.

About Palo Alto Networks

Palo Alto Networks is the world’s cybersecurity leader. We innovate to outpace cyberthreats, so organizations can embrace technology with confidence.

We provide next-gen cybersecurity to thousands of customers globally, across all sectors. Our best-in-class cybersecurity platforms and services are backed by industry-leading threat intelligence and strengthened by state-of-the-art automation.

Whether delivering Next-Generation Firewalls, pioneering Agentic AI security, or driving continuous frontier defense via Unit 42, we are committed to helping safely navigate the evolving digital landscape.

omri@omrihurwitz.com
