cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DFIR is the one security purchase evaluated under the worst possible conditions: mid-breach, counsel on the line, adversary still inside.

What separates firms then isn’t marketing it’s responder bench depth, forensic rigor that survives litigation, and how fast a qualified human reaches your keyboard. This ranking scores the capability itself; its sibling piece on IR retainers covers the contract vehicles.

Google (Mandiant) takes 1; CrowdStrike and Unit 42 complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Mandiant the deepest nation-state and APT response bench in commercial practice.

• Podium: Mandiant (APT depth), CrowdStrike (telemetry-accelerated response), Unit 42 (scale with platform reach).

• Capability lens: this ranking rates investigation muscle forensic rigor, eradication discipline, litigation survivability not retainer pricing (see the retainer-services ranking for contract strategy).

• 2026 theme: extortion economics the firms with ransomware-negotiation fluency and recovery discipline carry the caseload reality.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: responder bench depth, forensic/litigation rigor, threat-actor knowledge currency, eradication-and-recovery discipline, global reach, and insurer/counsel ecosystem standing.

Weights: bench depth 25%, forensic rigor 20%, actor knowledge 20%, recovery discipline 20%, reach/ecosystem 15%.

The 2026 DFIR Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Google (Mandiant) — Best APT/Nation-State Response Bench

Snapshot: Engagement + retainer structures | Two decades of frontline APT work | Google-scale intel fusion

Why it earns 1: When the intrusion is sophisticated enough to make the news, Mandiant is usually already in the building.

The bench has worked more nation-state casework than any commercial rival, the actor knowledge updates from live engagements, and Google’s acquisition added telemetry and analytics scale without diluting the responder culture.

For the worst day imaginable, it remains the reference call.

Pros: APT casework depth; actor-attribution authority; intel-fused investigation.

Cons: Premium rates; demand queue at major-event peaks.

Bottom line: The firm the other firms cite in their reports.

2. CrowdStrike — Best Telemetry-Accelerated Response

Snapshot: Services + retainer tiers | Falcon-deployed investigation speed | eCrime fluency

Why it ranks here: CrowdStrike’s responders arrive with a weapon others lack: Falcon deployed across the estate in hours, turning forensic collection from weeks of disk imaging into days of telemetry.

The services arm pairs that speed with deep eCrime fluency ransomware operators tracked by its own intel. Fastest time-to-visibility in the ranking; platform deployment is part of the method.

Pros: Deployment-speed advantage; eCrime depth; intel-services fusion.

Cons: Method assumes Falcon rollout; premium economics.

Bottom line: Speed as a forensic strategy.

3. Palo Alto (Unit 42) — Best Platform-Scaled Response

Snapshot: Engagement + retainer credits | Large global responder bench | Cortex/XSIAM-era tooling

Why it ranks here: Unit 42 built response at portfolio scale: a large global bench, methodology sharpened across a heavy caseload, threat intel from Palo Alto’s telemetry base, and investigation tooling riding Cortex.

Retainer credits flexing into proactive work make it a program partner, not just an emergency number.

Pros: Bench scale; caseload breadth; flexible retainer credits.

Cons: Platform-coupled tooling preferences.

Bottom line: Enterprise response with a platform engine behind it.

4. Kroll — Best Insurer/Counsel-Channel Response

Snapshot: Panel-based engagements | Breach-counsel ecosystem fluency | Notification/regulatory machinery

Why it ranks here: Kroll dominates the lane where most mid-market breaches actually route: cyber-insurance panels and breach counsel.

The machinery around the forensics privileged-investigation discipline, notification logistics, regulatory filings, litigation support is as developed as the investigation itself. If your incident starts with an insurer’s phone tree, Kroll is likely on the list.

Pros: Panel ubiquity; legal-process fluency; end-to-end breach logistics.

Cons: Elite-APT depth concentrated in the firms above.

Bottom line: The breach-counsel ecosystem’s workhorse.

5. Sygnia — Best Hands-On-Keyboard Containment

Snapshot: Engagement-based | Elite operator culture | Active-adversary specialization

Why it ranks here: Sygnia’s reputation grew from engagements where the adversary was still typing: live containment, adversary eviction under fire, and post-incident hardening delivered by a deliberately senior bench.

Boutique scale is the trade for operator density fewer bodies, each one you’d want in the room.

Pros: Senior-operator density; live-eviction craft; hardening follow-through.

Cons: Boutique capacity; book early via retainer.

Bottom line: The special-forces call for active intrusions.

6. Secureworks — Best Research-Fed Response

Snapshot: Services + Taegis-era delivery | CTU intel lineage | Sophos-family integration underway

Why it ranks here: Secureworks’ IR arm draws on Counter Threat Unit research and two decades of casework, with Taegis telemetry accelerating investigations in covered estates.

The Sophos acquisition folds the bench into a larger family service-line continuity is the diligence question while the responder quality lineage stands.

Pros: Research-fed methods; platform-accelerated collection; tenure depth.

Cons: Acquisition-era structure clarity.

Bottom line: Proven bench confirm the post-acquisition shape.

7. Cisco (Talos IR) — Best Network-Depth Response

Snapshot: Retainer + engagement tiers | Talos intel at backbone scale | Network-forensics strength

Why it ranks here: Talos IR brings the network operator’s eye: packet-level forensics, infrastructure-scale intel from Cisco’s visibility, and particular strength where the investigation lives in routers, VPNs, and traffic the lanes endpoint-first firms under-weight.

For network-centric estates and OT-adjacent incidents, the fit is structural.

Pros: Network-forensic depth; Talos intel; infrastructure fluency.

Cons: Brand gravity in pure-endpoint casework.

Bottom line: The responders who read packets natively.

8. Arete — Best Ransomware-Caseload Specialization

Snapshot: Insurer-panel engagements | High-volume extortion casework | Recovery+negotiation machinery

Why it ranks here: Arete built its practice where the caseload actually is: ransomware triage, negotiation support, decryption logistics, restoratio executed at a volume that compounds into pattern knowledge of specific extortion crews.

For the mid-market ransomware event routed through insurance, it’s a specialist with the reps.

Pros: Extortion-case volume; recovery machinery; insurer integration.

Cons: Scope concentrated on the ransomware lane.

Bottom line: Ransomware reps, by the thousand.

9. NCC Group — Best Technical-Assurance-Adjacent DFIR

Snapshot: Engagement + retainer | Pentest-heritage technical depth | UK/EU response strength

Why it ranks here: NCC’s response arm inherits its assurance DNA: responders who think like the attackers its testers emulate, strong malware-analysis craft, and UK/European response presence with regulatory fluency.

A technically serious mid-ranking pick, strongest where European jurisdiction and offensive-informed analysis matter.

Pros: Offense-informed forensics; EU presence; malware-analysis depth.

Cons: Global bench scale versus the majors.

Bottom line: The tester’s eye applied to the breach.

10. Booz Allen — Best Government-Grade Response

Snapshot: Contract vehicles + commercial engagements | Cleared-personnel depth | Critical-infrastructure fluency

Why it ranks here: Booz Allen’s DFIR strength is the government lane: cleared responders, national-security-grade process, and critical-infrastructure incident fluency that commercial boutiques can’t staff. Commercial enterprises in defense-adjacent or regulated-infrastructure sectors get a bench shaped for their constraints.

Pros: Clearance depth; CI/OT fluency; federal-grade process.

Cons: Commercial-market agility versus pure-plays.

Bottom line: When the incident needs a clearance.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Choose the Bench Before the Breach Chooses For You

DFIR bought mid-incident is bought at maximum price and minimum leverage the insurer’s panel decides, the queue decides, the first available team decides.

Pre-select instead: match the firm’s signature lane to your realistic worst case (nation-state exposure → Mandiant/CrowdStrike-tier; ransomware probability → Arete/Kroll’s insurer machinery; active-adversary fear → Sygnia’s operators; OT estate → Talos/Booz Allen fluency), then meet the actual regional team bench quality is a people question, and “who exactly responds to us, from where, in how many hours” belongs in writing.

Align the choice with counsel and insurer early so privilege structure and panel approval exist before the clock starts, and run one tabletop with the chosen firm annually; a team that has seen your network map investigates measurably faster.

The retainer mechanics credits, response-time SLAs, proactive-use terms are the sibling ranking’s subject, but one rule crosses both: the firm you’d want is the firm you’ve already met.

FAQs

Who are the best DFIR companies in 2026? Mandiant for APT depth, CrowdStrike for telemetry speed, Unit 42 for scale, Kroll for the insurer/counsel channel, Sygnia for live containment, with Secureworks, Talos IR, Arete, NCC, and Booz Allen by lane.

DFIR firm versus IR retainer same decision? Related but distinct: this ranking rates investigation capability; the retainer decision adds contract mechanics (SLAs, credits, panel status) ideally you pre-contract the capability you want.

How fast should response start? Remote responder engagement within hours under retainer; meaningful on-estate visibility inside twenty-four to forty-eight ask each firm for their actual medians, not their marketing.

Does our cyber insurance choose our firm? Panels constrain the list, but pre-approved exceptions are negotiable at policy-writing time name your preferred firm in the policy, not during the incident.

What makes forensics litigation-grade? Chain-of-custody discipline, privileged-engagement structure through counsel, and reporting that survives deposition ask for redacted sample reports and their courtroom track record.

Verdict

Ten firms, one buying truth: breach-day quality is decided before breach day. Mandiant for the nation-state call, CrowdStrike for speed, Unit 42 for scale, Kroll and Arete for the insurance-rail reality, Sygnia for the live fight, Secureworks and Talos and NCC and Booz Allen for their lanes pick the bench that matches your worst case, meet the humans, structure the privilege, and rehearse once a year.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The dirty secret of SIEM ownership: the license is half the cost, and the unstaffed half tuning, content, triage is where programs quietly die. Managed SIEM rents that discipline, in flavors that matter more than brands: vendors managing their own platform, operators managing yours, and services where ownership is genuinely shared.

The ranking scores ten providers on tuning quality, model flexibility, and cost honesty. Splunk takes 1 on managed-platform depth; Rapid7 and Secureworks complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Splunk the deepest managed bench for the market’s most powerful platform.

• Podium: Splunk (platform depth), Rapid7 (turnkey bundle value), Secureworks (Taegis-transparent co-management).

• Model question first: vendor-managed (Splunk, Sumo, Devo), operator-managed-yours (deepwatch, ReliaQuest, BlueVoyant), or platform-bundled (Rapid7, Arctic Wolf) the model decides your lock-in and exit math.

• Brand note: LogRhythm’s managed lane now ships from the merged Exabeam company confirm entity and roadmap in contracting.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: tuning/detection-content quality, ownership-model flexibility, transparency (console and case access), platform expertise depth, escalation maturity, and cost predictability.

Weights: tuning quality 25%, model flexibility 20%, transparency 20%, platform depth 20%, cost predictability 15%.

The 2026 Managed SIEM Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Splunk — Best Managed Depth on the Deepest Platform

Snapshot: License + managed-service contracts | Splunk-delivered and partner-delivered tiers | ES content mastery

Why it earns 1: Splunk’s managed lane answers Splunk’s own complexity: vendor and certified-partner services that run ingestion, tuning, and Enterprise Security content at the depth the platform rewards.

If you’ve committed to Splunk’s ceiling, managed delivery from inside the ecosystem extracts it at pricing that reflects both halves of the commitment under the Cisco portfolio.

Pros: Platform mastery; content depth; ecosystem bench.

Cons: Total-cost stacking (license + service); Cisco-era packaging watch.

Bottom line: Maximum Splunk, rented.

2. Rapid7 — Best Turnkey Managed Bundle

Snapshot: Per-asset managed tiers | InsightIDR + MDR analysts | VM-context fusion

Why it ranks here: Rapid7 collapses the managed SIEM question into one bill: InsightIDR as the platform, Rapid7 analysts as the staff, vulnerability context in the same pane, per-asset pricing a budget meeting can approve.

The mid-market reality check it’s the fastest route from no-SIEM to monitored outweighs the single-vendor telemetry ceiling for its buyers.

Pros: One-bill simplicity; fast time-to-monitored; accessible pricing.

Cons: Platform lock; enterprise-custom ceilings.

Bottom line: The managed SIEM most mid-market teams actually finish deploying.

3. Secureworks — Best Transparent Co-Management

Snapshot: Taegis subscriptions + managed tiers | Shared-console co-management | CTU detection content

Why it ranks here: Secureworks built co-management as a first principle: your analysts and theirs working the same Taegis console, detection content from CTU research, and graduated ownership so internal capability can grow without re-platforming.

The Sophos acquisition folds it into a larger ecosystem whose roadmap deserves written confirmation; the co-managed model remains the category’s reference.

Pros: True shared-console model; research-fed content; capability-growth path.

Cons: Taegis-platform coupling; acquisition-era diligence.

Bottom line: Co-management done as architecture, not marketing.

4. deepwatch — Best Managed-Splunk Specialization

Snapshot: Managed tiers | Named squads on your Splunk | Maturity scoring

Why it ranks here: deepwatch does one thing at depth: run enterprise Splunk estates with named squads, detection engineering, and hygiene scoring that tells you how your deployment ranks.

For the large Splunk-committed estate that doesn’t want vendor-delivered services, it’s the specialist alternative with continuity baked into the model.

Pros: Splunk-specialist depth; squad continuity; benchmarking.

Cons: Single-platform focus by design.

Bottom line: Your Splunk, their obsession.

5. ReliaQuest — Best Manage-Your-SIEM Operations

Snapshot: GreyMatter platform | Operates across your SIEM/EDR/cloud | Detection unification

Why it ranks here: ReliaQuest manages the SIEM you own Splunk, Sentinel, QRadar through GreyMatter’s unification layer, adding detection-as-code discipline across the whole stack rather than one console.

It’s the anti-lock-in managed answer: your licenses, your data, their operating rigor.

Pros: SIEM-agnostic operations; unified detection layer; sunk-cost respect.

Cons: Enterprise-weight platform and pricing.

Bottom line: Keep your SIEM; rent the discipline.

6. Arctic Wolf — Best Concierge-Wrapped SIEM Function

Snapshot: Per-user/asset subscription | Aurora platform ingestion | Concierge team delivery

Why it ranks here: Arctic Wolf delivers the SIEM function broad telemetry ingestion, correlation, retention, triage without selling you a SIEM at all: Aurora ingests, the Concierge team interprets, and the customer never touches a query language.

For teams that want outcomes rather than consoles, the abstraction is the product.

Pros: Zero-console burden; named-team continuity; broad ingestion.

Cons: Not your SIEM portability and query freedom traded away.

Bottom line: The SIEM you never have to see.

7. BlueVoyant — Best Microsoft-Estate Managed SIEM

Snapshot: Managed service tiers | Sentinel-specialist operations | MXDR for Microsoft lineage

Why it ranks here: BlueVoyant concentrated where the market moved: managed Sentinel at specialist depth data-connector hygiene, analytics-rule engineering, cost-tier tuning that keeps consumption honest plus Defender-stack response.

For E5-committed estates, it’s the focused alternative to generalist MSSPs running Sentinel as one of many.

Pros: Sentinel depth; consumption-cost tuning; Microsoft-stack response.

Cons: Microsoft-centric by design.

Bottom line: Sentinel estates’ specialist bench.

8. Sumo Logic — Best Vendor-Managed Cloud-Native Option

Snapshot: Credits/consumption | Vendor-operated SaaS + managed add-ons | Dual-use analytics

Why it ranks here: Sumo’s cloud-native SaaS already removes infrastructure ownership; its managed and partner layers add content and monitoring atop.

For teams whose logs serve both security and observability, the dual-use consolidation keeps total spend saner than running parallel stacks.

Pros: No-infrastructure baseline; dual-use economics; consumption flexibility.

Cons: Managed-service depth varies by partner.

Bottom line: The cloud-native path of least ownership.

9. Devo — Best High-Velocity Data Managed Service

Snapshot: Platform + services | Hot-data architecture | SOC-services layer

Why it ranks here: Devo’s always-hot architecture query years without rehydration pairs with managed SOC services for estates whose defining problem is data velocity and uncompromised cloud logging : telecoms, large retail, high-event-rate operations.

It’s a performance-first pick with a services layer, strongest where speed-at-volume is the purchase driver.

Pros: Hot-retention performance; velocity economics; services layer.

Cons: Brand gravity and content ecosystem versus leaders.

Bottom line: For estates that measure ingest in terabytes per day.

10. LogRhythm (Exabeam) — Best Mid-Market Managed Lineage

Snapshot: Platform + partner-managed tiers | Merged-company mid-market base | Partner delivery network

Why it ranks here: LogRhythm’s large mid-market install base carries a mature partner-managed ecosystem, now operating under the merged Exabeam behavioral analytics portfolio.

Existing estates get continuity economics; new buyers should ask the merged-roadmap question directly which platform line, which managed partners, what investment trajectory.

Pros: Install-base continuity; partner network; mid-market pricing.

Cons: Post-merger roadmap clarity is the homework.

Bottom line: Continuity pick for existing estates; diligence pick for new ones.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Decide Whose SIEM Dies If You Leave

The managed SIEM decision is an exit-math decision wearing a service contract. Vendor-managed and bundled models (Splunk-delivered, Rapid7, Arctic Wolf) are fastest to value and hardest to leave the detections, dashboards, and history live in their world.

Operator models (deepwatch, ReliaQuest, BlueVoyant) cost more coordination but leave you owning the platform, content, and data when the contract ends.

Price both paths across three years including the exit scenario: data export, detection-rule portability, and historical-retention transfer.

In the pilot, audit tuning honestly ask for the before/after alert-volume numbers on their last three onboardings and the detection-content changelog they’d commit to monthly.

Confirm the two merged-entity roadmaps here (Secureworks–Sophos, LogRhythm–Exabeam) in writing. And measure the metric the category exists for: analyst-confirmed true-positive rate per hundred alerts escalated to you, quarter over quarter.

FAQs

What are the best managed SIEM services in 2026? Splunk for vendor-managed depth, Rapid7 for turnkey bundles, Secureworks for co-management, deepwatch and ReliaQuest and BlueVoyant for operating your own SIEM, with Arctic Wolf, Sumo Logic, Devo, and LogRhythm/Exabeam by model fit.

Managed SIEM versus SOCaaS? Managed SIEM scopes to the platform (ingestion, tuning, content, triage); SOCaaS wraps broader SOC function around it many contracts blend both, so scope beats label.

Should we keep owning the SIEM license? Yes if exit optionality or data sovereignty matters: operator models preserve ownership; bundled models trade it for speed.

What does good tuning look like? Falling alert volume with rising true-positive rate, a monthly detection-content changelog, and consumption costs that trend flat as telemetry grows.

What’s the hidden cost in managed SIEM? Exit: unexportable detections and historical data re-ingestion write portability into the original contract, not the renewal.

Verdict

Ten providers, three ownership models, one math problem: entry speed versus exit freedom. Splunk’s depth, Rapid7’s bundle, Secureworks’ shared console, deepwatch and ReliaQuest and BlueVoyant running what you own, Arctic Wolf hiding the console entirely, Sumo and Devo as cloud-native lanes, the LogRhythm lineage under Exabeam model the three-year total with the breakup included, demand the tuning changelog, and sign the version of the contract your future self can leave.

articles.description:
Building a 24/7 SOC takes roughly a dozen analysts before vacation math works which is why SOC-as-a-Service became the mid-market’s default answer and the enterprise’s pressure valve. The post Top 10 Best SOC-as-a-Service Providers in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Building a 24/7 SOC takes roughly a dozen analysts before vacation math works which is why SOC-as-a-Service became the mid-market’s default answer and the enterprise’s pressure valve.

The 2026 field divides by philosophy: concierge models that assign you named humans, platform models that sell detection engineering at scale, and bring-your-own-stack operators who run the tools you already own.

Arctic Wolf takes 1; Expel and eSentire complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Arctic Wolf the concierge model at category-defining scale.

• Podium: Arctic Wolf (concierge scale), Expel (transparency and automation ethos), eSentire (response authority).

• Philosophy split: concierge (Arctic Wolf, eSentire), platform-transparent (Expel, Rapid7), BYO-stack (ReliaQuest, deepwatch, Proficio, Novacoast) decide whether they bring the stack or run yours.

• 2026 theme: response authority the providers willing to contain, not just notify, separate from the alert-forwarders.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: detection/response outcomes, response authority (containment actions, not just alerts), stack flexibility, transparency (console/case visibility), named-team continuity, and commercial accessibility.

Weights: outcomes 25%, response authority 20%, transparency 20%, stack flexibility 20%, continuity 15%.

The 2026 SOCaaS Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Arctic Wolf — Best Concierge Security Operations

Snapshot: Per-user/asset subscription | Concierge Security Team model | Aurora platform telemetry

Why it earns 1: Arctic Wolf productized the thing small teams actually lack: a named squad that knows your environment.

The Concierge Security Team owns your account’s triage, tuning, and quarterly posture work atop the Aurora platform’s telemetry breadth security operations as a relationship, not a ticket queue, delivered at a scale no other concierge model matches.

Pros: Named-team continuity; posture work included; telemetry breadth.

Cons: Platform lock to Aurora; enterprise-custom depth versus BYO operators.

Bottom line: The strongest “we’ve got you” in the category.

2. Expel — Best Transparent, Automation-Led SOC

Snapshot: Tech-stack-based pricing | Workbench transparency | Automation-heavy triage

Why it ranks here: Expel runs the glass-walled SOC: every investigation visible in Workbench as it happens, findings written in plain English, and automation (their bots) doing the repetitive triage so analysts spend minutes on judgment.

It runs atop your existing stack EDR, cloud, SIEM scoring it for signal quality and telling you honestly what to fix.

Pros: Investigation transparency; automation efficiency; BYO-stack respect.

Cons: Wants a decent existing stack to shine.

Bottom line: The SOC that shows its work.

3. eSentire — Best Response Authority

Snapshot: Service tiers | Atlas platform | 24/7 threat response unit

Why it ranks here: eSentire’s pitch is verbs: isolate, kill, contain authority written into the service, with its own threat response unit executing within minutes rather than emailing you at 3 a.m.

Atlas-platform telemetry plus original threat research back the muscle. For buyers whose nightmare is the un-actioned alert, this is the design center.

Pros: Containment authority; response speed culture; original research.

Cons: Full value needs you granting real response permissions.

Bottom line: Hire it to act, not to notify.

4. ReliaQuest — Best Bring-Your-Own-Stack Operations

Snapshot: GreyMatter platform subscription | Stack-agnostic unification | Detection-as-code ethos

Why it ranks here: ReliaQuest’s GreyMatter sits above whatever you already bought SIEM, EDR, cloud, identity unifying detection and response across it without rip-and-replace.

The model respects sunk investment and kills the single-vendor telemetry tax; its ceiling is that unification quality tracks the quality of what you feed it.

Pros: True stack agnosticism; unified detection layer; enterprise fit.

Cons: Garbage-in constraint; enterprise-weight platform.

Bottom line: The SOC layer for estates that refuse lock-in.

5. Rapid7 — Best Platform-Bundled SOC Service

Snapshot: Per-asset MDR tiers | Insight platform native | D&R + VM fusion

Why it ranks here: Rapid7’s managed SOC rides its own platform: InsightIDR detection, managed by Rapid7 analysts, with vulnerability context from InsightVM in the same pane.

The bundle economics are the argument detection, response, and exposure management in one per-asset bill a mid-market CFO can parse.

Pros: Bundle value; VM-context fusion; accessible packaging.

Cons: Single-platform telemetry view.

Bottom line: The tidy all-Rapid7 answer at mid-market price.

6. deepwatch — Best Splunk-Centric Managed SOC

Snapshot: Managed service tiers | Splunk-native operations | Squad-based delivery

Why it ranks here: deepwatch built its service as Splunk operations perfected: your Splunk (or theirs), run by named squads with detection engineering, hygiene scoring, and maturity benchmarking layered on.

For the large Splunk-committed estate that wants the platform’s ceiling without staffing it, the specialization is the value.

Pros: Splunk mastery; squad continuity; maturity benchmarking.

Cons: Splunk-centric by design.

Bottom line: Splunk estates’ outsourcing shortcut.

7. Huntress — Best Affordable Managed SOC for SMBs

Snapshot: Predictable endpoint-based pricing | 24/7 SOC monitoring | Managed EDR with active threat remediation

Why it ranks here: Huntress stands out for making managed security operations accessible to small and mid-sized businesses. Its 24/7 Security Operations Center combines managed endpoint detection, threat hunting, and automated response to identify and stop attacks before they spread.

The platform focuses on ransomware, persistent threats, and suspicious endpoint activity, helping organizations strengthen security without building an expensive in-house SOC.

Pros: Affordable and predictable pricing; 24/7 human-led SOC; strong ransomware protection; automated threat containment.

Cons: More endpoint-focused than full-scale enterprise SOC platforms; advanced SIEM and custom detection capabilities are limited compared with larger providers.

Bottom line: The practical, cost-effective managed SOC choice for SMBs that need reliable threat detection and response without enterprise-level complexity.

8. Sophos MDR — Best AI-Powered Managed Detection and Response

Snapshot: MDR Essentials and Complete tiers | 24/7 expert-led SOC | AI-assisted threat detection and response

Why it ranks here: Sophos MDR combines AI-powered detection with round-the-clock human expertise to identify, investigate, and contain threats across endpoints, networks, cloud environments, and identity systems.

Its flexible service tiers, broad third-party integrations, and incident response capabilities make it a strong choice for organizations seeking enterprise-grade security operations without building an in-house SOC.

Pros: 24/7 threat monitoring; AI-assisted investigations; broad security integrations; active threat containment.

Cons: Advanced response capabilities depend on service tier; full value may require deeper Sophos ecosystem integration.

Bottom line: The AI-powered managed SOC choice for organizations seeking continuous protection and expert-led response.

9. Proficio — Best Co-Managed Flexibility

Snapshot: Co-managed/full-managed tiers | ProSOC model | SIEM-flexible delivery

Why it ranks here: Proficio built its niche on meeting you where you are: co-managed SIEM (yours or theirs), graduated response authority via ActiveDefense, and healthcare/mid-enterprise vertical depth.

It’s the flexible mid-tier operator for teams that want partnership gradients, not binary outsourcing.

Pros: Co-managed gradient; vertical focus; SIEM flexibility.

Cons: Scale and research depth versus majors.

Bottom line: Outsource exactly as much as you want.

10. Novacoast — Best Services-Depth Boutique

Snapshot: Custom service engagements | Identity+security services lineage | novaSOC operations

Why it ranks here: Novacoast pairs its SOC service with unusual bench depth in identity and security engineering the boutique that can also fix what monitoring finds.

For buyers wanting a services partner with a SOC rather than a SOC with upsells, the shape fits; brand reach is the honest constraint.

Pros: Engineering bench; identity depth; partnership posture.

Cons: Boutique scale; regional gravity.

Bottom line: The engineer’s SOCaaS pick.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Grant the Verbs or Keep the Pager

The SOCaaS value cliff sits at response authority: a provider allowed only to email you is a very expensive smoke detector.

Decide before procurement which actions you’ll delegate host isolation, account disable, token revocation under what guardrails, and shortlist only providers contractually comfortable executing them; then test with an unannounced drill in the pilot and measure minutes-to-containment, not minutes-to-email.

Choose the philosophy honestly: strong existing stack → BYO operators (Expel, ReliaQuest, deepwatch); thin stack and thin team → concierge platforms (Arctic Wolf, eSentire); somewhere between → co-managed gradients (Proficio).

Interrogate continuity who exactly works your account, their tenure, and what happens when they leave and write telemetry sovereignty into the contract: your logs, exportable, with exit assistance.

The provider’s own metrics deserve audit too: ask for their median containment times across clients, and how they’re measured.

FAQs

Who are the best SOC-as-a-Service providers in 2026? Arctic Wolf leads the concierge model, Expel for transparency, eSentire for response authority, ReliaQuest and deepwatch for BYO-stack operations, with Rapid7, Alert Logic, Cybereason, Proficio, and Novacoast by fit.

SOCaaS versus MDR versus MSSP? Heavily overlapping labels: MDR is the detect-respond core, SOCaaS wraps it in full SOC function (triage, tuning, posture), MSSP is the widest umbrella including device management contract scope matters more than the acronym.

Should the provider run our stack or theirs? Good existing telemetry favors BYO operators; greenfield or thin stacks favor platform-native providers switching stacks mid-contract is the expensive mistake.

What response authority should we grant? Host isolation and account disable under written guardrails is the common baseline; start with after-hours authority if full delegation feels early.

How big must we be before building our own SOC? The usual arithmetic says roughly a dozen security FTEs before 24/7 in-house coverage beats renting most organizations below a few thousand employees rent.

Verdict

Ten providers, three philosophies, one cliff: authority. Arctic Wolf’s concierge squads, Expel’s glass walls, eSentire’s containment verbs, ReliaQuest and deepwatch running your stack, Rapid7’s tidy bundle, Alert Logic’s value tiers, Cybereason’s operation lens, Proficio’s gradient, Novacoast’s bench pick who may act at 3 a.m., write it down, and drill it before the adversary does.

articles.title: Critical ChatGPT Flaw Allowed Attackers to Hijack Accounts and Steal Private Conversations With One Link
articles.description:
A critical ChatGPT flaw that let a malicious shared conversation run attacker-controlled JavaScript in another user’s signed-in session. The attack could list private chats, read conversations never shared with the attacker, and send stolen data to an outside server. Opening one crafted link was enough in the final demonstration. OpenAI fixed the issue on October […]

The post Critical ChatGPT Flaw Allowed Attackers to Hijack Accounts and Steal Private Conversations With One Link appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical ChatGPT flaw that let a malicious shared conversation run attacker-controlled JavaScript in another user’s signed-in session. The attack could list private chats, read conversations never shared with the attacker, and send stolen data to an outside server. Opening one crafted link was enough in the final demonstration.

OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26, 2026, according to Parameter’s technical disclosure, published by Mukul Goyal on October 28. The company classified the report as P1 and awarded a $5,000 bounty. The demonstrated account access came through the victim’s active browser session, rather than a stolen password.

The exploit combined an interactive graph with ChatGPT’s HTML Preview feature. Preview normally runs code inside a restricted frame on a separate web address, preventing it from directly reading the main ChatGPT page. That boundary initially worked as intended.

ChatGPT Flaw Exploited With One Link

The graph, however, loaded MathLive, a math library that added a message listener to the main page for its virtual keyboard. Through the browser’s postMessage interface, the isolated Preview could send instructions to that listener. MathLive accepted keyboard changes without properly checking the sender’s origin or requiring an approved source window.

One message supplied a keyboard layout containing attacker-controlled HTML. Another opened the keyboard, placing that HTML into the real ChatGPT page through innerHTML. A helper called createHTML passed the content through without removing unsafe markup.

This differs from the previously reported ChatGPT sandbox flaw that exposed Gmail data, which used shared internal storage. Here, the escape crossed a browser boundary through messages trusted by a privileged page component.

HTML injection alone did not immediately execute JavaScript. The researchers inserted an iframe using srcdoc, which stores an embedded page’s HTML directly in an attribute. Because this new frame lacked sandbox restrictions, it inherited ChatGPT’s web origin and could access the parent page.

ChatGPT’s Content Security Policy blocked inline scripts but allowed scripts from YouTube. The researchers found that YouTube’s oEmbed endpoint returned an attacker-supplied JSONP callback as JavaScript, even when reporting an invalid callback. Loading that response provided the final step needed to run code as chatgpt.com.

The researchers then placed both the graph and HTML Preview inside a public conversation. An earlier version required clicking Preview. The final version opened it automatically and was reproduced three times in a separate account, with execution appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.

Private Chat Theft and OpenAI’s Fix

The payload read session details already available to ChatGPT’s frontend and called authenticated conversation APIs. It retrieved a private conversation unrelated to the shared link, then sent a small selected value to a research server through an image request.

Unlike the separately reported ChatGPT GitHub connector flaw, this attack did not depend on repository instructions or connected tools. Its access came directly from JavaScript running within the trusted website.

Parameter submitted the report on October 18. OpenAI reproduced the issue and raised its priority on October 21. By October 26, both affected web frontend versions rejected the reported MathLive messages. The case highlights why cross-frame receivers must verify both sender origin and source window, while untrusted HTML must remain sandboxed throughout rendering.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

The post Top 10 Best Managed Security Service Providers (MSSP) in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hiring an MSSP is hiring a co-pilot for your worst day, and the market now spans three species: security-born specialists, telecom-scale operators with backbone visibility, and consulting giants wrapping managed detection in transformation services.

The ranking below scores ten providers on what contracts rarely capture detection quality per dollar, escalation honesty, and whether the analyst on your ticket knows your estate. Secureworks takes 1; IBM and Accenture complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Secureworks security-born heritage with Taegis-platform transparency; note its Sophos acquisition reshapes the roadmap.

• Podium: Secureworks (platform transparency), IBM (enterprise scale+consulting), Accenture (transformation-fused security operations).

• Species split: security-born (Secureworks, Trustwave), telecom-scale (Verizon, BT, Orange, NTT, LevelBlue), consulting-led (Accenture, Deloitte, IBM) match the species to what you’re really buying.

• 2026 theme: platform transparency MSSPs that let you see their console beat black-box monthly PDFs.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: detection/response quality signals, platform transparency (customer console access, co-managed options), service breadth, global delivery, vertical expertise, and commercial flexibility.

Weights: detection quality 25%, transparency 20%, breadth 20%, global delivery 20%, commercial flexibility 15%.

The 2026 MSSP Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Secureworks — Best Platform-Transparent MSSP

Snapshot: Taegis-based subscriptions | Security-born heritage, CTU research | Sophos acquisition integration underway

Why it earns 1: Secureworks built what most MSSPs resist: a platform customers see into. Taegis gives co-managed visibility your analysts and theirs in the same console backed by Counter Threat Unit research and two decades of incident-floor experience.

The Sophos acquisition folds it into a larger MDR family; buyers should confirm service-line continuity and platform roadmap in writing.

Pros: Console transparency; research pedigree; co-managed model maturity.

Cons: Acquisition-era roadmap diligence required.

Bottom line: The transparency benchmark verify the post-acquisition contract terms.

2. IBM — Best Enterprise-Scale Security Operations

Snapshot: Custom enterprise contracts | Global SOC network + X-Force | Consulting integration

Why it ranks here: IBM pairs a global managed-security footprint with X-Force research and the consulting muscle to rebuild what monitoring reveals.

For complex, regulated, multi-national estates wanting one accountable throat to choke across operations and transformation, few match the span. The trade: enterprise process weight and enterprise pricing.

Pros: Global scale; X-Force integration; regulated-industry depth.

Cons: Process weight; premium economics.

Bottom line: The safe-pair-of-hands pick for enterprise complexity.

3. Accenture — Best Transformation-Fused Security Services

Snapshot: Program-based contracts | Managed services + transformation | Deep vertical practices

Why it ranks here: Accenture sells security operations as part of becoming a different company: managed detection woven into cloud migration, identity modernization, and OT programs, vertical practices that defend enterprise architecture and threat response.

Where the buying problem is “run it and fix it,” the integrated model is the point.

Pros: Transformation fusion; vertical depth; global bench.

Cons: Pure-monitoring buyers pay for integration they don’t use.

Bottom line: Buy when operations and transformation share a roadmap.

4. Verizon — Best Network-Backbone Visibility

Snapshot: Service tiers | Backbone telemetry + DBIR research lineage | NDR-strong portfolio

Why it ranks here: Verizon’s differentiator flows from the network it runs: backbone-scale threat visibility, network-centric managed services, and the research culture behind the DBIR.

For estates where network telemetry is the spine distributed retail, logistics, carrier-adjacent the vantage point is structural.

Pros: Backbone visibility; network-service depth; research culture.

Cons: Endpoint/cloud-native depth versus security-born rivals.

Bottom line: The network operator’s view of your threats.

5. NTT Data — Best Global Delivery Footprint

Snapshot: Regional service contracts | Global SOC mesh | Strong APAC/JP presence

Why it ranks here: NTT’s managed security rides one of the largest global delivery networks: follow-the-sun SOCs, sovereign-aware regional operations, and particular strength where APAC coverage decides the deal.

For multinationals needing consistent service from Tokyo to Frankfurt to São Paulo, the footprint is the feature.

Pros: Geographic mesh; APAC depth; carrier-grade infrastructure lineage.

Cons: Service consistency varies by region reference-check your regions.

Bottom line: Coverage-map winner for true multinationals.

6. Orange Cyberdefense — Best European Security Operations

Snapshot: Service packages | European SOC network + CERT | Sovereignty-conscious delivery

Why it ranks here: Orange Cyberdefense is Europe’s security-operations heavyweight: dense regional SOCs, a respected CERT and research arm, and delivery models built for GDPR-and-sovereignty-first procurement.

For European estates wanting scale without US-cloud entanglement questions, it’s the natural shortlist leader.

Pros: European density; sovereignty posture; research credibility.

Cons: Thinner presence outside EMEA.

Bottom line: The European answer, by design.

7. Deloitte — Best Risk-and-Board-Aligned Services

Snapshot: Program contracts | Cyber risk + managed operations | Regulatory fluency

Why it ranks here: Deloitte’s managed security arrives wrapped in risk language boards understand: quantification, regulatory mapping, audit-ready reporting , with operations delivered beneath that umbrella.

Strongest where the CISO’s hardest audience is the audit committee, not the adversary.

Pros: Board-grade reporting; regulatory fluency; risk integration.

Cons: Hands-on-keyboard depth varies by practice.

Bottom line: Security operations that speak fluent audit-committee.

8. LevelBlue (AT&T) — Best Carrier-Heritage Threat Visibility

Snapshot: Service tiers | AT&T Cybersecurity lineage, USM platform | Alien Labs intel

Why it ranks here: LevelBlue the spun-out AT&T Cybersecurity business carries carrier-scale visibility, the USM platform, and Alien Labs (OTX lineage) intelligence into an independent MSSP play.

The spin-out brought focus; buyers should confirm service continuity and investment trajectory post-separation.

Pros: Carrier-heritage visibility; OTX community intel; accessible packaging.

Cons: Post-spin-out trajectory diligence.

Bottom line: Carrier DNA at independent-MSSP economics.

9. Arctic Wolf — Best Concierge-Led Security Operations

Snapshot: Subscription-based | Aurora security operations platform | 24×7 MDR + Concierge Security

Why it ranks here: Arctic Wolf combines continuous monitoring with a dedicated security operations team that investigates and responds to threats across endpoint, network, identity, cloud, and other telemetry.

Its Concierge Security model gives organizations ongoing access to security experts, making it a strong fit for mid-market and enterprise teams that want managed detection and response without building a large in-house SOC.

Pros: 24×7 monitoring; dedicated security team; broad telemetry coverage; guided response; strong mid-market fit.

Cons: More MDR-focused than a traditional full-spectrum MSSP; advanced managed database-security needs may require additional tools.

Bottom line: A hands-on security operations partner for organizations that want continuous monitoring, expert guidance, and managed response.

10. BT — Best UK/Commonwealth Enterprise Fit

Snapshot: Managed service contracts | UK SOC network + government pedigree | Network-integrated delivery

Why it ranks here: BT’s managed security leans on national-infrastructure pedigree: UK-sovereign operations, government-grade clearances, and network-integrated delivery for estates already running BT connectivity.

Strongest in UK and Commonwealth procurement; a regional pick ranked honestly as one.

Pros: UK sovereignty; clearance depth; network integration.

Cons: Global breadth versus multinationals above.

Bottom line: The UK-first shortlist entry.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Contract the Escalation, Not the Dashboard

MSSP disappointment is usually a contract defect: the glossy SOC tour never promised who calls whom, how fast, with what authority.

Write the escalation matrix into the MSA severity definitions, notification SLAs in minutes, containment authority boundaries, named-analyst continuity and test it quarterly with injected scenarios you don’t announce.

Demand console access or structured data export so your team sees raw signal, not monthly PDF theater; an MSSP that resists transparency is telling you something.

Reference-check within your vertical and your regions specifically, probe analyst-turnover and account-team tenure, and confirm the two acquisition-era roadmaps on this list (Secureworks–Sophos, LevelBlue post-spin-out) in writing.

Finally, keep sovereignty of your own telemetry: log retention in your tenancy, export rights on exit, and a termination-assistance clause the breakup terms are part of the service.

FAQs

Who are the best MSSPs in 2026? Secureworks leads on platform transparency, IBM and Accenture for enterprise scale, Verizon, NTT, Orange Cyberdefense, Deloitte, LevelBlue, Trustwave, and BT by geography and specialty.

MSSP versus MDR what’s the difference? MDR is a focused detect-and-respond service, usually platform-native; MSSP is the broader managed-operations umbrella (monitoring, device management, compliance, often MDR inside). Many buyers actually need MDR plus specific managed services.

What should MSSP SLAs cover? Notification time by severity in minutes, containment authority boundaries, analyst continuity, console/data access, and exit terms not just uptime.

How do we test an MSSP before signing? Scenario injection during the pilot: a simulated credential compromise and a planted beacon
, measured on detection, escalation accuracy, and narrative quality.

Consulting-led or security-born provider? Buying transformation alongside operations favors consulting-led; buying detection excellence standalone favors security-born transparency.

Verdict

Ten providers, three species, one contract truth: you’re buying escalation behavior at 3 a.m., not a dashboard at the demo.

Secureworks for transparency, IBM and Accenture for enterprise span, Verizon and LevelBlue for carrier eyes, NTT and Orange and BT for geographic truth, Deloitte for the boardroom, Trustwave for the data layer write the matrix, test it unannounced, and keep your exit keys.

articles.description:

The company disconnected selected internal and customer-facing systems to contain the threat, interrupting digital services used by hearing aid wearers and hearing care professionals. The post Hackers Breach WS Audiology IT Systems, Disrupting Widex and Signia Hearing Aid Services appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WS Audiology (WSA), the parent company of Widex and Signia, is investigating a cybersecurity incident after unauthorized parties accessed parts of its IT infrastructure.

The company disconnected selected internal and customer-facing systems to contain the threat, interrupting digital services used by hearing aid wearers and hearing care professionals.

However, WSA said the hearing aids themselves were not affected. The incident highlights how disruption to supporting applications can affect patients even when medical devices keep working.

A similar distinction emerged during the Quest Diagnostics platform breach, where access to one service was suspended while core operations continued.

For WSA customers, the immediate impact involved app controls, fitting tools, and remote support rather than a confirmed failure of hearing aid hardware.

Reporting from Hearing Tracker noted the unauthorized access and service interruptions, but did not identify malware, a ransomware family, or an attacker.

Its October 30 report quoted WSA’s response and described problems reported by users. The available evidence therefore supports reporting an IT security breach, not attributing the incident to a specific malicious program.

Hackers Breach WS Audiology IT Systems

WSA said it acted immediately after identifying the incident and worked with its global IT partners to contain it. The company described the affected environment as its own IT infrastructure.

Business operations and core services continued, although protective shutdowns caused interruptions. Restoration was proceeding in phases, with affected systems brought back according to priority.

Widex Compass Cloud, used by hearing professionals for fitting and fine-tuning, was taken offline as a precaution. By the October 30 update, WSA said it was fully functional again, allowing Widex Allure and Allure AI fittings to proceed normally.

A spokesperson emphasized that the security threat was not caused by the company’s cloud-based software and that Compass Cloud had been disconnected deliberately.

Taking systems offline can create visible disruption even when the shutdown is a defensive decision. During the New York Blood Center incident, selected systems were similarly disconnected during containment.

That case involved confirmed ransomware; WSA’s disclosure does not establish the same cause. The comparison concerns the response measure, not a shared attacker, infection method, or malware family.

The Widex MOMENT app was among the services most affected. HearingTracker reported that some wearers could not access listening settings even though their devices continued amplifying sound.

One forum participant described being unable to select a preferred classroom preset while teaching. Other users reported difficulty reaching app controls, showing how software availability can influence everyday communication without disabling the underlying device.

WSA expected the MOMENT app to return over the weekend following its October 30 statement. Signia TeleCare was expected back early the following week, while Signia hearing aids could still be fitted and adjusted.

These were recovery estimates, not confirmation that restoration had finished. WSA also said its e-commerce sites remained functional and existing orders continued to be processed and shipped.

Investigation Leaves Attack Method and Data Exposure Unclear

The public account does not identify how the intruders entered WSA’s environment, which systems they accessed, or whether they stole information.

No exploited vulnerability, compromised account, or encryption activity was disclosed. Those gaps matter because unauthorized access, service disruption, and data theft are separate findings. Evidence of one does not automatically prove the others.

The CareCloud IT infrastructure breach illustrates why that distinction matters: restoring service and investigating possible patient information exposure were separate tasks.

WSA’s application outages likewise do not establish that patient records were stolen. Customers and clinics need further findings before drawing conclusions about confidentiality, the full scope of access, or any notification obligations arising from this incident.

HearingTracker also referenced a separate July 2024 WSA breach affecting a local retail IT system serving Bloomhearing operations. That earlier incident exposed patient and employee information, according to the report.

However, the current disclosure provides no basis for linking the two events. Treating them as one campaign would go beyond the available evidence.

articles.description:
Reddit plans to make its platform a primarily logged-in service, tightening access to public discussions as it seeks to curb unauthorized data scraping. Chief Executive Steve Huffman announced the shift in an October 29 post, explaining that account-based access would help protect Reddit’s content, improve recommendations, support advertising, and meet changing safety rules. The company […]

The post Reddit Plans Mandatory Logins to Block AI Bots From Scraping User Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Reddit plans to make its platform a primarily logged-in service, tightening access to public discussions as it seeks to curb unauthorized data scraping.

Chief Executive Steve Huffman announced the shift in an October 29 post, explaining that account-based access would help protect Reddit’s content, improve recommendations, support advertising, and meet changing safety rules.

The company has not announced a global rollout date. The proposal marks a major change for a website that has allowed people to read most discussions without signing in for two decades.

However, Reddit has not confirmed that every page will require an account. Tests in selected markets outside the United States will help determine which content remains open to visitors.

Reddit plans to require logins to curb AI data scraping, as CEO Steve Huffman said most unauthorized data collection occurs through public pages that allow bots to access discussions without accounts.

Reddit Requires Login to Block AI Data Scraping

In his announcement, Huffman described the problem as “the scraping and stealing of Reddit’s data.” Reddit will continue licensing content through commercial agreements, which he said provide rules governing permitted uses and presentation.

The planned restrictions therefore target unauthorized collection rather than ending all commercial access to Reddit discussions. The move also serves business goals beyond blocking AI bots. Logged-in activity helps Reddit recommend communities and show more relevant advertisements.

Huffman said personalization becomes increasingly important as the platform grows. At the same time, accounts encourage visitors to join communities, vote, and comment instead of only reading posts.

The wider challenge is controlling automated access without making websites harder for ordinary readers to use. CybersecurityNews previously covered Cloudflare’s AI Labyrinth, which directs unwanted crawlers toward AI-generated pages to waste their resources. That approach targets crawler behavior rather than requiring every reader to sign in.

Another related development is Cloudflare’s acquisition of Human Native, aimed at giving content owners more control over AI data access.

Together, these developments show how websites are exploring technical controls and licensing models to manage automated collection. Reddit’s proposal puts authentication at the center of its own access strategy.

Huffman said the change will not require users to supply their real names or verify their identities. Reddit also plans a rebuilt incognito mode in its mobile app, allowing read-only browsing and searching without affecting a logged-in account. Users can turn off personalization, although Huffman argues that recommendations will become less useful.

According to IGN’s report, Reddit still wants visitors to reach shared posts and content linked from search results. Huffman also described logged-out access to the front page as important.

Those boundaries remain unsettled, making the coming tests crucial for readers, moderators, and publishers that link to Reddit. The announcement outlines a planned access change, not a completed platform-wide lockdown or a proven end to AI scraping.

According to the supplied report from Dark Web Intelligence, the actor offered the alleged […]

The post Hackers Claim to Have Stolen 30GB of Data From Frooti Maker Parle Agro appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A dark web forum post claims 30GB of data linked to Parle Agro, the company behind Frooti, Appy Fizz, Bailley and Hippo, has been leaked. Dark Web Intelligence highlighted the claim, but the alleged theft and any system breach remain unverified.

According to the supplied report from Dark Web Intelligence, the actor offered the alleged archive as a free download. The post did not describe its contents, show sample records, or provide a file listing.

Those gaps leave basic questions unanswered, including whether the files belong to Parle Agro and whether they contain current information. The reported 30GB figure describes the claimed archive size, not the number of people or business records potentially affected.

Without access to verified evidence, it is not possible to determine whether the material contains internal documents, personal information, duplicate files, or unrelated data.

Parle Agro Stolen Data Claim

The Dark Web Intelligence report also provides no confirmed explanation of how the actor allegedly obtained the files. No entry point, attack timeline, or evidence of continued access to company systems is established.

Calling this a confirmed ransomware attack or identifying a specific security flaw would go beyond the information available. The supplied analyst note raises another concern.

The actor reportedly posted several similar dumps, meaning the alleged Parle Agro archive could contain recycled or incorrectly labeled material. That possibility requires investigation rather than acceptance of the forum claim at face value.

Cyber Security News previously covered a disputed HSBC data breach claim, which the bank rejected after reviewing the advertised sample. That case shows why an underground listing alone cannot prove that an organization lost data.

If the archive contains genuine business records, the risks could extend beyond public exposure. Supplier details, employee information, and payment documents could help criminals write convincing phishing emails or impersonate trusted business contacts. These remain possible risks, not confirmed findings about the alleged Parle Agro files.

A separate invoice fraud campaign covered by Cyber Security News showed how attackers reused stolen customer information to create personalized payment demands.

Real transaction details can make fraudulent messages appear credible to recipients who recognize the names, amounts, or business relationships involved.

For organizations assessing such claims, useful evidence includes file dates, document ownership, matching internal records, and access logs.

Reviewing those details could help distinguish a genuine incident from old, duplicated, or falsely attributed material. The claimed archive size alone cannot answer those questions.

For now, the available evidence supports reporting an alleged Parle Agro data leak, not a confirmed breach. The source report offers no verified sample, file inventory, or reliable account of the alleged intrusion.

Until stronger evidence emerges, claims about affected employees, customers, suppliers, or business systems should remain clearly identified as unknown rather than presented as facts.

articles.title: Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents to Automate Active Directory Attacks, Kerberoasting, and Lateral Movement
articles.description:
Hackers are now using an open-source AI tool called ARTEX to run large parts of a network break-in on their own. The tool can map a Windows network, steal service account passwords, and try to spread to domain controllers with very little human help. It does this in seconds, not hours. ARTEX is a multi-agent […]

The post Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents to Automate Active Directory Attacks, Kerberoasting, and Lateral Movement appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are now using an open-source AI tool called ARTEX to run large parts of a network break-in on their own. The tool can map a Windows network, steal service account passwords, and try to spread to domain controllers with very little human help.

It does this in seconds, not hours. ARTEX is a multi-agent penetration testing and command-and-control platform written in Go. Security teams built this kind of tool for testing, but criminals and suspected state-linked groups have picked it up.

Its original author took the code down from GitHub in October 2026 because of the abuse, yet copies still spread through community forks, including ScopeWeaver and a paid version called ARTEX PRO.

Researchers at Google Cloud’s Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant identified the activity during incident response work.

They have seen ARTEX used since late August 2026. Victims include organizations in government, technology, chemicals, manufacturing, and telecommunications.

Microsoft has also tied the tool to a China-linked group in a campaign against Microsoft 365 tenants that used stolen ConnectWise credentials.

Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents

ARTEX splits the attack into six sub-agents. The attacker gives it a goal and some stolen credentials, and the framework turns that goal into commands. In several cases, the intruders handed ARTEX valid logins and told it to carry out the later stages.

Once inside, ARTEX ran PowerShell scripts against a domain controller and a federation server. These scripts checked usernames, listed managed service accounts, and reviewed Active Directory Certificate Services templates.

They also mapped thousands of security accounts across forests. In one case, the tool pulled more than 110,000 Active Directory objects and read the Domain Admins group.

Kerberoasting was a key step. ARTEX asked for service tickets for accounts tied to service names, which attackers can crack offline to recover passwords.

This is the same basic trick seen in the Ghost SPN Kerberoasting technique, but here a machine did the work. After an offline cracking pause, the tool ran DCSync scripts and took the domain krbtgt key, cloud sync credentials, and domain controller hashes.

Stealing these hashes is dangerous because it can lead to forged tickets, as we explained in our report on how attackers impersonate domain controllers.

ARTEX also tried to move onto domain controllers with Pass-the-Ticket, WinRM, Kerberos relay, and Pass-the-Hash scripts. It failed in one case because of Windows service token limits, and endpoint protection blocked the rest before defenders cut off the server.

Machine Speed, Noisy Traces, and Wider Trend

Google said the tool works at a speed no human could match. Single bursts of activity ran for about 2 to 25 seconds, and one case showed 27 events in 23 seconds. When a script was too large, ARTEX trimmed it and relaunched it in about 10 seconds.

Wiz tracks one ARTEX campaign that Google calls UNC7228, which overlaps with Microsoft’s STORM-0940. That actor often went from its first hacked account to deep system access in about four hours, and once in 15 minutes.

The tool is also sloppy. In one case it created 240 log events while trying to plant web shells through MySQL log files, and its sub-agents seemed to overwrite each other.

Google says ARTEX trades stealth for speed, which gives defenders something to catch. The trend is spreading, too. Another group used AI agents to reach domain admin, as seen when Aur0ra ransomware operators used Cursor agents.

Google says these tools do not change attack methods. They only cut the time needed to chain them together. Its advice is to isolate admin systems, use short-lived credentials, limit access, segment networks, and watch for odd behavior.

Google also says static indicators will miss much of this activity, because attackers use valid accounts and normal admin tools.

articles.title: VOLTA Malware Steals Gmail and Discord Sessions, Then Uses AI to Build Detailed Victim Profiles
articles.description:
A new Windows infostealer called VOLTA does more than steal passwords. After it grabs Gmail, Discord and other logins, it asks an AI model to study the loot and write a report on how much the victim is worth. The idea is simple: steal everything, then let AI sort it out. The malware calls itself […]

The post VOLTA Malware Steals Gmail and Discord Sessions, Then Uses AI to Build Detailed Victim Profiles appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new Windows infostealer called VOLTA does more than steal passwords. After it grabs Gmail, Discord and other logins, it asks an AI model to study the loot and write a report on how much the victim is worth.

The idea is simple: steal everything, then let AI sort it out. The malware calls itself “VOLTA-AUTODOXER.” It deletes itself after running, which makes it harder to find. It is also a sign of where cybercrime is heading.

Criminals have already tried AI for victim sorting, as in the Dolphin X AI profiler reported earlier this year, but VOLTA pushes the idea further by using a commercial AI service as its analyst.

Researchers at Cisco Talos noted the malware after it surfaced through their CAIRN research effort, which looks for hacking tools that use AI.

Talos published its findings on October 31, 2026, and wrote that VOLTA is a mature stealer with an optional AI layer added at the end. Talos also did not track whether VOLTA has been used in the wild, according to WIRED.

VOLTA Malware Steals Gmail and Discord Sessions, Then Uses AI

VOLTA starts like most stealers. It pulls saved passwords, cookies and payment cards from Chromium-based browsers.

It also hits Firefox, Thunderbird, Outlook, Slack, Steam, Battle.net, Telegram, Roblox and Discord. It takes Microsoft OAuth tokens, SSH keys, cloud-provider files and saved Wi-Fi passwords too, and it can crack crypto wallet vaults on the spot.

The second stage is what sets it apart. Using the victim’s own logged-in Gmail session, VOLTA searches the inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal.

These receipts help it confirm the victim’s home address. It also calls stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions to read order history, and it reuses the Discord token to fill in the account profile.

A live Rolimons lookup puts a price on any Roblox items. Session theft like this is not new, and an older stealer, FleshStealer harvesting Discord tokens, showed how a stolen token can give an attacker lasting access.

Stolen sessions matter because they can skip passwords and sometimes two-factor prompts. The attacker simply acts as the logged-in user.

Talos says much of VOLTA’s token theft depends on getting around Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption. Chrome added that feature to protect cookies, but infostealers have been finding ways around Chrome’s cookie protection since it launched.

How the AI Builds the Victim Profile

VOLTA saves everything it learns into a file called Identity_Report.txt. The file includes location, home address, employer, an estimated birth year, the last four digits of cards and Slack workspaces.

It sends this file to OpenRouter, an AI gateway, with instructions to act as “a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment”.

The reply must include a section called “WHAT THEY’RE WORTH,” which ranks valuables as low, medium or high. A second section, “THEIR OPSEC,” judges the victim’s password habits and security level.

The default model is Claude Opus 4.6. If that model refuses the request, VOLTA tries Kimi K2 and then Gemini 2.5 Flash. It checks replies for phrases like “I can’t” to spot a refusal. The temperature is set low, at 0.2, to keep answers steady and accurate.

The AI call runs from the victim’s own computer and network. The results come back as AI_Analysis.txt, and both files leave in a zip called volta_dox.zip. Talos believes VOLTA is sold as a builder.

Each buyer fills in six slots, such as a Telegram channel and API keys, and gets a custom build. The buyer then gets ranked reports in Telegram.

No attacker-owned servers were seen, so defenders cannot simply block one command server. Similar builder-style tools, like this Python MaaS infostealer builder, already let low-skill criminals run large theft campaigns.

Talos suggests blocking Chrome from starting with the –headless flag unless a known developer process launches it. Users who suspect an infection should keep the %APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt log, which shows what was taken.

They should also revoke tokens and reset passwords from a clean device, and move crypto funds to a new wallet if the seed phrase sat in plain text.

articles.title: TightVNC Pre-Auth RCE Vulnerability Lets Hackers Execute Code on Windows PCs, PoC Released
articles.description:
A TightVNC Viewer vulnerability can let attackers execute code on Windows PCs before a password prompt appears. Research credited to SeongJoon Cho of SSD Labs Korea includes proof-of-concept exploit code targeting TightVNC 2.8.88 x64. The attack uses a malicious VNC server to send screen data that corrupts the viewer’s memory. The affected component is the […]

The post TightVNC Pre-Auth RCE Vulnerability Lets Hackers Execute Code on Windows PCs, PoC Released appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A TightVNC Viewer vulnerability can let attackers execute code on Windows PCs before a password prompt appears. Research credited to SeongJoon Cho of SSD Labs Korea includes proof-of-concept exploit code targeting TightVNC 2.8.88 x64. The attack uses a malicious VNC server to send screen data that corrupts the viewer’s memory.

The affected component is the viewer, not simply any Windows machine running a TightVNC server. Attackers need either network access to a viewer in Listening Mode or a user who connects the viewer to an attacker-controlled server. The supplied disclosure does not establish active exploitation.

The flaw begins when the server announces its screen size through the Remote Framebuffer protocol (RFB). TightVNC calculates the memory needed to hold that screen, but converts the result into a 32-bit integer. Large dimensions cause the value to wrap around, leaving a smaller allocation than expected.

In the reported example, a server announces a 32,768-by-32,769 screen using 32 bits per pixel. The viewer allocates only 128 KB while retaining dimensions representing more than 4 GB of pixel data. Later screen updates write outside that small buffer because the pointer calculation lacks a check against the allocated size.

TightVNC Pre-Auth RCE Vulnerability

The PoC turns this memory corruption into code execution. It first changes an outgoing buffer’s length to leak nearby memory, revealing addresses needed to bypass address randomization.

It then redirects a function call and uses return-oriented programming, which reuses existing code, to launch a process through Windows’ CreateProcessW function.

Listening Mode exposes the viewer on TCP port 5500 and, according to the disclosure, accepts incoming server connections without a password or IP restriction.

An attacker who can reach that port can target the viewer directly. An outbound connection to a rogue support server creates another route, with exploitation occurring before authentication.

These conditions differ from VNC connection hijacking that relies on weak passwords. They also differ from remote access tools disguised as installers, where users install legitimate software under pretenses. Here, the attack targets memory handling inside the viewer itself.

The researchers say the vendor did not respond and patched the issue on October 3, 2026. However, TightVNC’s official release notices identify October 2 and October 5 security updates, so the exact fix date remains unclear. The vendor says versions 2.8.89 and 2.8.90 address Viewer security issues and recommends 2.8.90 for that branch.

Administrators should update affected viewers, turn off unnecessary Listening Mode, restrict port 5500 to trusted systems, and avoid untrusted VNC servers. Network restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching the vulnerable viewer.

articles.title: Hackers Target 61 GitHub Repositories With Command Injection Attacks to Steal CI/CD Secrets
articles.description:
Hackers targeted 61 public GitHub repositories in a coordinated command injection campaign designed to steal data from automated development systems. Radware researchers identified 83 malicious issues, pull requests, and comments posted on September 1, 2026, with evidence that injected commands executed inside two GitHub Actions workflows. The findings show how routine project discussions can become […]

The post Hackers Target 61 GitHub Repositories With Command Injection Attacks to Steal CI/CD Secrets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers targeted 61 public GitHub repositories in a coordinated command injection campaign designed to steal data from automated development systems.

Radware researchers identified 83 malicious issues, pull requests, and comments posted on September 1, 2026, with evidence that injected commands executed inside two GitHub Actions workflows. The findings show how routine project discussions can become entry points into software build systems.

According to Radware’s investigation, 77 malicious items appeared within about 43 minutes. Six more followed in a second wave lasting roughly two minutes.

Targets included Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave Browser, MLflow, ToolJet, and PX4-Autopilot. Their inclusion does not mean every project was breached.

The campaign exploited workflows that placed user-controlled text directly into shell scripts. GitHub Actions can automatically respond when someone opens an issue, submits a pull request, or posts a comment. These tasks may check titles, assign labels, or send notifications.

Hackers Target 61 GitHub Repositories

Attackers placed Bash command substitution expressions, written as $(), inside that content. When a vulnerable workflow inserted the text into executable shell code, Bash treated the embedded expression as a command rather than ordinary text. Wrapping the inserted title in double quotes did not prevent execution.

The payload ran env to collect environment variables, encoded the output with Base64, removed newline characters, and used curl to attempt an HTTP POST request.

Every verified payload pointed to 54.205.16[.]142 on port 8443, with a separate collection identifier for each attempt. Despite the port number, the connection used HTTP rather than HTTPS.

The risk depended on what each job could access. Environment variables could contain service tokens, deployment credentials, or internal settings.

GitHub Actions secrets are not automatically available to every workflow, so execution alone does not establish that sensitive credentials were stolen.

In PX4-Autopilot, a pull request posing as a documentation correction carried the payload in its title. A title-checking workflow inserted that title into a Bash command invoking Python. Logs showed a command-substitution warning and returned content beginning with GIF89a, replacing the malicious expression.

In Snouzy/workout-cool, an issue notification workflow inserted the attacker’s title directly into a Bash variable assignment. A warning tied to that line confirmed command substitution. A later Discord request failed because its body contained invalid JSON, although that failure did not prove successful data theft.

Radware did not confirm stolen secrets, repository write access, source code changes, or compromised releases. Researchers also found signs that some participating accounts may have been hijacked, including one owner publicly denying opening a malicious issue.

The findings complement earlier reporting on GhostAction credential theft and the tj-actions supply chain attack. Those incidents used different routes but also put CI/CD secrets at risk.

Maintainers should pass untrusted titles through environment variables instead of inserting them into shell source, avoid eval, and limit workflow permissions.

Teams finding execution evidence should review available secrets, rotate potentially exposed credentials, inspect audit logs, and investigate unexpected outbound traffic. Keep notification jobs separate from privileged release workflows to reduce the damage an injected command could cause.
