articles.title: Aur0ra Ransomware Hackers Use Cursor AI Agents to Gain Domain Admin Access and Steal Data
articles.description:
Ransomware crews are now giving the hardest parts of a network break-in to AI coding tools. A group linked to Aur0ra ransomware used Cursor AI agents to go from stolen passwords to domain admin access, the highest level of control in a Windows network. From there, it collected data and prepared to deploy ransomware. The […]

The post Aur0ra Ransomware Hackers Use Cursor AI Agents to Gain Domain Admin Access and Steal Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ransomware crews are now giving the hardest parts of a network break-in to AI coding tools. A group linked to Aur0ra ransomware used Cursor AI agents to go from stolen passwords to domain admin access, the highest level of control in a Windows network. From there, it collected data and prepared to deploy ransomware.

The group behind Aur0ra, also spelled Aurora, is tracked as GOLD OGRE. Human operators supplied VPN access, targets and goals, and the agents handled most of the work with little help. This lowers the skill needed to run a full intrusion.

It also matters for every company that relies on Active Directory, as shown in an earlier report on Aurora that covered the same crew’s use of AI planning.

Analysts at Sophos identified the activity while studying an AI-assisted testing framework built with Cursor. The company’s Counter Threat Unit published research on that framework in May 2026.

Aur0ra Ransomware Hackers Use Cursor AI Agents

The framework had tested several endpoint detection and response (EDR) products, including Sophos’s own agent. Later, according to the full Sophos analysis, the same infrastructure was seen hosting Cobalt Strike for Aur0ra operations. Sophos said it warned affected customers and worked with law enforcement to notify other victims.

In late August, the analysts recovered Cursor files tied to both the ransomware work and the evasion testing. The attackers used Cursor to climb from credential access to domain administrator.

They got past AI safety rules by describing the work as an authorized red team job or “diagnostics testing.” Cursor’s Composer model ran many of the intrusions, along with models from Anthropic, xAI and Moonshot.

The group used Anthropic almost entirely at first, then added the others as it moved from building tools to breaking into networks. Other crews have been caught using Claude AI to plan ransomware work too, so the habit is spreading.

Once given access, the agents mapped the network and checked for weak paths to powerful accounts. They ran commands, moved from machine to machine, and searched file shares, user documents, backup stores and cloud-linked storage.

They tried password spraying, Kerberoasting, NTLM coercion and relay, and pulled credentials from files and backups. Operators also used common tools like SharpShares and NetExec, which appear in Gentlemen ransomware EDR killers reporting as well.

In some victim networks, the agents reached domain management access, and three of those victims later appeared on the Aur0ra leak site.

Stolen files were staged and sent to S3-compatible storage. Sophos saw one operator use a VeeamTransport command to copy data to a bucket on a server at 152[.]236[.]4[.]14. Logs also showed Russian shortcuts typed on a Cyrillic keyboard layout, which suggests the operators speak Russian.

Third-Party Findings, Shared Tools and Defense Steps

In late August 2026, Gambit Security and CloudSEK published reports that appeared to rely on the same exposed open directory at 172[.]86[.]113[.]245.

It held Windows and Linux (ESXi-ready) versions of the Aur0ra ransomware, shell history and Cursor chat logs. Gambit also noted a Claude 4.5-Sonnet agent in semi-automated intrusions.

That fits with a Claude Code ransomware case in which an operator let the model fix its own commands until a task worked.

Gambit described agents installing a VPN client, scanning subnets with Nmap or NetExec, and mapping the domain with BloodHound.

They also tried NTLM relay through PetitPotam, Coerce Plus and PrinterBug, and used Certipy for certificate abuse. Sophos found the same tools in its own testing framework, but only one SOCKS-related IP address overlapped between the two sets of infrastructure.

Sophos researchers say with high confidence that GOLD OGRE used AI to test how well tools evade detection, then gave similar technology to associates running Aur0ra.

They also expect other ransomware groups to build AI agents like Cursor into their work. Basic defenses still help, including patching internet-facing devices, phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and close watch on EDR alerts.

Since the AI speeds up each stage, a fast response matters more. Sophos also advises limiting how far an intruder can move by segmenting critical servers, isolating backups, reviewing domain administrator rights, using privileged access management and applying application controls.

articles.title: Hackers Build Fake Polymarket Platforms That Rig Trades and Block Cryptocurrency Withdrawals
articles.description:
Criminals are copying the look of Polymarket, one of the biggest prediction market sites. They use the copies to take cryptocurrency from people who think they are placing real bets. Once a victim deposits money, the site decides every win and loss, and withdrawals stop working. The scams are not one-off websites. Three Russian-speaking “traffer” […]

The post Hackers Build Fake Polymarket Platforms That Rig Trades and Block Cryptocurrency Withdrawals appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Criminals are copying the look of Polymarket, one of the biggest prediction market sites. They use the copies to take cryptocurrency from people who think they are placing real bets.

Once a victim deposits money, the site decides every win and loss, and withdrawals stop working. The scams are not one-off websites.

Three Russian-speaking “traffer” teams, called AtlasCore, PolyFucked and Magnetic Team, sell ready-made fake prediction markets to affiliates.

Affiliates bring in the victims, and the team supplies the website, admin panel, crypto payment system and technical support.

Earlier cases such as fake Polymarket trading tools drained wallets with malware. This newer wave skips the malware and relies on a rigged platform instead.

Researchers at Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified the three teams and the tools they sell. They have watched the groups adapt since spring 2026.

Their Insikt Group report says the teams copied established fraud methods and applied them to the growing interest in Polymarket and Kalshi.

Hackers Build Fake Polymarket Platforms

The fake sites copy the real thing closely. They show YES/NO bets, probability charts, trading volumes and live market activity. Some even import data from the public Polymarket API, so the numbers look real.

Behind the screen, the operator controls the result. Code from AtlasCore’s fake sites lets an operator set a “win chance” for each victim. A value of 0 means the victim always loses, and 100 means they always win. This can apply to every user or to one person.

Magnetic Team adds a “Boost” tool with a target win rate, a balance cap that holds back payouts once a victim’s balance grows, and a forced-loss pause after several wins in a row.

Magnetic Team also fakes the crowd. It claims more than 3,000 bots trading across more than 5,000 markets, each acting like a different kind of trader, so the order book looks busy and natural.

Withdrawals are where victims get stuck. The panels hold ready-made error messages and fee settings. Magnetic Team’s “withdrawal funnel” gives one excuse after another, such as identity checks, anti-money-laundering reviews, VIP upgrade fees, an “Account Protection Score” and withdrawal taxes. The aim is to keep the victim paying and never let them cash out.

The sites also collect personal data. Victims are asked for card numbers, CVV codes, passport or driver’s license photos and a selfie holding the document.

Magnetic Team can create up to 20,000 deposit wallets per blockchain. Their private keys are exposed and can be exported the moment money arrives, so funds can be swept out quickly.

This fits a wider pattern. The DCloud Uni-App scam network also shows victims fake trading activity before their money disappears.

AI and Affiliate Money Help the Scam Spread

The affiliate deals are attractive. AtlasCore advertises 70% to 80% of net profit, PolyFucked offers at least 60%, and Magnetic Team pays a base of 70% of victim deposits.

AtlasCore’s Telegram channel claimed about $10.97 million in deposits between May 2 and September 18, 2026. PolyFucked claims about $2.4 million in quarterly turnover. Both figures come from the criminals themselves and may be inflated.

AI lowers the effort needed to run these campaigns. AtlasCore’s manuals teach affiliates to build fake influencers by blending photos of two real people, then post short reaction videos on Instagram.

They also tell affiliates to strip metadata so the content is not labeled as AI-made. PolyFucked shares prompts for making logos with AI image tools.

AI also handles the chat with victims. Code from the fake sites shows operators connecting a language model to answer support messages and translate victim replies into Russian. If one model refuses a request, the system switches to a model from another provider.

Magnetic Team’s code also looks AI-assisted, with heavy English comments and notes about bug fixes, though Insikt says this is a judgment based on style and not confirmed.

This matches what OpenAI found in a scam networks using ChatGPT case, where fraud groups used AI for fake personas and translation.

Treat any prediction market that is not on the official Polymarket or Kalshi domain as suspect. Be careful with sites promoted by influencers on Instagram or Telegram.

A site that asks for ID documents or card details before you can withdraw should raise alarms. Watch for sudden fees or “verification” steps when you try to cash out.

Reviewing crypto phishing warning signs helps spot these tricks early. Security teams can block the domains and IPs below and watch for new lookalike domains.

articles.title: Critical Drupal Commerce Vulnerability Could Let Hackers Buy Products for Just $0.01
articles.description:
Drupal has warned that hackers are actively exploiting a highly critical security flaw in Commerce Core, putting online stores at risk of financial losses. Tracked as CVE-2026-118539, the vulnerability lets attackers bypass access checks in the module used to sell products and services on Drupal websites and connected shopping applications. The warning raises concerns about […]

The post Critical Drupal Commerce Vulnerability Could Let Hackers Buy Products for Just $0.01 appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Drupal has warned that hackers are actively exploiting a highly critical security flaw in Commerce Core, putting online stores at risk of financial losses.

Tracked as CVE-2026-118539, the vulnerability lets attackers bypass access checks in the module used to sell products and services on Drupal websites and connected shopping applications.

The warning raises concerns about unauthorized changes to store data and transactions. However, Drupal has not confirmed that attackers can buy products for exactly $0.01.

The public advisory does not document that price, describes a potential financial impact, and does not name the fields attackers can change or explain how observed attacks worked.

Published on October 28, 2026, the official Drupal security advisory identifies insufficient protection around certain routes and entity fields. Routes handle requests to website functions, while entity fields hold data associated with site records. Missing access checks can let someone reach functions or data they should not control.

Critical Drupal Commerce Vulnerability

Drupal assigned the flaw a risk score of 21 out of 25, placing it in its “Highly critical” category. This is Drupal’s own security scale, not a CVSS score. The assessment indicates that exploitation requires no authentication and affects all configurations of vulnerable module versions.

The rating also identifies possible exposure of some private information and changes to some data. Drupal has confirmed active exploitation but has not published affected store names, attack volumes, or a detailed attack method. The advisory does not establish remote code execution or full website takeover.

Commerce Core supports shopping carts, checkout forms, and separate applications connected through APIs. Its project page reports more than 42,000 websites using the module. That figure reflects reported installations, not the number of stores confirmed vulnerable or compromised.

The vulnerability affects Commerce Core versions before 2.41 and versions from 3.0.0 up to, but not including, 3.3.13. Administrators running the 3.x branch should install Commerce Core 3.3.13. Sites using earlier versions should upgrade to Commerce Core 8.x-2.41, following Drupal’s published guidance.

These are Commerce module updates, separate from Drupal core security releases. Earlier coverage of a critical Drupal remote code execution vulnerability concerns a different flaw. Store owners should check the installed Commerce package rather than assume a recent Drupal core update fixed this issue.

Drupal explicitly advises affected sites to audit orders for inconsistencies because exploitation is already underway. Beyond applying the update, a practical review should compare recorded orders with expected prices and payment records, investigating unexplained differences rather than treating them as proof of compromise.

This threat differs from Magecart attacks that target online checkout pages and steal customer payment details. Here, Drupal’s warning centers on broken access controls and possible merchant losses.

Researchers Dan Puccetti, Marcus Johansson, and Robert Snyder reported the vulnerability. Prompt patching and order checks remain the immediate priorities for affected online stores.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Passwordless Telnet to Infect Linux Devices With New Kairos DDoS Botnet
articles.description:
A new botnet called Kairos is spreading to Linux devices through a very old mistake: a Telnet service that accepts the root user with no password. Once inside, the attackers install a small Go-based program that turns the device into a node for DDoS operations. The campaign shows that basic security gaps still give attackers […]

The post Hackers Exploit Passwordless Telnet to Infect Linux Devices With New Kairos DDoS Botnet appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new botnet called Kairos is spreading to Linux devices through a very old mistake: a Telnet service that accepts the root user with no password.

Once inside, the attackers install a small Go-based program that turns the device into a node for DDoS operations. The campaign shows that basic security gaps still give attackers an easy path in.

Kairos does not use a complex exploit or a zero-day flaw. The attackers connect to exposed Telnet services and log in as root with an empty password.

Weak remote access has fueled many botnets before, including a VOIP-based botnet attacking routers that also relied on default Telnet logins.

Analysts at Nozomi Networks identified the malware after their honeypots recorded three different IP addresses delivering Kairos samples.

The Nozomi Networks Labs report describes it as a previously undocumented DDoS bot for Linux. The three samples were the same program.

They differed only in the hard-coded command-and-control (C2) address and the Go compiler patch level, versions 1.27.0 and 1.27.1. This suggests the operator recompiles one codebase for each C2 server.

Hackers Exploit Passwordless Telnet

Every observed infection began the same way. The attacker guessed the default Telnet login, user root with an empty password. The operator then ran a short set of shell commands.

First, uname -m checked the device’s processor type, and the payload requested later, x86_64, matched it. This hints that the operator keeps a separate build for each architecture.

Next, the commands moved into the /tmp folder, removed leftovers from earlier attempts, and downloaded the malware.

The dropper tries several download methods in turn: wget, curl, BusyBox wget, and finally TFTP. Each downloaded copy gets full permissions with chmod 777 and runs in the background.

The BusyBox and TFTP fallbacks keep the loader working on small embedded systems that lack common tools. In the sample chain, the server at 172[.]86[.]85[.]39 hosted the payload on TCP port 8080 and also served as the C2 on port 9999.

Once running, the bot connects to its single hard-coded IP address and sends a plain-text beacon, REGISTER linux amd64 <NumCPU>. It then sends a blank line every two seconds to keep the session alive.

If the link drops, it tries again every five seconds with no limit. The C2 can send only three commands: hold, which starts a flood, !ka, which stops all attacks and pauses the bot, and !ku, which lets it accept attacks again. Similar Telnet-driven threats include the Tengu Mirai botnet that reboots IoT devices when someone tries to remove it.

How Kairos Floods Targets and How to Defend Against It

Kairos does not send huge amounts of traffic. Instead, it opens hundreds or thousands of real TCP connections to a victim and keeps them open. The bot starts 128 workers per CPU core, with a minimum of 256, so a 16-core device opens 2,048 connections per attack.

Each worker finishes a normal handshake, then sends one space character every five seconds to hold the socket open. If the target refuses the connection, the worker retries every 100 milliseconds, which creates a fast “connect storm.”

The victim’s service slowly runs out of room and stops accepting real users. The bot is simple and has weaknesses. It has no persistence, no self-spreading, no command execution, and no anti-analysis features.

It tries to hide by renaming itself [kworker/0:1] to look like a Linux kernel thread. However, tools like ps and the /proc folder still show the real name.

Since the bot completes real handshakes, its source IP is also visible to the victim. This is unlike KATARU IoT malware strain, which adds privilege escalation and encrypted C2 traffic.

Defenders should disable Telnet, replace default or empty passwords, and block outbound traffic to the known C2 addresses on ports 9999 and 8080.

Since the C2 address changes with each build, Nozomi advises relying on code-based detection. Teams can add an IDS rule for the plain-text REGISTER linux beacon and deploy the published YARA rule.

They should also alert on any “kernel worker” process holding many outbound connections. Exposed services remain a common entry point, as seen when a cPanel authentication bypass flaw was used to drop Mirai malware.

articles.title: Hackers Use Zero-Click Coruna and DarkSword Exploits to Steal Sensitive Data From iPhones
articles.description:
Hackers are using two powerful iPhone exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, to break into phones and steal private data. The victim only has to open a web page. There is no app to install and no prompt to accept. The scale is larger than many people expected. Researchers found 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code. These […]

The post Hackers Use Zero-Click Coruna and DarkSword Exploits to Steal Sensitive Data From iPhones appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using two powerful iPhone exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, to break into phones and steal private data. The victim only has to open a web page. There is no app to install and no prompt to accept.

The scale is larger than many people expected. Researchers found 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code. These sites choose an exploit chain based on the iOS version on the phone.

iPhones on iOS 17.2.1 or older get the original Coruna kit. Newer iPhones on iOS 18 get a chain built from DarkSword. Earlier reporting on the Coruna and DarkSword kits already showed how outdated iPhones are at risk from a single website visit.

Analysts at Zimperium’s zLabs team identified and documented this activity in a detailed technical report published on October 29, 2026.

They recovered both the browser code and the native payloads. They also matched 93 of the domains to 21 tracking servers.

Hackers Use Zero-Click Coruna and DarkSword Exploits

The infection starts with a page that looks normal. Zimperium found dating sites built for users in Brazil, Nigeria, and Indonesia.

It also found AI-companion chat sites, crypto promotions, and streaming pages. While the visitor sees the decoy, a hidden frame loads the exploit in the background.

Some pages tell TikTok users to tap “Open in browser” so the link opens in Safari, which is the browser the exploit needs. Nothing looks wrong on screen, so advice like “watch for strange behavior” does not help here.

Next, a script checks the iOS version and picks the right path. The Coruna chain uses CVE-2022-48503, a WebAssembly flaw in Safari, to read and write browser memory.

It then bypasses pointer authentication, an Apple protection that signs code addresses so tampering is caught. After it escapes the browser, the native modules read and write kernel memory and change code-signing settings.

They talk to their servers over encrypted traffic with certificate checks turned off. They also delete crash logs and Safari website data to cover their tracks.

The DarkSword chain works in steps. Browser code runs first. It then breaks out through the GPU process and moves into mediaplaybackd, a system media service.

In Zimperium’s test on an iPhone running iOS 18.6.2, the phone contacted the command server 144 times and pulled seven extra modules.

One module was built to read Telegram’s local storage. The phone then sent out its Apple Notes database and a list of 214 installed apps.

The same kit has also appeared across DarkSword’s growing web infrastructure that operators replace within days, as DarkSword’s growing web infrastructure reporting from Censys showed.

Supply Chain Delivery and Ways to Stay Safe

Not every infection starts with a bad link. SafeDep found matching Coruna code inside the backdoored art-template npm package that many developers had pulled into their sites.

Any site using the bad versions served the exploit to its own visitors, so no suspicious lure domain was needed. Domain blocklists miss this route completely.

Zimperium also spotted a fake jquery.min.js file loaded from a look-alike Google domain on a comic site, which then started the Coruna chain.

Who is behind it remains unclear. Coruna was first built by a nation-state actor for targeted work, but its leak spread the toolkit to many groups.

Some recovered code has Chinese-language comments. Zimperium says that only describes how the code was written, not who deployed it, so it ties its conclusions to the code and infrastructure only.

The best defense is patching, because every CVE in these chains is already fixed. Apple even pushed an expanded iOS 18.7.7 update to more devices to block DarkSword, so users should check Settings for the newest version offered for their phone.

People at higher risk, such as journalists, activists, and executives, should turn on Lockdown Mode. Everyone should treat unexpected “Open in Safari” prompts as a stop sign.

Security teams should require patched iOS builds on all devices, including personal ones used for work. Mobile threat defense tools can flag odd crashes, unexpected restarts, and disabled code signing.

Teams should also keep diagnostic logs for high-risk users, because the malware deletes local traces. Site owners should audit third-party scripts and enforce a strict Content Security Policy.

articles.title: Hackers Weaponize OpenAI API in NIK C2 Framework for Credential Theft and Remote System Control
articles.description:
A new malware framework called NIK C2 is turning the OpenAI API into a tool for cybercriminals. Its Windows implant can dump passwords, record every keystroke, take hidden control of a desktop, and send the stolen data to an AI model for analysis, all inside the same session. The tool is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows […]

The post Hackers Weaponize OpenAI API in NIK C2 Framework for Credential Theft and Remote System Control appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new malware framework called NIK C2 is turning the OpenAI API into a tool for cybercriminals. Its Windows implant can dump passwords, record every keystroke, take hidden control of a desktop, and send the stolen data to an AI model for analysis, all inside the same session.

The tool is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access program. It talks to its server over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443.

It also uses an HTTP backup channel that checks in about every 250 milliseconds. All traffic is locked with AES-256-GCM encryption, and the implant rotates between three server tiers so a single takedown does not cut it off.

Researchers at Cisco Talos identified the malware and published their findings on October 29, 2026. Talos found a live server in the wild and said, with moderate confidence, that NIK C2 is a working framework and not a proof of concept.

The samples point to at least three versions, which suggests a skilled team that keeps adding features. Abusing OpenAI is not new.

The earlier OpenAI Assistants API backdoor called SesameOp used the service to hide its command traffic. NIK C2 goes a step further by using the model as a built-in analyst.

Hackers Weaponize OpenAI API

The AI feature runs through a command named ai_generate. The operator sends a prompt, an API key, and a model name.

The implant builds a request and sends it to the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint from the victim’s computer. It waits up to 60 seconds, reads the answer, and returns the text to the attacker’s panel along with token-usage counts. If no model is named, it defaults to gpt-4.

The most worrying detail is the key fallback. If the attacker leaves out an API key, the implant reads the OPENAI_API_KEY variable on the victim’s machine.

OpenAI then bills the victim, and the logs show the victim’s key, so nothing points back to the attacker. Talos calls this a deliberate design choice. This kind of AI-enabled malware is getting more attention from defenders.

Talos has also released the open-source CAIRN toolkit, which hunts for AI endpoints, prompt templates, and API-key patterns inside suspicious files. Because normal apps use the same AI services, blocking those domains alone is not practical.

Credential Theft, Remote Control, and Screen-Locking Ransomware

The implant supports more than 52 commands. For theft, it copies browser databases from Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, and Firefox. It also grabs saved Wi-Fi passwords, Discord tokens, and desktop crypto wallets such as Exodus, Electrum, and Bitcoin Core.

It also targets wallet extensions such as MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet, and Phantom. Two search patterns hunt the whole disk for files with names like “seed,” “mnemonic,” “private,” or “secret.”

A keylogger streams each keystroke live to the attacker. Hidden VNC gives full desktop control that the victim cannot see. The implant also offers proxy tunnels and RDP session control to move deeper into a network.

To stay hidden, the implant renames itself to names like svchost.exe and csrss.exe and patches AMSI so PowerShell scripts are not scanned.

It also skips the UAC prompt with a fodhelper trick. It marks itself as a critical process, so ending it in Task Manager triggers a Blue Screen of Death.

The ransomware module is simple but fast. It backs up the Master Boot Record, writes an HTML lock screen with the attacker’s Bitcoin or USDT wallet details, and opens it through the Windows mshta.exe utility, a trusted tool that attackers often misuse.

A registry Run key named “SystemLock” brings the screen back after every restart. It does not encrypt files, so it leaves little forensic evidence. A separate bootkit-prep feature checks UEFI, BIOS, and Secure Boot status.

articles.title: Researchers Hacked Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop Embedded Browsers
articles.description:
Security flaws in the embedded browsers of Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop could enable code execution, file theft, and address-bar spoofing on developer machines. The findings published on October 29 show how browser features built into AI assistants can break security boundaries when given extra access to their host apps. The […]

The post Researchers Hacked Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop Embedded Browsers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security flaws in the embedded browsers of Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop could enable code execution, file theft, and address-bar spoofing on developer machines.

The findings published on October 29 show how browser features built into AI assistants can break security boundaries when given extra access to their host apps.

The researchers named the attack class EMBRACE, short for an embedded browser trusted like a real one. These are separate flaws sharing one design problem. Features meant to help assistants preview projects, read pages, and track tabs gave untrusted content powers it should not have.

According to Forever report, Cursor exposed a window.cursorBrowser.send() bridge that allowed any loaded page to send content into the agent’s instruction box without a user gesture.

Embedded Browser Flaws in Popular AI Coding Tools Exploited

Attackers could abuse its element-selected channel to hide instructions inside HTML attributes. The visible item looked harmless, while the agent received command fragments and instructions to join them into an npm installation command.

A single Enter keypress could approve execution. When Cursor’s sandbox blocked installation, the agent independently retried outside it, allowing the package’s preinstall script to launch Calculator.

Success depended on the model and was not guaranteed. The finding adds another browser entry point to risks covered in earlier Cursor prompt injection research.

GitHub Copilot’s browser preview accepted address updates supplied by the page itself. It checked the address format but did not confirm that the reported location matched the page actually loaded.

Researchers made an attacker-controlled page display github.com/login in the preview’s address bar. The agent also received that false location, although the page remained on the attacker’s server. A fake login form could therefore appear beneath a trusted address and mislead both the user and the assistant.

Claude Desktop and VS Code restricted file access on the main page but failed to apply the same checks inside web workers, which run scripts in the background. A malicious local preview could start a worker and read files outside its project folder.

Codex needed no worker bypass. Researchers found that its local pages could fetch files elsewhere on the machine directly. On macOS, the team usedDS_Store metadata to discover filenames and expand the search across folders.

Their test collected SSH keys, .env files, npm tokens, and private documents. The demonstration sent data to a local receiver. An attacker could instead use a remote server.

Delivery required opening a malicious local page, potentially through a link generated by the assistant itself. These findings sit alongside earlier Claude sandbox escape coverage.

Forever Security says Cursor patched its flaw on October 1. GitHub independently fixed the spoofing issue in Copilot 1.1.29 on October 13, after researchers confirmed it in version 1.1.27.

At publication, Codex and VS Code remained unpatched. Microsoft rejected the report on Workspace Trust, while OpenAI did not respond. Anthropic accepted its issue after an initial rejection, but the report gives no clear patch status.

The vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each […]

The post Palo Alto Confirms Active PHP2Shell Exploitation Targeting Exposed PAN-OS Management Interfaces appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. In its October 29, 2026, update, Unit 42 said it independently verified attacker tools used to combine the PHP flaws with a Linux kernel vulnerability and gain root access.

The vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each carry a critical CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. They can allow remote code execution without a login. Palo Alto said roughly 0.02% of its global installed base had public management interfaces configured and was impacted. Its teams have contacted those customers individually, according to the Unit 42 threat brief.

The confirmation updates the earlier picture covered in Cyber Security News’ report on PHP vulnerabilities affecting PAN-OS, when the vendor had not reported malicious exploitation against its products.

PHP2Shell Enables Remote Code Execution

Both flaws involve unsafe memory handling when PHP stops processing a request after an error. CVE-2026-109618 affects out-of-memory handling through longjmp(), a function that jumps out of the current operation. That sudden exit can leave request data partly initialized. Cleanup routines may then read or act on that invalid data, creating a path to code execution.

CVE-2026-109619 leaves shared internal state pointing to memory that PHP has already freed. A later request handled by the same worker can reach those stale references before normal setup resets them. Attackers can use this condition to make the process execute their code.

The PHP Group’s security advisory identifies PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed deployments as exposed. Fixed releases are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Unit 42 counted more than 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable worldwide. That figure describes possible PHP exposure, not confirmed breaches or affected Palo Alto firewalls.

Dream Research reported finding campaign artifacts showing 25 compromised PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. The count included three systems in a US government-affiliated environment.

The attacker used a custom PHP2Shell implementation aimed at the PAN-OS management web server. Crafted upload requests created memory pressure, leaked an address, and manipulated memory structures to execute commands as the restricted nobody user. A separate Linux kernel flaw, Fragnesia, tracked as CVE-2026-46300, then enabled root access.

Cyber Security News’ report on the 25-server campaign explains the wider impact. Dream found evidence of webshell placement, internal tunneling, LDAP credential extraction, and Active Directory enumeration. However, it could not confirm whether later password spraying or attempts to create backdoor accounts succeeded.

This confirmation should not be confused with Unit 42’s retracted October 23 update. That earlier account linked activity at a European government agency to PHP2Shell, but investigators could not establish that these specific flaws provided initial access. The October 29 update separately confirms the PAN-OS campaign.

PAN-OS Patches and Immediate Protection

Palo Alto’s security advisory limits the affected surface to the management HTTPS interface and XML API. PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama are covered. GlobalProtect portals, gateways, Clientless VPN and Captive Portal are not affected by these PHP flaws. A dataplane interface is exposed only when a management profile is attached.

Administrators should immediately remove public management access, allow only trusted internal IP addresses, and install the correct PAN-OS hotfix. Fixed options include 12.2.4-h1, 12.1.10-h3, 11.2.16-h1, 11.1.16-h4 and 10.2.18-h13, with additional fixes for other maintenance releases. Palo Alto says these updates address both PHP vulnerabilities and interrupt the observed chain.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.description:
Trezor has warned that a suspected hardware implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 could steal recovery phrases and send them over a mobile network. The warning covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onward, although only one suspected device has been reported. In its October 30 security notice, Trezor urged affected users […]

The post Trezor Warns of Suspected Spy Implant in Crypto Wallet That Could Steal Recovery Phrases appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Trezor has warned that a suspected hardware implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 could steal recovery phrases and send them over a mobile network. The warning covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onward, although only one suspected device has been reported.

In its October 30 security notice, Trezor urged affected users to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed. The company has not examined the device and has received no reports of stolen funds from CryptoBilis buyers.

The March cutoff is a precautionary scope for customer action, not proof that every device sold since then was altered. The confirmed extent and operation of the suspected Trezor implant remain subject to laboratory examination.

Suspected Implant Targets the Wallet Screen

The report came from a customer in Indonesia who bought the Safe 5 through CryptoBilis on Tokopedia in August 2026. Trezor received the disclosure on October 28, reviewed photos, and interviewed the customer by video. The device is being sent to its security lab.[trezor]

According to the report, an extra circuit board sits between the wallet’s main board and screen. It contains a cellular module and antenna. The added hardware allegedly reads information shown on the display, including the wallet backup, and sends it over a mobile network while the device is plugged in.

That would make the screen connection a possible theft point. Rather than needing to break the wallet’s core security, an attacker could capture the recovery words when they appear during setup. This remains a reported method, not a finding confirmed through Trezor’s own testing.

A stolen recovery phrase can let someone restore a wallet elsewhere and control its funds. Cybersecurity News has also covered fake crypto wallet screens that seek the same secret through false recovery prompts. The suspected implant would target displayed information instead of relying on a user entering words into fake software.

The warning follows a separate investigation involving Ledger wallets supplied by CryptoBilis. According to Trezor, Ledger began investigating customer fund losses on October 9 and later confirmed physical tampering in some devices.

Cybersecurity News previously reported Ledger’s confirmation of an unauthorized hardware implant in a CryptoBilis device. Trezor removed CryptoBilis from its authorized reseller network on October 9 and began checking customer devices.

Despite the shared reseller, Trezor has not identified the attackers or confirmed that the same group targeted both brands. It is working with Ledger and other parties investigating the incident. Trezor also credited SEAL 911, the Security Alliance’s emergency response service, for helping with the report and customer support planning.

The customer who reported the suspected Trezor implant had already moved his funds before finding it. Trezor says it has received no reports involving other resellers. Its warning also covers stores selling devices supplied by CryptoBilis, not just purchases made directly from the reseller.

What Affected Trezor Owners Should Do

Trezor says moving the existing wallet backup onto another device does not fix the risk. Users need a fresh wallet with a newly generated seed, then must transfer their funds to it. Anyone who has not set up an affected device should leave it unused and never enter an existing recovery phrase.

If another secure hardware wallet is unavailable, Trezor recommends temporarily using a software wallet or familiar exchange. Its sending guide explains the transfer process. Users should carefully check the full receiving address before sending funds.

Customers should not rely on weighing or opening their devices to rule out tampering. Trezor says weight differences can have other causes and there is no dependable home inspection method.

Eligible CryptoBilis buyers can contact official Trezor Support for a replacement shipped directly or a voucher covering a new device. They should keep the original wallet. Trezor also warns that scammers may exploit the incident through fake emails, letters, or calls. Support will never ask for a recovery phrase.

TRM Labs describes the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft ever recorded, with most of the stolen funds transferred out within about 20 minutes of the attack. Its investigation attributes the operation to TraderTraitor, a […]

The post Binance Faces Largest Crypto Heist – $6.36 Billion Reportedly Stolen by North Korean Group appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Binance reportedly lost approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency on October 29, 2026, after an attacker drained wallets across ten blockchains.

TRM Labs describes the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft ever recorded, with most of the stolen funds transferred out within about 20 minutes of the attack.

Its investigation attributes the operation to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group known for targeting cryptocurrency platforms and financial organizations to steal digital assets.

According to TRM, Binance acknowledged a security incident, suspended withdrawals on several networks, and said user funds were safe. The reported loss exceeds four times the $1.5 billion Bybit theft.

Earlier reporting on the Bybit multistage attack investigation explains how compromised infrastructure enabled another major cryptocurrency theft, although Binance’s initial entry point remains unknown.

Binance Hit by Biggest Crypto Heist in History

Researchers from TRM identified malicious sweeper contract activity that allowed the attacker to repeatedly drain a Binance Ethereum hot wallet.

Their published Binance hack analysis describes harmful smart contract code rather than a named endpoint malware family. TRM attributes the operation to TraderTraitor with high confidence, citing blockchain records and intelligence gathered outside the blockchain.

Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft. The operator received three small Tornado Cash withdrawals starting October 28, then deployed and tested attack code against several wallets.

A final rehearsal preceded installation of the same code on a Binance hot wallet by approximately four hours, suggesting a planned operation rather than an opportunistic transfer.

The first recorded theft occurred on the XRP Ledger between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, when five Binance wallets transferred 233.46 million XRP.

Solana and Optimism transfers followed. At 20:20 UTC, a Bitcoin hot wallet sent 18,270 BTC to the attacker, who immediately split the funds into smaller amounts through a peel chain.

Ethereum activity exposed the attack’s central technical feature: EIP-7702 delegation. This mechanism lets a wallet authorize smart contract code to control its behavior.

At 20:20 UTC, the operator submitted 50 authorizations signed by Binance’s wallet, directing it toward an attacker-controlled sweeper. Unlike previously documented TraderTraitor cloud compromise campaigns, this report does not establish how access was first obtained.

Each authorization covered a consecutive nonce, the counter used to track wallet activity. Preparing multiple signatures increased the chance that one would match the wallet’s current counter when executed.

One matched. Three minutes and 24 seconds later, a single sweep transferred 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including 1.615 billion USDT.

The delegation remained active, allowing six further sweeps as fresh deposits arrived. The compromised wallet also controlled execution for another Binance smart account, enabling the removal of 823 million USDC.

Meanwhile, wallets across other networks produced ordinary signed transfers. TRM therefore suspects compromised signing infrastructure, not an Ethereum-only authorization phishing incident. Binance had not published a root cause in the report.

Frozen Funds, Laundering Activity, and Defensive Priorities

TRM valued the stolen assets at their prices when transferred, producing the $6.36 billion estimate. Ethereum accounted for approximately $3.79 billion, followed by Bitcoin at $1.47 billion and Tron at $628 million.

Its figures reflect blockchain observations through October 30 at 00:30 UTC, meaning subsequent movements or price changes could alter later assessments.

Issuers and network responders restricted approximately $2.7 billion. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial froze stablecoins, while Arbitrum’s Security Council removed 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB from the attacker’s control.

These actions limited access to funds; they did not establish that the assets had been returned to Binance. The attacker also converted approximately 325 million USDT into roughly 122,300 ETH through market makers and trading contracts.

Another wallet deposited 60 million USDT into Aave and borrowed about 19,760 ETH. Earlier investigations into Lazarus cryptocurrency laundering networks illustrate why tracing counterparties matters, although those findings should not be treated as proof of participants in this incident.

TRM recommends screening deposits and trading counterparties, alerting on unexpected wallet delegations, and rejecting unapproved EIP-7702 authorizations.

Exchanges should separate signing systems and approval paths across blockchains and wallet tiers. Treasury teams also need tested revocation procedures because a malicious delegation can keep redirecting incoming funds after the initial theft.

articles.title: Unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Claude Code Relays Disable AI Sandboxes and Redirect Enterprise Data
articles.description:
An unauthorized AI relay service is installing genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools on company computers, then changing their settings to send requests through third-party servers. The setup also removes sandbox controls, creating a path for sensitive business data to leave approved systems. Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team documented the activity in an October […]

The post Unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Claude Code Relays Disable AI Sandboxes and Redirect Enterprise Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An unauthorized AI relay service is installing genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools on company computers, then changing their settings to send requests through third-party servers. The setup also removes sandbox controls, creating a path for sensitive business data to leave approved systems.

Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team documented the activity in an October 29 report. Researchers observed the service across a dozen organizations since early 2026.

Most were in mainland China, with other deployments involving multinational firms connected to South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia. Affected industries include semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, electronics, petrochemicals, and data center services.

The key distinction is configuration. Researchers found neither a modified client nor a vulnerability in Codex or Claude Code. The genuine tools follow settings introduced by the relay.

Sandbox Controls and Credentials Replaced

Users appear to run a setup command themselves, often within minutes to half an hour of installing an AI coding tool through npm. Researchers found no automated or exploit-based delivery.

A fileless PowerShell or bash script arrives from a lookalike domain such as vibe.aiok[.]me. It checks for Node.js and the requested coding tool, installs missing components, and then applies the relay settings. Because users receive a working application, the extra setup can look routine.

The script rewrites ~/.codex/config.toml or ~/.claude/settings.json. It changes base_url or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to relay-controlled infrastructure and installs relay-issued credentials. User-level environment variables preserve these settings after a restart.

For teams examining unfamiliar setup scripts, ANY.RUN’s interactive sandbox offers a separate analysis environment with live interaction and reporting. This differs from the coding agent’s own sandbox, which limits actions during normal use.

In Codex, the script sets sandbox_mode to danger-full-access. It also enables network access for the write sandbox and disables telemetry and error reporting through DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1. These changes remove safeguards while suppressing signals that might otherwise reach the vendors.

On one host, the script ran claude /logout, removed ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, then ran claude /login. This cleared an existing session before relay credentials took over. Researchers could not establish whether every deployment followed that sequence, reads the Symantec report.

The service rotated through at least eight domains imitating OpenAI or Anthropic services. Its subscription-style Claude tokens could suggest pooled account resale, but researchers said this was not proof of its business model.

Related reporting on Codex and Claude Code hijacking through Downloads folders shows a separate route to endpoint redirection. Here, however, the setup script changes the settings directly rather than relying on malicious instructions inside files.

The relay can see prompts, files, and secrets sent through it, and could alter responses. With sandbox protection removed, a malicious response could lead to commands running with the user’s account privileges. Symantec found no evidence that the operator had exploited this position. Observed redirection must not be confused with confirmed data theft.

Separate coverage of AI coding agent security flaws highlights why permission controls matter. This case adds another concern: genuine software can become unsafe when an unapproved service controls its settings.

Defenders should review endpoint URLs, sandbox settings, and user-level credential variables. PowerShell or bash download-and-execute commands shortly after npm installation deserve attention.

Network monitoring should flag coding tools contacting destinations outside approved AI endpoints. Relay-issued variables also warrant review because other applications may inherit them. These checks help separate sanctioned deployments from unapproved access without treating every legitimate AI installation as malicious activity.

Investigate suspicious scripts before they reach developer systems. Explore ANY.RUN’s interactive analysis features to observe behavior, inspect network activity, and support incident triage.

The post CISA Warns of GitLab Integer Overflow Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-97229. This GitLab vulnerability could allow code execution without logging in.

CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 29, 2026, confirming evidence of active exploitation and raising the urgency for organizations running affected GitLab servers.

The vulnerability affects GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. It involves an integer overflow or wraparound caused by insufficient checks on regular expressions inside CI/CD configurations. A specially crafted expression could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server.

Cybersecuritynews.com previously covered the technical details in its report on the GitLab code execution vulnerability. Regular expressions are text patterns used to match or filter data. In this case, the dangerous input reaches GitLab’s regular expression compiler through a CI/CD configuration.

These configurations define automated development tasks. Processing a malicious pattern could affect the server itself, not just cause a pipeline task to fail.

GitLab Integer Overflow Vulnerability Exploited

An integer overflow occurs when a calculation produces a number outside the range a program can store. The resulting value can become unexpectedly small or negative. MITRE’s CWE-190 description explains that these errors can cause crashes, memory corruption, or unauthorized code execution, depending on how the software uses the value.

GitLab assigned the flaw a maximum CVSS score of 10.0. Earlier reporting identified affected versions as 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.4, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. Those branches received fixes on October 12. Administrators should review their installed release and follow the current vendor update guidance.

The supplied catalog entry lists November 1, 2026, as the remediation deadline and marks forensic triage as required under BOD 26-04. It lists ransomware use as unknown. That status does not establish a ransomware link, and CISA’s public alert does not identify attackers, victims, or the scale of exploitation.

CISA’s October 29 alert explains that BOD 26-04 requires federal civilian agencies to prioritize high-risk vulnerabilities on exposed assets.

The directive also requires, where applicable, checks for signs that attackers compromised a system before updates were applied. CISA encourages other organizations to adopt similar risk-based patching practices.

Administrators must also avoid confusing this issue with CVE-2026-110264, a separate GitLab regular expression vulnerability disclosed later in October.

Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of that separate GitLab server vulnerability explains that installing the earlier CVE-2026-97229 update does not fix the newer issue.

Reviewing both advisories helps teams choose an update that addresses both vulnerabilities rather than leaving another code execution path open on their GitLab servers.

articles.description:

Ivanti confirmed attacks against a limited number of customers and released additional fixes on October 29, 2026, following its initial October patches. Volexity tracked UTA0576 activity to October 3 and, during […]

The post Ivanti Connect Secure 0-Days Exploited in the Wild to Gain Unauthenticated Root Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are chaining zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances to gain unauthenticated root access, exposing stored credentials and sensitive Active Directory data.

Ivanti confirmed attacks against a limited number of customers and released additional fixes on October 29, 2026, following its initial October patches.

Volexity tracked UTA0576 activity to October 3 and, during an October 5 investigation, identified a compromised, fully patched Ivanti appliance running version 22.8R2.4 (Build 19097) during an investigation on October 5, highlighting the flaws’ ability to bypass existing protections.

According to Volexity’s technical analysis, the attack began with an authentication bypass in welcome.cgi, the public login script. A mismatch between the requested URL and the X-DSCGI-PATH header let the attacker reach a protected upload handler without signing in.

The upload handler, wu.cgi, wrote incoming content to a predictable temporary location before checking whether it was a valid ZIP file. The attacker uploaded a Perl script and sent parallel requests to execute it before the appliance deleted it. This timing flaw delivered code execution as the appliance’s cgi-server user.

The attacker then abused the privileged dsinvoked service. By changing library code in memory and altering a maintenance task in the DSCache configuration store, UTA0576 caused the service to run attacker-controlled code as root. The payload then restored the changed settings and memory to hide its activity.

Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Days Exploited

Earlier CybersecurityNews coverage of the Ivanti authentication bypass (CVE-2026-104935) detailed the initial disclosure and affected releases.

Ivanti also tracks CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS 8.6) for authentication bypass and code execution, CVE-2026-111357 (CVSS 8.8) for privilege escalation, and CVE-2026-118527 (CVSS 4.3) for a predictable-filename weakness.

UTA0576 did not install a backdoor or web shell. Instead, it repeated the exploit chain for each command and received results through HTTPS responses. This reduced the need to leave persistent access tools on disk.

After gaining control, the attacker extracted stored domain credentials and used the VPN appliance’s Active Directory service account to query internal systems. Targets included Windows LAPS administrator passwords, BitLocker recovery keys, and password-containing attributes.

The operation also involved password spraying, username collection, and packet analysis to recover credentials from network traffic. Related reporting on Active Directory credential theft details how the compromised gateway became a starting point for wider access. Volexity assessed that these actions prepared the attacker to move into other systems.

The October 29 update supplied for this report identifies 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6 as releases resolving all disclosed vulnerabilities on those branches. Administrators should follow Ivanti’s advisory and select the correct upgrade for their appliance platform.

Detection needs more than a clean integrity check. Volexity found that memory-only changes and restored settings escaped Ivanti’s Integrity Checker.

Defenders should examine unusual welcome.cgi traffic, mismatched request paths and headers, suspicious files in /tmp/, and connections from the VPN into internal systems.

Suspected compromises require memory, disk, and network analysis because the attacker also removed selected debug and audit log entries. A clean check alone cannot rule out this compromise.

The post Microsoft Fixes Remote Desktop Connection Failures Following Recent Updates appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft resolved a Windows 11 issue that blocked non-admin users from connecting via Remote Desktop when Administrator protection was enabled, releasing fixes on October 28, 2026, for connection failures with error 0xC000000D.

The bug appeared after the September 22 non-security preview update, KB5124010, or later updates. Affected users could see the message, “The token that was passed to the function is invalid.”

Microsoft’s release health notice identifies enterprise-managed computers acting as Remote Desktop hosts as the main systems affected.

Microsoft opened its investigation on October 13. As detailed in Cyber Security News’ earlier coverage of the Remote Desktop connection failures, the problem prevented standard users from reaching remote systems where Administrator protection was active. The failure could occur regardless of how administrators enabled that feature.

Microsoft lists Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, 26H1, and 26H2 as affected platforms. Its notice does not list Windows Server as affected by this particular issue. That scope matters because other recent Remote Desktop problems have involved different Windows releases and separate update failures.

Administrator protection limits how applications gain administrator rights. Instead of leaving those rights available throughout a session, it grants temporary access for approved tasks.

Microsoft Fixes Windows 11 Remote Desktop Failures

Cyber Security News’ explanation of Windows 11 Administrator protection describes how this approach helps reduce the risk of malware making unwanted system changes.

The setting may already be active in managed environments. Microsoft says its Windows 11 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 security baselines enable Administrator protection by default unless an organization changes the policy. Businesses using those baselines should therefore check affected hosts rather than assume the feature was never enabled.

According to Microsoft’s release health advisory, updates released on or after October 28 resolve the issue. Systems running an applicable fixed update no longer need the temporary workaround. Microsoft recommends installing the latest security update available for the device to receive relevant fixes and improvements.

The KB5127936 release notes explicitly confirm the Remote Desktop repair. This non-security preview update applies to Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, raising their builds to 26200.9818 and 26300.9818, respectively.

Administrators managing other affected versions should check the package offered for their specific Windows release instead of treating KB5127936 as a universal installer.

For affected computers still running older updates, Microsoft allows administrators to temporarily turn off Administrator protection through their existing management tools. The documented workaround involves resetting the “User Account Control Type Of Admin Approval Mode” policy through Microsoft Intune or Group Policy.

Because this workaround turns off a security feature, it should remain temporary. After deploying the appropriate fixed update, IT teams should verify Remote Desktop access using a non-admin account and review any policy changes made during troubleshooting. This confirms remote access works without leaving the earlier workaround in place unnecessarily.

articles.title: Researcher Uses Claude AI to Extract Internal Anthropic Binary and Recover Google Cloud Token
articles.description:
A security researcher got Claude AI to hand over an internal Anthropic program and a memory dump that held pieces of a working Google Cloud token. The findings were published on October 29, 2026. They show how a helpful chatbot can expose the systems that run it. The work started with a plain question about […]

The post Researcher Uses Claude AI to Extract Internal Anthropic Binary and Recover Google Cloud Token appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A security researcher got Claude AI to hand over an internal Anthropic program and a memory dump that held pieces of a working Google Cloud token.

The findings were published on October 29, 2026. They show how a helpful chatbot can expose the systems that run it. The work started with a plain question about the sandbox, the locked-down space where Claude runs code.

Claude’s answers led the researcher to a downloaded binary, a memory file, and a rebuilt Google service account ID token that Google accepted as valid. Anthropic later said the sandbox findings did not break its threat model.

Chris Davis, a senior security consultant at Bishop Fox, wrote up the research. Researchers at Bishop Fox noted that the post was meant as an interesting look inside Claude’s sandbox, not a formal vulnerability disclosure.

No malware was involved. Everything in the Bishop Fox blog post came from normal chat requests and some careful follow-up work.

Researcher Uses Claude AI

Davis asked Claude, running on an Enterprise account, whether its sandbox was a virtual machine. Claude said it was a gVisor container running Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, and it listed mounted folders and tools.

In later answers it named a program at /process_api running as process ID 1. It described the program as a Rust-built control daemon that handles processes, file mounts and host communication.

Davis then found that the file-download feature accepted an absolute path. When he asked for /process_api, the service returned a 3,179,528-byte file that appeared to be Anthropic’s own sandbox orchestration binary.

He reverse-engineered it and confirmed that Claude’s description was accurate. He also repeated the tests in unrelated chat sessions to rule out made-up answers.

Next, he asked Claude for the full memory of process ID 1, framing the request as a test comparing human and computer memory. Claude produced a dump that contained broken pieces of JSON Web Tokens.

This resembles the earlier Claude Code sandbox bypass that exposed credentials, but here the sandbox itself leaked the secrets.

Some signature bytes were missing, so Davis wrote a Python script that tried candidate values against Google’s public OAuth keys until the signature verified.

About one in three memory requests produced usable token material. The script found two token types: EdDSA tokens made by Anthropic’s systems and Google Cloud service account ID tokens. Google’s token-info API accepted the rebuilt Google token.

Why the Network Bypass and Anthropic’s Response Matter

The binary refused connections that came from inside its own container. It ran with a –block-local-connections flag and reset requests from 127.0.0.1.

Davis noticed the container held the CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_NET_RAW permissions. Claude’s safeguards blocked a direct request to build a tunnel.

A short hint, “IP_FREEBIND,” was enough for Claude to work out the method on its own. This looks like an indirect prompt injection attack in spirit, because a small nudge steered the model.

Claude set up a virtual network address and connected from it, so the service saw a source that was not local. The /mount_root endpoint answered with a 101 Switching Protocols reply, which confirmed the block was bypassed.

Davis stopped there. Attempts to mount file systems failed, and he found no other use for the tokens. He submitted six observations through Anthropic’s bug bounty program.

Anthropic said the sandbox items did not meet its security threshold, and it marked the two Enterprise control items informational or duplicate.

One of those items let a user change a profile name field that the web client had locked. Aviatrix’s threat research summary describes the same chain as a path from conversation to credential harvesting.

The reasoning behind Anthropic’s answer is that its security boundaries sit outside the untrusted sandbox. Even so, Davis suggested several fixes.

They include blocking model access to infrastructure memory, wiping credentials from memory once they are no longer needed, and limiting the download API to user folders such as /mnt/user-data.

He also suggested removing the extra network permissions and treating every local interface address as local. For defenders, the lesson is that AI helpers can reveal their own internals when asked politely.

Anthropic’s own testing shows how capable these models have become, including Claude building working exploit chains in lab conditions. Teams should keep secrets out of any process an AI tool can read.

articles.title: Top 10 Best UEBA Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:

UEBA baselines how every user and entity normally acts, then surfaces the deviation: the service account suddenly browsing HR files, the engineer’s badge in one country and login in another. cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Stolen credentials beat most controls because they are the control which is why behavior became the detection substrate. UEBA baselines how every user and entity normally acts, then surfaces the deviation: the service account suddenly browsing HR files, the engineer’s badge in one country and login in another.

One honest note up front: our source list named ten brands, but Exabeam and LogRhythm merged into a single vendor, so we rank nine platforms honestly rather than pad. Exabeam takes 1 on the lineage that defined the category.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Exabeam (including LogRhythm) timeline-stitched behavioral analytics remain the reference.

• Podium: Exabeam, Securonix (cloud-native UEBA-SIEM), Microsoft (estate-bundled behavioral analytics).

• Honest count: nine platforms, not ten the Exabeam–LogRhythm merger collapsed two roster slots.

• Market reality: standalone UEBA is nearly extinct it now lives inside SIEMs, identity platforms, and data-security stacks; the buying question is which stack gets your behavioral layer.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: baseline/model quality, insider-threat depth, entity coverage (users, hosts, service accounts, machines), SIEM/stack integration, investigation ergonomics, and pricing accessibility.

Weights: model quality 25%, insider depth 20%, entity coverage 20%, integration 20%, ergonomics 15%.

The 2026 UEBA Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Exabeam (incl. LogRhythm) — Best Behavioral Timelines

Snapshot: Identity-based pricing | Machine-built session timelines | Merged LogRhythm install base

Why it earns 1: Exabeam’s timelines remain the category’s signature: every event in a user’s session stitched automatically into a narrative, with each anomaly scored in context the hours of manual log correlation an insider investigation used to cost, done by machine.

The LogRhythm merger adds a large mid-market base; buyers should confirm which product line carries which capability forward.

Pros: Timeline reconstruction; insider/credential-abuse depth; lateral-movement chains.

Cons: Post-merger product-line clarity needs probing.

Bottom line: The investigation-speed benchmark in behavioral analytics.

2. Securonix — Best Cloud-Native UEBA-SIEM

Snapshot: Identity-based pricing | UEBA-born SIEM, Snowflake-backed | Threat-chain models

Why it ranks here: Securonix grew from UEBA into a full SIEM without losing the behavioral spine: threat chains that link anomalies into attack narratives, identity-priced licensing, and cloud-native scale.

For buyers wanting behavior-first detection as the SIEM rather than inside one, it’s the purest expression available.

Pros: UEBA-native architecture; threat-chain correlation; pricing clarity.

Cons: Pure-play fighting suite bundles.

Bottom line: Behavior analytics that grew a SIEM, not the reverse.

3. Microsoft — Best Estate-Bundled UEBA

Snapshot: Bundled in Sentinel/Defender/Entra licensing | Estate-wide identity signal | Copilot-era fusion

Why it ranks here: Microsoft’s behavioral analytics ride the estate: Sentinel UEBA entities, Defender’s identity-threat detections, Entra’s risk engine all drawing on sign-in, email, endpoint, and collaboration signal no third party sees as natively.

The marginal cost is near zero for E5-class estates; the ceiling is depth tuning versus the specialists.

Pros: Signal breadth; bundled economics; identity-risk fusion.

Cons: Specialist-depth tuning and insider-program workflow trail leaders.

Bottom line: The default behavioral layer for Microsoft-first estates.

4. Varonis — Best Data-Centric Behavior Analytics

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Data-access behavioral baselines | Automated remediation

Why it ranks here: Varonis watches behavior where damage happens the data: who touches which files, mailboxes, and SaaS objects, baselined per user, with alerts on the access pattern that precedes exfiltration and automation that revokes exposure.

For insider-risk programs centered on data theft, it’s the sharpest lens in the ranking.

Pros: Data-access depth; exposure remediation; insider-exfil focus.

Cons: Data-centric scope pair for network/endpoint behavior.

Bottom line: UEBA aimed at the crown jewels.

5. Vectra AI — Best Network+Identity Attack Signal

Snapshot: Per-entity pricing | Attack Signal Intelligence | Hybrid/cloud coverage

Why it ranks here: Vectra detects behavior from the wire and the identity plane: AI models tuned to attacker tradecraft (privilege abuse, lateral movement, C2) rather than generic anomalies, scored per entity and prioritized by attack urgency.

Less an insider-program tool, more a precision early-warning radar for active intrusion behavior.

Pros: Attacker-behavior precision; low alert noise; hybrid reach.

Cons: Insider-workflow depth is not the design center.

Bottom line: Behavioral detection aimed at intruders, not just insiders.

6. Splunk UBA — Best Splunk-Estate Behavioral Add-On

Snapshot: Add-on licensing | ML models over Splunk data | ES integration

Why it ranks here: For Splunk estates, UBA layers unsupervised models over data already ingested, feeding risk-scored anomalies into Enterprise Security’s correlation. The value case is incremental: no new data pipeline, familiar workflow.

Standalone ambition is limited by design this is Splunk’s behavioral organ, not an independent platform.

Pros: Zero-new-pipeline economics; ES fusion; model breadth.

Cons: Tied to Splunk’s cost base and roadmap.

Bottom line: The behavioral layer Splunk shops already half-own.

7. Gurucul — Best Model-Transparent Risk Engine

Snapshot: Identity/platform pricing | Open ML model library | Unified risk scoring

Why it ranks here: Gurucul’s differentiator is transparency: a large, inspectable model library buyers can tune, extend, or audit valuable where compliance demands explainable scoring plus unified risk across users, entities, and access.

It punches above its brand weight technically; market gravity is the constraint.

Pros: Model transparency; risk unification; tuning freedom.

Cons: Smaller ecosystem than suite rivals.

Bottom line: The explainability pick for regulated insider programs.

8. Rapid7 — Best Bundled Mid-Market UEBA

Snapshot: Per-asset bundle | InsightIDR-native UEBA | MDR pairing

Why it ranks here: Rapid7 bakes behavioral detection into InsightIDR at mid-market economics: user baselines, impossible-travel and credential-abuse detections, deception points, all in the per-asset price. Depth ceilings apply, but for teams buying their first behavioral layer, the bundled path is the realistic one.

Pros: Bundle economics; operational simplicity; MDR option.

Cons: Specialist-depth ceiling.

Bottom line: First behavioral analytics most mid-market teams actually deploy.

9. Forcepoint — Best Risk-Adaptive DLP Behavior

Snapshot: Per-user suite | Behavior-driven DLP policy | Insider-risk lineage

Why it ranks here: Forcepoint’s behavioral engine exists to modulate data controls: risk-adaptive protection that tightens DLP enforcement as a user’s risk score rises printing spikes, USB anomalies, pre-resignation patterns.

It’s UEBA as a policy actuator rather than an investigation platform, strongest inside data-protection programs.

Pros: Behavior-to-enforcement loop; insider-risk lineage.

Cons: Analytics scoped to the data-protection mission.

Bottom line: Behavior analytics that move the DLP dial.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Pick the Stack That Owns Your Behavioral Layer

Standalone UEBA is a shrinking aisle; the real decision is which platform family hosts your behavioral brain.

SIEM-centered SOCs choose between the merged Exabeam lineage, Securonix, or their incumbent’s add-on; data-theft-centered insider programs start at Varonis or Forcepoint; Microsoft estates should exhaust bundled capability before buying anything.

Pilot with your own worst cases: replay a known insider incident and a credential-compromise drill through each finalist and compare time-to-narrative how long until an analyst can tell the story.

Interrogate baseline hygiene (how models handle job changes, contractors, service accounts the false-positive factories), demand explainable scoring if HR or legal will act on alerts, and settle the Exabeam–LogRhythm product-line question in writing before contracting.

Finally, align privacy counsel early: behavioral monitoring of employees carries works-council and jurisdiction obligations that are cheaper to design in than retrofit.

FAQs

What are the best UEBA tools in 2026? Exabeam (with LogRhythm) leads, with Securonix, Microsoft, Varonis, Vectra AI, Splunk UBA, Gurucul, Rapid7, and Forcepoint by stack fit.

Why nine platforms instead of ten? Exabeam and LogRhythm merged into one vendor we rank the merged entity once.

Is standalone UEBA dead? Mostly absorbed: it lives inside SIEMs, identity platforms, and data-security suites buy the behavioral layer where your detection stack already lives.

UEBA versus ITDR what’s the difference? Overlapping lenses: UEBA baselines all behavior broadly; ITDR focuses on identity-infrastructure attack paths (AD, Entra, Okta). Mature programs run both signals.

What makes UEBA pilots fail? Dirty identity data and unmanaged service accounts clean the identity inventory first, or baselines learn noise.

Verdict

Nine platforms, one merger honestly counted, one principle: behavior is the only signal credentials can’t fake for long.

Exabeam for timelines, Securonix for behavior-born SIEM, Microsoft for bundled estate signal, Varonis for the data lens, Vectra for intruder behavior, Splunk and Rapid7 for their estates, Gurucul for explainability, Forcepoint for enforcement replay your worst day through the finalists and buy the one that tells the story fastest.
