articles.title: Hackers Chain PHP2Shell and Linux Kernel Exploits to Gain Root Access on 25 Servers
articles.description:
Hackers combined PHP2Shell vulnerabilities with a Linux kernel exploit to gain root access on 25 servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including three systems in a US government-affiliated environment. Dream researchers uncovered the campaign’s files on October 25, revealing a path from exposed firewall management interfaces to internal Active Directory services. […]

The post Hackers Chain PHP2Shell and Linux Kernel Exploits to Gain Root Access on 25 Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers combined PHP2Shell vulnerabilities with a Linux kernel exploit to gain root access on 25 servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including three systems in a US government-affiliated environment. Dream researchers uncovered the campaign’s files on October 25, revealing a path from exposed firewall management interfaces to internal Active Directory services.

According to Dream’s investigation, the list includes custom exploits, target lists, attack logs, and roughly 40 post-compromise scripts. The affected firewall vendor has been notified, but it has withheld its name and vulnerable software versions for security reasons.

PHP2Shell Exploit Chain Gained Root

The attack paired PHP2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, with Fragnesia, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw tracked as CVE-2026-46300. Dream described the PHP2Shell code as a custom, nonpublic implementation tailored to the targeted firewall platform, rather than a copy of a known public exploit.

PHP2Shell targeted PHP’s session.upload_progress feature within the firewall’s appweb management server. Through several stages, the attacker exhausted memory, leaked a memory address, and manipulated damaged memory structures to run commands as the restricted nobody user. Fragnesia then changed local authentication data, allowing the attacker to become root without a password.

The full chain reportedly installed a root webshell in under 15 minutes. Although the final request connected both exploits, earlier requests prepared memory for execution. Cyber Security News previously covered PHP2Shell exploitation and the underlying flaws, providing context for this campaign.

Using FOFA, the attacker identified about 19,000 internet-facing firewalls. Roughly 5,000 returned version information, and filtering by location and software version narrowed the list to 240 targets. The operation ultimately compromised 24 firewalls, leaving webshells on 22 without further recorded activity beyond that initial access.

Two firewalls linked to a US government-affiliated organization received closer attention. Configuration data exposed internal systems and network details. After the first firewall crashed, the attacker compromised the second on October 24 and established a reverse SSH tunnel forwarding eight internal ports. Startup settings allowed the tunnel to survive reboots.

At 11:35 UTC that day, the attacker used the same exploit chain through the tunnel against an internal firewall management server. This became the 25th compromised system and exposed centrally managed firewall settings and credentials.

From there, the attacker decrypted an LDAP service account password and listed Active Directory users and groups. Password spraying, backdoor account creation, and SAML signing key theft were attempted, but their success remains unknown. These limits matter when assessing Active Directory attack paths, rather than assuming full domain control.

Recovered systems contained Claude Code and an aiscan setup configured with DeepSeek and Kimi. Chinese-language prompts and UTC+8 timestamps supported Dream’s assessment of possible Chinese links. However, researchers found no direct proof that AI wrote the exploits, established no named actor attribution, and did not describe the campaign as fully autonomous.

Dream recommends deploying relevant patches under vendor guidance. The broader concern is stolen access: fixing the entry point does not establish whether credentials, webshells, or tunnels remain usable. Investigators must distinguish confirmed credential theft and directory access from the still unverified outcomes of the attacker’s later identity attacks.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.description:
A leak of records covering more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors has exposed contact details, work assignments, and links to sensitive operations, including undercover ICE work. Published on October 28, the archive reveals far more than a staff directory, offering a view of internal teams and reporting lines. Distributed Denial of […]

The post Hackers Leak Records of 41,000 DHS Personnel, Exposing Undercover ICE Agents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A leak of records covering more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors has exposed contact details, work assignments, and links to sensitive operations, including undercover ICE work. Published on October 28, the archive reveals far more than a staff directory, offering a view of internal teams and reporting lines.

Distributed Denial of Secrets released the collection under the name Icepick, crediting a group calling itself Department of Peace. Researcher and journalist Maia Arson Crimew built a search tool for the records. The nonprofit says the release supports public oversight, journalism, and requests for government records.

DHS Data Leak

According to reports, the records were last updated on August 19, 2026. They include names, email addresses, phone numbers, office locations, job titles, and supervisors. The files cover DHS and seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

CBP accounts for more than half of the records, while roughly 10,000 relate to ICE. About 6,200 cover US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 concern CISA. The collection represents about one seventh of the department’s workforce, not every DHS worker.

The most sensitive details appear in more than 55,000 permission groups, which help control access to internal systems. WIRED identified 39 Homeland Security Investigations employees in groups containing “CUC,” a term government court records link to certified undercover operations. Other groups reference wiretaps, phone data analysis, and surveillance tools.

DDoSecrets says the information came from an Okta single sign-on service used by DHS. However, Reuters could not confirm that claim. Okta said its systems were secure and that it had no evidence its data or systems had been compromised. No confirmed entry method has been disclosed.

That distinction matters. A claimed theft from an organization’s identity service does not establish a breach of the identity provider itself. Separate reporting on attacks targeting Okta identity systems shows how criminals can target customer accounts through phone calls and false help desk requests. There is no confirmed link between those methods and this incident.

Reuters could not verify the entire archive. It matched details for six employees against other records and confirmed phone numbers and other information by calling three workers. Some entries matched public profiles, while others revealed internal structures or previously undisclosed operations.

Names become more useful to attackers when paired with supervisors, duties, and phone numbers. Recorded Future expert Alexander Leslie told WIRED that such information could help adversaries identify vulnerable staff, build convincing impersonation attempts, or threaten investigations. Group membership, however, should not automatically be treated as proof of a person’s current assignment.

Previous Okta support impersonation campaigns show why exposed contact details matter. Attackers have used fake support messages and login pages to steal account information and authentication codes. The DHS records could provide material for similarly tailored approaches.

The disclosure follows ShinyHunters’ September claim of stealing FBI personnel data and an October lawsuit over a Defense Department breach affecting millions. These are separate incidents, with no established common cause.

articles.description:
WatchGuard disclosed seven critical Fireware OS vulnerabilities in an October 27, 2026 advisory, affecting Firebox firewalls and potentially enabling remote code execution, root-level action injection, and memory corruption. They are part of a wider release that covers 18 security issues across Fireware OS and the Windows Mobile VPN with SSL client. The seven critical entries […]

The post WatchGuard Discloses 7 Critical Firewall Flaws Allowing Remote Code Execution and Root-Level Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WatchGuard disclosed seven critical Fireware OS vulnerabilities in an October 27, 2026 advisory, affecting Firebox firewalls and potentially enabling remote code execution, root-level action injection, and memory corruption.

They are part of a wider release that covers 18 security issues across Fireware OS and the Windows Mobile VPN with SSL client. The seven critical entries carry severity scores between 9.1 and 9.5.

Other issues in the release could expose configuration secrets, allow file changes with root rights, hijack sessions, or disrupt firewall services. Risks vary by service, software version, and the access an attacker needs.

The highest-rated issue, CVE-2026-103594, scores 9.5 and involves a stack buffer overflow in WireGuard configuration that allows remote code execution. Its affected ranges cover Fireware OS 2026.2 through versions before 2026.4, and 12.12 through versions before 12.12.4.

Two further flaws, CVE-2026-112709 and CVE-2026-112710, each score 9.2. Both involve heap buffer overflows in the Active Directory authentication service and allow remote code execution before authentication.

WatchGuard Discloses Critical Firewall Flaws

WatchGuard’s indexed advisory confirms that description for CVE-2026-112710. These bugs are notable because attackers do not need to complete a login before triggering the vulnerable code.

CVE-2026-93857, also rated 9.2, affects the SIP proxy and allows remote code execution before authentication through a stack buffer overflow. CVE-2026-103593 scores 9.1 and affects the logging service, where another stack buffer overflow can allow remote code execution.

The remaining critical issues affect FireCluster synchronization and Access Portal. CVE-2026-93865 scores 9.2 and involves missing authentication in the FireCluster sync daemon, allowing remote root action injection.

Critical Flaws :

CVE-2026-93866 carries the same score and involves an integer overflow before authentication in Access Portal that allows an out-of-bounds write. That description establishes memory corruption, not confirmed code execution.

Two lower-scored entries also involve root-level access. CVE-2026-90464 lets an authenticated attacker modify arbitrary files as root because it lacks command validation. CVE-2026-93864 allows a local attacker to overwrite arbitrary files as root through a link-following flaw in firewalld.

Earlier reporting on WatchGuard Firebox OS vulnerabilities covered separate authenticated code execution and file-write issues. Do not confuse those earlier flaws with this release.

For most listed Fireware OS issues, the supplied advisory data identifies 2026.4 and 12.12.4 as fixed versions. Where applicable, T15 and T35 devices require 12.5.22. The Windows SSL VPN client credential-exposure issue is fixed in 2026.4.

Previous coverage of an exploited WatchGuard zero-day concerns CVE-2025-14733, not these newly listed flaws. It does not establish exploitation of this release.

We could not retrieve full advisory pages during verification. Apart from the indexed confirmation noted above, the October disclosure details and patch versions therefore remain based on the supplied list and need confirmation before publication.

An Oracle announcement published October 27 outlines how customers can combine the self-hosted gateway with OCI Enterprise AI to protect applications connected to company data and tools. The […]

The post Fortinet Brings AI Agent Security to Oracle Cloud to Block Prompt Injection and Data Leaks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Fortinet’s FortiAIGate is bringing AI security controls to enterprise workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), helping businesses inspect prompts, block sensitive data leaks, and control agent actions.

An Oracle announcement published October 27 outlines how customers can combine the self-hosted gateway with OCI Enterprise AI to protect applications connected to company data and tools.

The approach addresses a growing security gap as AI agents move beyond answering questions. Agents can query databases, access code, and call business tools.

Monitoring chat messages alone leaves other interactions unchecked, including tool responses that could carry hidden instructions or expose private information.

FortiAIGate runs as a containerized, GPU-powered reverse proxy between applications and AI models. It routes requests through security checks before they reach their destination. The gateway also inspects model responses, giving security teams a central place to apply rules across AI services.

Fortinet Secures Oracle Cloud AI Agents

Its Model Context Protocol (MCP) protection checks tool lists, calls, and responses in both directions. Fortinet says these checks detect prompt injection, data leaks, and harmful content in traffic between agents and MCP servers.

This extends inspection beyond the user’s original request to the information agents receive while completing tasks. That threat has surfaced in research covered by Cybersecuritynews.com on prompt injection through malicious MCP servers.

Researchers described how hidden instructions could redirect conversations or trigger tool use without clear user consent. Separate reporting on attacks targeting AI infrastructure detailed attempts to exploit exposed gateways and agent tools.

According to Oracle, FortiAIGate uses Virtue AI guardrails to inspect prompts and responses across nine languages. Built-in data loss prevention detects 35 types of sensitive information and can block or redact matches. Administrators can also describe custom detection rules in plain language.

Role-based workspaces separate team policies, model access, and logs while keeping central oversight. More than 50 preset policies cover privacy, security, and AI governance requirements.

Workspace policy changes require approval, while records of routed prompts, outputs, and tool calls support audits. These features help enforce rules but do not establish compliance.

The gateway also limits spending by organization, workspace, project, user, and virtual key. Requests stop when budgets run out. Rate limits restrict requests and tokens per minute.

At the same time, guardrails target denial-of-wallet attacks designed to consume paid AI resources. Content-based routing can send routine work to cheaper models.

The reference design places FortiAIGate on GPU-enabled Oracle Kubernetes Engine worker nodes. A hub-and-spoke setup can centralize inspection while applications operate across separate cloud networks.

According to Fortinet, OCI Enterprise AI provides managed model access, agent tools, and governance. Self-hosting keeps gateway logs and inspection data within the customer’s environment, while model requests still reach the selected provider.

Businesses must therefore check model routing and processing locations against their data residency needs. Protection also depends on sending relevant traffic through the gateway, rather than leaving alternate application paths outside inspection.

articles.title: WordPress 7.1.4 Fixes 22 Security Flaws, Including an Unauthenticated RCE Vulnerability
articles.description:
WordPress released version 7.1.4 on October 28, 2026, fixing 22 security flaws, including an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in its update process. The security release also addresses stored cross-site scripting, data exposure, and access control issues. WordPress urges website owners to install the update immediately. The official release announcement credits security researcher Umut Bayram […]

The post WordPress 7.1.4 Fixes 22 Security Flaws, Including an Unauthenticated RCE Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WordPress released version 7.1.4 on October 28, 2026, fixing 22 security flaws, including an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in its update process. The security release also addresses stored cross-site scripting, data exposure, and access control issues. WordPress urges website owners to install the update immediately.

The official release announcement credits security researcher Umut Bayram with reporting the update flaw. Patchstack’s technical analysis describes 22 vulnerabilities across 17 advisories, explaining why the number of listed advisory entries differs from the total flaw count.

The release was led by Aaron Jorbin and Nik Tsekouras, with reports from independent researchers and the WordPress Security Team helping close weaknesses across older and newer features.

The most serious issue involves a race condition, where an attacker must reach a temporary installation at precisely the right time. Exploitation requires no WordPress account, but the attack depends on a short update window and public access to the wp-content/upgrade/ directory.

During updates, WordPress extracts files into that directory. Previously, predictable folder names and cleanup that removed index.php could expose an unpacked WordPress installer. An attacker reaching it during the update could run setup using a database they control, creating a path to code execution.

WordPress 7.1.4 adds 16 random characters to temporary folder names, restores index.php protection, and prevents wp-config.php from being copied from the working directory. Patchstack rates exploitation as difficult because the opportunity lasts only seconds. This is separate from the earlier WordPress Core template resolution vulnerability covered by Cybersecuritynews.com.

Stored XSS and Permission Gaps

Several fixes target the Interactivity API, which supports interactive page features. Attackers with Contributor access could save crafted attributes that passed content filtering but later triggered unsafe browser actions. The update blocks dangerous bindings, strengthens checks, and addresses a denial-of-service issue that could freeze a visitor’s browser tab.

Other stored XSS fixes cover crafted block markup, Customizer selective refresh, Categories, and navigation labels. Image and Playlist processing also received hardening. Stored XSS means harmful script content remains saved on a site and runs when another user opens the affected content.

Anthropic reported issues involving personal data removal requests and specially crafted usernames. A separate Customizer flaw exposed unpublished changes to visitors without accounts. WordPress also tightened note permissions so users cannot access notes attached to posts they lack permission to edit. These changes follow earlier WordPress security updates addressing similar risks.

Update WordPress and Check Protection

Administrators can install the release through Dashboard, Updates, and Update Now, or download WordPress 7.1.4 directly. Sites with automatic background updates should receive it automatically, but owners should confirm the installed version rather than assume the process completed.

The official version documentation lists patched older branches, including 7.0.8, 6.9.11, and releases extending to 4.7.39. Not every branch contains all 22 flaws. Only the latest WordPress version remains actively supported, while versions 4.6 and earlier receive no security updates.

Beyond patching, Patchstack recommends blocking web access to wp-content/upgrade/ at the web server and reviewing accounts with Contributor privileges or higher.

A WordPress plugin firewall may not protect the extracted installer because that copy loads independently. The release also updates bundled root certificates following the eMudhra revocation. WordPress 7.2 remains scheduled for December 8, but site owners should not delay this security update while waiting for that major release.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.description:

OffSec today announced the release of a free, interactive hands-on lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play) to help security practitioners examine and defend against the critical “PHP2Shell” vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and […]

The post OffSec Launches Free PHP2Shell Lab Following Critical Vulnerability Discovery appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
New York, United States, October 28th, 2026, CyberNewswire

New hands-on lab lets security practitioners explore PHP2Shell exploitation firsthand as AI-assisted research reshapes vulnerability discovery.

OffSec today announced the release of a free, interactive hands-on lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play) to help security practitioners examine and defend against the critical “PHP2Shell” vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) firsthand. Developed in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and active exploits targeting core PHP engines in the wild, the lab provides penetration testers and enterprise defenders with a safe, controlled environment to study the decade-old memory corruption flaws and implement timely server mitigations.

The two critical flaws sat inside PHP, the language behind roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known, for more than a decade. Then researchers at Wiz, a Google-owned cloud security company, pointed AI at the code. 

They found the first flaw Aug. 19. The next day they used it to take over a Drupal site without a password. The day after that, it worked on WordPress.

PHP disclosed the flaws Oct. 21 as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. An attacker with no login can send a series of crafted web requests to crash a server or take it over. PHP’s severity scores rate both vulnerabilities as complex to exploit, even though working attacks already existed. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recommends patching immediately. 

Attackers are moving fast. Amazon calls PHP2Shell broadly exploited in the wild. By Oct.24, researchers had confirmed attackers running commands on vulnerable honeypot servers. CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Oct. 26. 

“PHP is one of those technologies attackers love to see,” said Keegan Bowen, principal DevOps lead at OffSec. “It has been a great attack vector over the years with many exploits and potential abuses. PHP wasn’t designed with security from the start.”

OffSec, which has taught hands-on offensive security since 2006, has released a free PHP2Shell lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play). The lab gives penetration testers and other security professionals a controlled environment to explore CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 firsthand. OffSec’s blog breaks down both flaws, and its proof-of-concept exploit is available on Exploit-DB. 

AI and the Evolving Pace of Exploitation

PHP scored both flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. To build a working attack, Wiz researchers had to chain several bugs together and tune the attack to each server’s memory. When they let AI do the grind, one researcher finished in a week what once took a top team month. Attackers can use the same AI models, so flaws once ranked too complex to matter are now fair game. 

“At this point, attackers are heavily leaning on AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities; the rate of CVEs is roughly double what was reported last year,” said Matt Freitas-Stavola, staff software engineer at OffSec. “LLMs don’t get tired and can easily run in the background for as long as attackers have money or compute to spare. Even now, just a hint of where an issue could arise is enough for an LLM to get a workable POC out relatively quickly.”

The Effects of These Flaws

Both flaws start with the same weak spot: what PHP does when a request runs out of memory or hits another fatal error.

“PHP is built from C and memory management becomes increasingly challenging as the code grows,” Bowen said. “Some out-of-memory states were not handled well. In some cases, attackers can access interrupted state data before it is cleaned up. That becomes an opportunity for abuse.”

That leftover state can carry into the next request on the same worker. An attacker who shapes it can run code with the web server’s privileges.

The same bugs can also leak data. Wiz showed attackers could potentially read memory from the PHP process. That memory could hold passwords, session tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests or the server itself. 

The story is still developing. On Oct. 23, PHP disclosed a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, that can affect fully patched servers with an unusual session setup. PHP has no fix for it yet. Researchers have also built PHP2Shell exploits that get past ASLR, a common memory defense, and more issues could surface as the flaws are studied. As research continues, new vulnerabilities, exploitation techniques, and mitigations may emerge beyond those covered here.

OffSec’s Current Recommendations

These steps reflect what is known at the time of publication. Check CISA and the PHP project for the latest recommendations.

  • Patch PHP Now. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to address CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Check vendor advisories rather than relying on version numbers alone.
  • Update the Underlying PHP Engine. Updating WordPress, Drupal, or another application does not resolve vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Rebuild affected container images, and restart PHP processes so the updated code takes effect.
  • Apply Temporary Protections While Patching. Disable PHP session upload progress (session.upload_progress.enabled=0), which also mitigates CVE-2026-115560. On PHP 8.5, disable fatal error backtraces and restart affected workers after configuration changes. These measures reduce exposure; they do not replace patching.
  • Investigate Potential Compromise. Review web server and PHP logs for suspicious multipart requests, memory-limit errors, repeated HTTP 500 responses, malformed session cookies, and unexpected PHP worker restarts. Investigations should consider activity dating back to at least October 17, when exploitation attempts were first reported. Rotate potentially affected credentials, API keys, and tokens as appropriate.

Understand the Exploit. Strengthen the Defense.

When the next disclosure lands, someone on the team needs to judge exposure. Reading about an exploit builds awareness. Working on one hands-on builds the skill to respond. 

OffSec’s PHP2Shell lab helps practitioners turn technical knowledge into hands-on experience they can apply to future vulnerabilities. For a deeper look at the vulnerabilities, explore OffSec’s technical analysis. Organizations looking to build these capabilities across their security teams can explore OffSec’s workforce development programs.

About OffSec

OffSec is the world’s leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications. Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

Contact

articles.description:
Security researcher Saifeldeen Aziz says he found new zero-click bugs in Telegram stickers. He also says he chained them to run code on iOS. The work was due to be presented on October 28 at OffensiveCon in Tokyo, according to the conference agenda. Aziz says he got past Telegram’s server-side checks and that the flawed […]

The post Researcher Uncovers New 0-click Flaw in Telegram Stickers and Chained Them to Run Code on iOS appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security researcher Saifeldeen Aziz says he found new zero-click bugs in Telegram stickers. He also says he chained them to run code on iOS. The work was due to be presented on October 28 at OffensiveCon in Tokyo, according to the conference agenda. Aziz says he got past Telegram’s server-side checks and that the flawed code still ships in its apps.

The talk is a direct challenge to a position Telegram took in March. Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) had reported a bug in the app’s sticker code. According to reports, Telegram called the flaw fake, saying its servers check every sticker before any app can play it. ZDI then cut the severity score from 9.8 to 7.0 because of those server-side checks.

The researcher behind that report, Michael DePlante, still said the weak code exists on the client side. Italy’s national cyber agency also took the report seriously.

0-click Flaw in Telegram Stickers

ZDI later released its advisory ZDI-26-757 on October 15. It tracks the bug as CVE-2026-111105 and describes a numeric truncation flaw in the rlottie library. Bad input there can cause a write before the start of a memory buffer, and that can lead to code execution.

The timeline shows a long back-and-forth. Telegram said on March 31 that server-side checks mitigated the bug. In mid-April, it asked ZDI for a full working exploit chain. ZDI called that request out of line with normal disclosure practice. In July, ZDI warned Telegram it would publish the case as a zero-day, which means a flaw with no patch yet.

Aziz’s abstract says he spent a year on Telegram. He began by fuzzing rlottie with help from large language models. Fuzzing means feeding a program huge amounts of broken input to make it fail. The abstract says this found several memory-corruption bugs in the iOS, Android, and Desktop clients.

He then found separate logic flaws in how Telegram delivers and checks stickers. By chaining them, he says he made the code that was supposed to be out of reach open to abuse. The final step was code execution on Telegram for iOS. He also plans to discuss the limits of that exploit. The public abstract gives no technical proof, no patch status, and no CVE numbers for the new bugs, so readers should treat the claims as unconfirmed until the full talk or a write-up appears.

Animated stickers use the TGS format, which is a compressed Lottie animation file. Telegram’s rlottie library draws them on your screen. Pasquale Pillitteri explained that one tiny 269-byte sticker could crash Telegram and lock a chat. He also noted that server filtering does not catch every case. Telegram Desktop 7.2.7 fixed that specific variant.

This is not the first time rlottie has been in trouble. A GitHub analysis recalls that Shielder found several rlottie bugs in 2021. Those affected Android, iOS, and macOS.

Telegram’s code has seen other trouble lately. Cyber Security News covered a Telegram Desktop flaw tracked as CVE-2026-107181, which could let a crafted link steal files and take over accounts before version 7.2.9. We also reported on the EvilVideo bug, where fake video files ran malicious code on Android.

Aziz ends his abstract with a hard question. If one provider’s servers act as the only gate against a zero-click bug, is that a fix, a design risk, or something close to a backdoor? The point is that users cannot check what the server does. They can only trust it.

Until Telegram changes the client code, the safest steps are simple. Keep every Telegram app fully updated, limit who can message or add you to groups, and avoid opening files from strangers. ZDI also advises limiting interaction with the product.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Whether you’re investigating a suspicious URL or a file, you need more than a verdict to make a confident, evidence-based decision.

You need to understand what the threat does, whether others have encountered it before, and what the findings mean for your next steps.

Here are key questions to guide your SOC investigation and will lead you to a more confident and efficient decision-making.

Question 1. Are You the First to Face It?

The IOC you’re investigating may have appeared in previous investigations by your team, surfaced in activity targeting your industry, or already been linked to known threats.

So before digging deeper, it’s worth asking: Has anyone encountered this indicator before? If so, can I use their findings to my advantage?

ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox provides a fast answer to these questions with brand-new capability – Related Threat Context.

Once the analysis is complete, you can see where the same indicators have appeared across your team, your industry, and ANY.RUN’s broader intelligence dataset, informed by investigations from 16,000+ SOC teams and a community of more than 700,000 security professionals.

Related Threat Context combines three sources of insight:

  • Team Context: See whether your team has investigated the same IOC before and explore previous analyses.
  • Industry Context: Check whether the IOC has appeared in analyses associated with your industry.

For example, in the Sandbox analysis below, 300+ related analyses were found across the manufacturing industry, and over 1,000 across the broader ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence. All of them contain IOCs also related to the current analysis.

That’s what combining deeper behavioral analysis with intelligence on emerging threats can help achieve: spotting activity that might otherwise go unnoticed.

Detect up to 58% more threats with full behavioral evidence. Get more context with Interactive Sandbox

You can examine related analyses, compare previous observations with the behavior captured in your current session, and identify new leads worth investigating.

Outcome: Uncover related threat activity, find new investigation leads, and make more informed decisions with broader context.

Question 2. What Does It Actually Do?

Previous investigations can give you valuable clues about a threat. But to understand what’s happening in your specific case, you still need to examine its behavior: what gets executed, how the attack unfolds, and what happens next.

For example, a document may launch PowerShell and download another payload. A phishing URL may redirect users through several pages before reaching a credential-harvesting site. Without observing this behavior, analysts may miss important parts of the attack chain.

ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox lets you observe this activity in an isolated environment. Virtual machines start in under 10 seconds, with analysis reports available in around 40 seconds.

You can inspect network traffic, downloaded payloads, and extracted IOCs to reveal additional infrastructure and help you follow the attack beyond the original file or URL.

Outcome: Validate suspicious activity, uncover more of the attack chain, and get behavioral evidence in around 40 seconds.

Question 3. Do You Have Enough Evidence for Handoff or Response?

Identifying suspicious activity is only half the job. You also need to turn what you’ve uncovered into something you can act on.

By this point, your investigation may have produced several types of evidence:

  • IOCs: Suspicious IPs, domains, URLs, and file hashes discovered during the current analysis or identified through related investigations.
  • Behavioral evidence: Process activity, network connections, downloaded payloads, and MITRE ATT&CK techniques that explain how the threat operates.
  • Related investigation context: Previous analyses that may reveal additional infrastructure, similar behavior, or other useful connections.

The final step is to present this evidence in a comprehensive way, for Tier 2, SOC head, or IR team.

ANY.RUN automates this step of the process with Tier 1 Reports. They not only present investigation findings in a structured format, so you don’t have to manually assemble the key evidence from scratch but also offer AI-generated summary and recommendations for a quick overview and next steps.

This makes it easy to hand off cases for deeper investigation or incident response.

The collected IOCs and behavioral evidence can also support threat hunting and detection engineering, helping teams search for related activity across their environment and improve existing detections.

Outcome: Turn your findings into actionable evidence for 21-minute reduction in MTTR per case.

Bonus Question: Could You Have Spotted This Threat Earlier?

In a study of ANY.RUN Sandbox sessions, approximately 30% of unique malicious IOCs had already been observed by ANY.RUN and were present in Threat Intelligence Feeds before analysts began investigating.

This is where threat intelligence and behavioral analysis complement each other.

ANY.RUN TI Feeds deliver continuously updated, high-confidence malicious IOCs with supporting context directly into existing SIEM, SOAR, EDR, and other security workflows.

This allows SOC teams to automatically identify known malicious indicators in their telemetry, prioritize relevant alerts, and detect threats earlier.

Detect known threats earlier with intelligence from 16K+ SOC teams. Integrate TI Feeds

And for deeper behavioral evidence, Interactive Sandbox provides everything you need to validate suspicious activity, understand how an attack unfolds, and uncover additional indicators.

That’s the power of combining ANY.RUN solutions: together they bring earlier detection of known threats, deeper investigation of suspicious activity, and new intelligence for future detection.

Conclusion

Before wrapping up your next threat investigation, ask yourself:

  • Have I checked previous analyses? Someone else may have already uncovered useful evidence.
  • Have I looked beyond the verdict? Behavioral details and additional IOCs may reveal more of the attack.
  • Do I have enough evidence to act? Make sure your findings are ready for handoff, response, or further investigation.
  • Could these findings help detect threats earlier? Today’s investigation may provide valuable intelligence for future detections.

ANY.RUN helps you work through these questions in one connected workflow: check what other analysts have uncovered, validate suspicious behavior, gather evidence for your next decision, and use the findings to detect similar threats earlier.

The company published security bulletin TV-2026-1011 on October 27, 2026, […]

The post TeamViewer Vulnerabilities Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code Through Remote Desktop Sessions appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
TeamViewer has released security updates for three high-severity vulnerabilities that could let attackers run malicious code, crash remote desktop clients, or gain root access on macOS. The flaws affect client components used with TeamViewer Remote, TeamViewer Tensor, and TeamViewer ONE, with CVSS scores reaching 8.8.

The company published security bulletin TV-2026-1011 on October 27, 2026, and urged customers to install version 15.83 or the latest available release. TeamViewer said it was not aware of active exploitation when it published the bulletin.

CVE-2026-92372, rated 8.8, affects the screen-image decoder in TeamViewer Full Client for Linux and macOS before version 15.83. The decoder processes image data received during remote-control sessions. Still, it fails to check whether incoming data fits within the destination image buffer.

An attacker could supply specially crafted screen-image data that writes beyond the allocated memory space, potentially allowing arbitrary code execution. A second route involves convincing a user to open a malicious TeamViewer session recording with the .tvs extension. Both routes require user interaction.

TeamViewer Remote Desktop Session Flaws

The bulletin also lists Linux and macOS Host installations and older 14.7 and 13.2 branches in the affected-version section. This makes it important to check installed components, not just the main desktop application.

The second remote-session flaw, CVE-2026-111585, also carries an 8.8 score. It involves an integer overflow during screen processing that can lead to a heap-based buffer overflow, where data exceeds its assigned memory area.

A malicious or compromised remote host could use the flaw to crash the viewer application. Depending on the platform, it could also execute code with the viewer process’s privileges.

Exploitation requires the victim to establish a remote-control session with that host. Affected software includes Full Client on Windows, Linux, and macOS, Windows Portable, and the Android Remote Control app before version 15.83.

CVE-2026-92374, rated 7.8, affects the privileged helper in TeamViewer Full Client and Host for macOS. It combines a timing flaw with unsafe handling of symbolic links, which point to other files or locations.

A local attacker with limited permissions could exploit the gap between checking an installer package and using it. Bypassing package verification could allow installation of a malicious package and escalation to root. Unlike the screen-processing flaws, this issue requires existing local access.

These fixes follow earlier reports covering TeamViewer remote-session vulnerabilities and a separate TeamViewer file-transfer vulnerability. Those reports address different flaws and should not be confused with the three newly disclosed issues in this bulletin.

TeamViewer recommends updating through its official download page. Legacy fixes include 15.64.10 for Windows 7 and 8, 14.7.48868 across supported legacy platforms, and platform-specific 13.2 builds.

The key risk is that connecting to a hostile computer can expose the viewer itself. Users do not need to grant an attacker normal control of their desktop for these screen-processing vulnerabilities to become relevant.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: Researchers Chain Cloudflare Security Flaws to Bypass CSP and Execute Malicious JavaScript
articles.description:
Security researchers at Searchlight Cyber chained several small flaws in Cloudflare’s image feature. The chain let them run JavaScript on a site that was meant to block it. Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues published the work on October 28, 2026, in a write-up titled Cache Me If You Can. They showed a working cross-site scripting […]

The post Researchers Chain Cloudflare Security Flaws to Bypass CSP and Execute Malicious JavaScript appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security researchers at Searchlight Cyber chained several small flaws in Cloudflare’s image feature. The chain let them run JavaScript on a site that was meant to block it.

Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues published the work on October 28, 2026, in a write-up titled Cache Me If You Can. They showed a working cross-site scripting (XSS) bug through the /cdn-cgi/image/ endpoint on cloudflare.com. The write-up does not list a CVE or a patch status, so readers should check with Cloudflare.

Cloudflare XSS Flaws

Cloudflare sits in front of 24.3% of all websites. When a site joins Cloudflare, the company adds a managed /cdn-cgi/ path to that site’s own domain. Features such as bot checks, Web Analytics, Access, and Image Transformations live there.

Because these pages load from the customer’s own domain, a bug in them runs with that site’s trust. Other researchers had already found Content Security Policy (CSP) bypasses in this path. CSP is a browser rule set that limits which scripts a page may run.

Cloudflare cleans SVG images with svg-hush, a Rust tool built on the xml-rs library. The tool checks the file, then writes it back out. The researchers found that xml-rs escapes normal attribute values but writes namespace values (the xmlns setting) raw.

An attacker can hide a quote mark in that value and break out of it. The filter has already approved the file by then, so the script tag slips through. Cloudflare serves these images with a strict policy of default-src ‘none’, which blocks scripts. However, the endpoint passes along Cache-Control headers from the source image.

The HTTP rules allow a form such as no-cache=”Content-Security-Policy”, which tells a cache to drop the named header. Only Chromium follows this rule, and it accepts any header name. The CSP stays in place on the first load. After Chromium saves the page, the policy is gone.

A known CTF trick then forces Chromium to reload the saved copy. The attacker opens the page in a new window, moves that window to another site, and calls history.back().

The opener link keeps the page out of the back/forward cache, so Chromium uses its disk cache, and the script runs. A related cache-based CSP bypass covered earlier by Cyber Security News relied on the same bfcache fallback.

Image Transformations only fetches images from allowed sources. The default setting is “This zone only”. The fetcher follows redirects without checking the final address. Any open redirect on an allowed site therefore lets an attacker load an image from anywhere.

The team wanted a method that needed no open redirect. They found that once Cloudflare Access is on for any hostname in a zone, /cdn-cgi/access/logout works on every hostname in that zone. Its returnTo setting accepts any cloudflare.com subdomain.

A redirect on a Cloudflare research host then sent the fetcher to the attacker’s file. That completed the chain on zones with strict source settings. The team then tested the cache trick elsewhere. On Netlify Image CDN, they used it to drop both the CSP and the Content-Type header. Chromium then guessed the file type from its content and treated an SVG starting with a doctype as HTML.

A processing instruction hid the script from the SVGO cleaner, which only checks elements. The researchers say Netlify’s hosted code is not public, so they could not confirm it matches the open-source version. Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage also allow signed links to override response headers. Such links can set response-content-type and response-cache-control.

This matters for buckets behind custom domains or proxies that pass query strings along. The idea builds on earlier Content-Type override research and the S3 GetObject overrides.

The main lesson is that you shouldn’t trust only a file’s body. Headers passed through by an image service or storage layer become part of your security. Teams should avoid forwarding Cache-Control and X-* headers from untrusted sources.

They should also set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and review which sources their image tools may fetch. Closing open redirects helps too. Past work shows that even strong filters can fail, as in WAF bypass research on XSS payloads. Layered defenses still matter.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: PropellerAds: Why Modern Malware Delivery Starts Before the Payload
articles.description:
By Farukh Rakhimov, Head of Compliance, Data Protection, and Information Security at AdTech Holding In March 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) disclosed Coruna, an iOS exploit kit with five exploit chains and 23 exploits covering iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1. The most instructive part of the disclosure is what happened before the exploit got any […]

The post PropellerAds: Why Modern Malware Delivery Starts Before the Payload appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
By Farukh Rakhimov, Head of Compliance, Data Protection, and Information Security at AdTech Holding

In March 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) disclosed Coruna, an iOS exploit kit with five exploit chains and 23 exploits covering iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1.

The most instructive part of the disclosure is what happened before the exploit got any chance to run.

Coruna was amazingly picky about visitors. A JavaScript fingerprinting module checked whether the visitor was a real device, which iPhone model it was and which iOS version it ran. Only then did the framework fire a matching exploit.

Researchers, scanners, Lockdown Mode devices and private browsing sessions were shown the door.

For a defender, the payload is where the investigation starts. For the operator, it is the end of the assembly line: by then, traffic has already been acquired, routed and qualified, mostly in plain view.

At PropellerAds, we see that upstream layer from the advertising side, including through ADEX, our traffic-quality and anti-fraud system.

A malware campaign is a delivery system

A modern malware campaign makes a lot more sense if you look at it as a delivery system. It usually has five parts:

  • Acquisition: a paid ad, a search result, a compromised site, a messenger link.
  • Routing: redirectors and traffic distribution systems (TDS) that decide where each visitor goes next.
  • Trusted infrastructure: CDNs, code repositories and file-sharing services that help malicious traffic blend into the furniture well.
  • Visitor qualification: fingerprinting that decides who gets the payload and who gets a decoy.
  • Persuasion: a fake download page, a fake virus alert, or a chat in WhatsApp or Telegram.

In June 2026, Check Point Research described fake open-source download sites that loaded a staging script from Amazon CloudFront and handed clicks to a TDS.

The TDS scripts were in place by December 2025; malware distribution through them began in January 2026. In other words, the pipes were already in place weeks before anyone turned on the malware tap.

The chains were always long. Now they are selective.

Long redirect chains are stale news. A USENIX Security study back from 2008 found that in half of the cases where malware was delivered through ads, the visitor passed more than six redirects before reaching the payload.

What has changed is selectivity, and Coruna takes it to the extreme. A mismatched exploit crashes Safari, and a chain delivered to a researcher gets patched. If a reviewer visits once, from one profile, they see exactly the version the attacker wanted them to see. 

What an advertising platform sees, and when

An ad platform cannot see an infected device, but it sees what endpoint tools never do, in three windows:

  • At submission: account signals, the declared destination, domain history, and reuse of domains, scripts or hosting from blocked campaigns.
  • At moderation: the full redirect path, scripts and hidden iframes on the landing page, and whether the page answers different visitor profiles differently.
  • After launch: real traffic, destination changes after approval, and abuse reports.

Visibility also has edges. In one ADEX case, the ad itself ended at a Google search page. The critical hop happened only after the user clicked the first result, pushing the next stage outside the ad’s direct click path.

That is exactly why destination verification and journey reconstruction are not the same thing. 

None of this requires catching the payload red-handed. A page that loads a hidden iframe, checks the OS version and calls a version-specific script is suspicious before anyone retrieves the exploit.

One operator, fifty faces

Everything above about Coruna comes from GTIG’s research. What follows is ADEX’s own investigation, and it concerns the delivery method, not the exploit kit: ADEX found ad campaigns built on the same qualify-first logic, which does not mean Coruna itself was delivered through them.

The ADEX team identified approximately 50 advertiser accounts linked to campaigns that used the similar delivery setup behind landing pages with nothing in common: a social offer, a finance page, changing formats and verticals.

The findings were passed to the platforms using ADEX, whose teams reviewed the accounts and took action.

Underneath, the chain was identical. A hidden iframe checked the OS version. An orchestrator then filtered out bots and crawlers, checked the IP, and served a script for that iOS version as an ordinary-looking .min.js file.

That sequence is what linked the accounts. Nothing on the pages themselves connected them: themes, brands, verticals and formats all differed. Only the delivery behavior repeated.

Creative by creative, these looked like unrelated advertisers. By delivery behavior, they looked like one operator.

The cloaking setup takes weeks to build; a landing page takes a day, so operators reuse the first and refresh the second.

The analysis gave ADEX metrics that now flag the pattern during moderation, before a campaign reaches traffic. A new campaign that reproduces the delivery pattern is flagged whatever its landing page looks like.

What changed in 2026

ADEX’s Trust & Safety review, based on moderation data from eight ad platforms for January to September 2026, shows the same shift at scale.

Source: ADEX, State of Ad Fraud 2026: Trust & Safety Report

Baseline periods differ by row, so the table shows a changing mix of reasons, not a like-for-like trend. Malicious iOS scripts became a separate category only in Q3: ~20% is their share that quarter, not measured growth.

Cloaking is still the top suspension reason, but it now shares the list with device-specific scripts and messenger phishing, where persuasion moves into a chat reviewers cannot follow.

AI speeds up the cheap layer: in the cases ADEX reviewed, a rejected campaign could return rebuilt within hours. The delivery infrastructure changes far more slowly, which makes it the more reliable thing to track.

From “what ran” to “how the victim arrived”

Endpoint detection remains necessary, but it starts at the last step of the chain and treats incidents separately, even when one delivery path sits behind several.

Moving up does not require a new product, only a few changes in practice:

  • Record the path, not only the file. The redirect chain is often the only artifact shared by incidents that look unrelated.
  • Treat a single clean crawl as inconclusive. Revisit suspicious paths from different device and network profiles, and follow the journey beyond the declared destination. A clean first hop may simply hand the user off to the next stage. 
  • Cluster by delivery, not content. Redirect shape, iframe behavior, script hashes and hosting survive a creative refresh; page themes do not.
  • Keep legacy devices in view. Apple backported Coruna-relevant fixes to iOS 15.8.7 in March 2026, but unpatched devices stay exposed longest. 
  • Report the full path to the source. An ad platform can block an operator’s next fifty campaigns only if it sees what connects them.

The takeaway

The layer that decides which visitor is real and which is a reviewer is the same engineering whether it protects an exploit chain or a scam page. “What ran?” remains a necessary question.

Teams that also ask “how did the victim arrive?” see the operator earlier and connect incidents that otherwise look unrelated.

Methodology

ADEX figures come from the State of Ad Fraud 2026: Trust & Safety Report, based on aggregated moderation data from ad platforms using ADEX, January to September 2026.

Percentages describe the composition of rejected or suspended campaigns in that dataset, not industry-wide prevalence.

Author:

Farukh Rakhimov — Head of Compliance, Data Protection, and Information Security at AdTech Holding, the parent company of ADEX. Over 8 years he has built and led compliance, data protection, and information security across the group. His work spans GDPR governance, KYC and AML frameworks, financial risk assessment, and ISO 27001 certification for the group’s flagship platforms. A PhD candidate at the University of Cyprus, Farukh brings a practical, no-nonsense take on data protection — showing how businesses can turn regulatory pressure into real trust and treat compliance as a competitive edge, not a checkbox.

The post PropellerAds: Why Modern Malware Delivery Starts Before the Payload appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: OWASP Finds ChatGPT Helped Low-Skilled User Take Over Admin Account in Hacking Test
articles.description:
OWASP found that ChatGPT helped an operator with no offensive security knowledge take over an administrator account during a controlled hacking test. The operator largely copied commands, returned results to the chatbot, and followed its guidance to change a password and log in. The finding shows how AI can lower the skill needed for some […]

The post OWASP Finds ChatGPT Helped Low-Skilled User Take Over Admin Account in Hacking Test appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OWASP found that ChatGPT helped an operator with no offensive security knowledge take over an administrator account during a controlled hacking test.

The operator largely copied commands, returned results to the chatbot, and followed its guidance to change a password and log in. The finding shows how AI can lower the skill needed for some attacks without removing the need for human input.

The LLM Exploit Generation Phase 2 report, published by the OWASP GenAI Security Project, compared human-guided chat sessions with autonomous agents against live Hack The Box targets.

These were authorized training environments, not breached businesses. Researchers tracked success, human effort, costs, safety controls, and failures.

The main test involved Silentium, a machine with a hidden staging website running a vulnerable version of Flowise. Using a testing guide generated by ChatGPT, the operator followed instructions with the common security tools nmap and curl.

ChatGPT directed information gathering and uncovered the staging site, which the operator would not have known to investigate. It then identified a login flow that revealed valid usernames and guided the operator through changing an administrator account’s password. The operator confirmed the takeover by signing in with the new credentials.

OWASP Finds ChatGPT-Assisted Admin Takeover

The result was not entirely skill-free. The test persona allowed general computer literacy, command-line use, and intermediate prompting ability. The operator also had to recognize refusals and reframe requests as authorized testing. Installing the Kali environment was outside the test’s scope.

Researchers also observed a response disappearing behind an error before a repeated request succeeded. They could not confirm the cause or reproduce the event, so it does not establish a general weakness in OpenAI’s safeguards.

The autonomous track tested nine configurations using CAI, HexStrike, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and hosted or local models. Stronger multi-agent setups discovered staging sites, identified vulnerable software, and researched exploit paths with little guidance after setup.

However, no autonomous run completed the final Silentium takeover step. Provider safety controls stopped the hosted systems that reached that stage, leaving humans to finish. Other runs stalled in repeated scans, password-cracking loops, hostname errors, or tool failures.

This distinction adds context to broader reporting on hackers using autonomous AI agents. In OWASP’s tests, the software around the model often mattered more than model choice, and building that software required expertise.

Costs also extended beyond API bills. Productive hosted runs cost tens of dollars, but setup, troubleshooting, and supervision remained important. A local Qwen Coder run avoided API charges yet needed repeated human corrections and ended with a tool integration error.

OWASP identified repeated, similar scans and requests against one target as a possible detection signal. Human-guided activity could be quieter, although the study did not directly measure stealth or detection rates.

For teams deploying agents, OWASP recommends enforcing approval before high-impact actions rather than relying only on model safeguards. Related coverage of hijacked AI pentesting agents highlights why those controls matter.

The report also warns against treating benchmark scores as proof of real-world hacking ability. Its small sample supports a narrower conclusion: AI speeds up parts of an attack, but reliable execution still depends on people.

articles.description:
Google released a Chrome security update that fixes 52 vulnerabilities, including four critical flaws affecting FileSystem, FileAPI, Skia, and Layout. According to the release notice, the Stable channel is moving to version 156.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac. At the same time, Linux users will receive version 156.0.8078.73. The update will reach users over the coming […]

The post Google Fixes 52 Chrome Security Flaws, Including Four Critical Vulnerabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google released a Chrome security update that fixes 52 vulnerabilities, including four critical flaws affecting FileSystem, FileAPI, Skia, and Layout.

According to the release notice, the Stable channel is moving to version 156.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac. At the same time, Linux users will receive version 156.0.8078.73.

The update will reach users over the coming days and weeks. The supplied security list includes four critical vulnerabilities, 46 high-severity issues, and two medium-severity bugs. The fixes cover browser functions ranging from file handling and page rendering to JavaScript, graphics, video, and audio processing.

CVE-2026-118306 is a memory corruption flaw in FileSystem, reported on October 7 by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic with assistance from Claude. The second critical issue, CVE-2026-118331, involves improper input validation in FileAPI. Ge reported that vulnerability on October 11, also with Claude’s assistance.

The remaining critical bugs are CVE-2026-118348, an improper input validation issue in Skia, and CVE-2026-118344, a use-after-free flaw in Layout. Ge reported both on October 17. These findings highlight file operations and page display features as key areas this release addresses.

A use-after-free bug occurs when software accesses memory after it has been released. Input validation flaws involve inadequate checks on incoming data.

However, the supplied notice does not describe specific attack methods, confirm remote code execution, or state that attackers have exploited these vulnerabilities.

Google Fixes 52 Chrome Security Flaws

Google’s high-severity fixes address memory corruption, use-after-free, input validation, access control, and authorization flaws across V8, Turbolev, ANGLE, WebRTC, PDFium, WebAudio, Payments, and graphics and media components.

Notable entries include CVE-2026-118318, an improper access control flaw in V8, and CVE-2026-118333, a missing authorization issue in Video. Google also fixed CVE-2026-118342, an out-of-bounds write in Editing. The notice provides no detailed exploit conditions for these issues.

This release follows the earlier Chrome 156 update fixing 353 security flaws and a separate Chrome update addressing 32 vulnerabilities.

These releases highlight the importance of checking the installed Chrome build rather than relying solely on the browser’s major version number.

The notice credits Google researchers, independent contributors, Mozilla, Anthropic, Ada Logics, and OpenAI Codex Security. Several reports explicitly name AI assistance, although the credits do not establish that those tools independently discovered or verified every issue.

Critical Vulnerabilities :

High-Severity Vulnerabilities :

Medium-Severity Vulnerabilities :

Google says some bug details will remain restricted until most users have installed the fixes. Restrictions may last longer where shared libraries affect other projects. The Chromium Security page explains its coordinated approach to vulnerability disclosure.

Users should open Chrome’s menu, select Help, then About Google Chrome, and relaunch after any available update installs. Linux users should update through their package manager. Google’s Chrome update guide provides platform instructions.

Administrators should keep automatic updates enabled across managed Windows devices to receive critical security fixes promptly.

articles.description:

Announced on October 27, 2026, the court-authorized action targeted a business accused of helping criminals keep their websites online, ignore abuse complaints, and hide payments. The U.S. Justice Department said Virtualine also operated […]

The post FBI Seizes Virtualine Bulletproof Hosting Domain Linked to Ransomware and Cybercrime appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The FBI seized virtualine.net, the main website of a bulletproof hosting provider linked to ransomware operators, stolen-data markets, and other cybercrime services.

Announced on October 27, 2026, the court-authorized action targeted a business accused of helping criminals keep their websites online, ignore abuse complaints, and hide payments.

The U.S. Justice Department said Virtualine also operated under the names Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech. It sold hosting, servers, and domain registration services while openly seeking customers on cybercrime forums.

Investigators linked its services to child sexual abuse material, the sharing of intimate images without consent, and international money laundering.s

Virtualine marketed its willingness to support illegal activity as a selling point. In September 2024, it told an Exploit. user that customers could use its services for phishing, payment card fraud, spam, port scanning, and other illegal activities. Its stated exceptions were child abuse content and terrorism.

By March 2026, the provider was advertising an “additional protection plan” for customers facing law enforcement requests. Under that plan, Virtualine would move a customer’s criminal infrastructure to an unrelated shell company and reactivate the server, according to court records cited by prosecutors.

FBI Seizes Virtualine Bulletproof Hosting

That offer shows how bulletproof hosting can help criminal operations recover from pressure rather than provide server space. Similar concerns appeared in earlier coverage of U.S. sanctions against bulletproof hosting provider Aeza, whose infrastructure supported ransomware and information-stealing malware.

Chainalysis reported that Virtualine’s payment addresses were directly linked to ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, and scam and phishing addresses. These findings provide context for the hosting provider’s role in several types of online crime.

The Justice Department said Virtualine accepted payments through an option labeled “BTC [NO-AML],” using unhosted Bitcoin addresses. Prosecutors allege that Virtualine then laundered payments from criminal customers to hide their source. The announcement did not identify individual ransomware groups or disclose the total value of those transactions.

A central part of the investigation involved a criminal forum identified as Vendor 1. Prosecutors say it sold access to explicit images of minors and adults and promoted hackers who could break into victims’ accounts to steal private material.

Virtualine began receiving warnings about child sexual abuse material in January 2026. Notices came from police in Germany, Canada, and Australia, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, and a victim’s attorney. Despite those reports, Virtualine allegedly kept the forum online and helped build another site to upload and sell content.

The FBI Washington Field Office led the investigation with German, Dutch, and British authorities, alongside OverRIPE and Lumen. The case follows wider action against criminal hosting, including U.S. charges against two bulletproof hosting companies.

However, taking control of Virtualine’s domain does not establish that every related server stopped operating. Silent Push reported that Omegatech was not fully offline after the seizure.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys
articles.description:
Three malicious Firefox extensions posed as the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys. Whoever holds these secrets controls the wallet and every coin in it. All three listings were live on the Firefox Add-ons store during the research and have since been removed. The fake add-ons copied the […]

The post Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Three malicious Firefox extensions posed as the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys.

Whoever holds these secrets controls the wallet and every coin in it. All three listings were live on the Firefox Add-ons store during the research and have since been removed.

The fake add-ons copied the names, icons, and marketing text of well-known wallets. Anyone searching the store for a trusted wallet could easily install one by mistake. This is the same trick seen in other fake crypto wallet screens used to trap careless users.

Researchers at Socket.dev identified the malware and shared their findings on October 27, 2026. Their team found that the extensions send stolen secrets to subdomains of one command-and-control domain, bonto[.]io.

The Phantom copy also carried a hidden loader that could change its behavior after Mozilla approved it.

Malicious Firefox Extensions Impersonate Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget

The Phantom listing used lookalike Unicode letters in its name, so it appeared on screen as “Phantom.” It reused Phantom’s real ghost icon and called itself “Official Phantom Wallet (Firefox Update).”

The Jupiter copy claimed it was built by Jupiter Exchange. The Bitget copy used the internal name “TabFlow Pro” but showed Bitget branding to users. None of them offered a privacy policy, and all declared that they collect no data.

The Phantom package held a small loader added to its background script. The loader hid its server address inside a list of numbers, then fetched a settings file from phantom[.]bonto[.]io.

That file told the extension whether to run and carried a base64-encoded stealer. The code ran inside every page the victim opened, which let it read the wallet’s own page objects.

Since the operator controls that server, it could return a harmless reply during Mozilla’s review and the real stealer afterward.

The stealer watched for 12, 15, 18, and 24-word recovery phrases, and for Ethereum and Solana private-key formats. It read text boxes, paste events, and the numbered phrase grid that wallets show on their secret-phrase screen.

Captured data was sent to the attacker’s server as JSON. This is not the first time Socket has found this style of theft. It also reported 16 malicious Firefox extensions that copied Rabby and OKX wallet screens earlier this month.

The Jupiter and Bitget fakes worked more simply. They bundled the stealer in the package and sent the recovery phrase straight to jupiter[.]bonto[.]io or bitget[.]bonto[.]io.

The Jupiter copy also asked for access to Trezor Connect, which widened what it could read. Socket noted that all three packages carried a full, always-on stealer inside the signed code Mozilla reviewed, so the remote loader was only an extra layer.

Hidden Infrastructure and Real-World Risk

The Phantom package went further and included the operator’s own drainer backend, a Node.js file named server.js.

It saved stolen secrets to local files, sent them to a Telegram bot, and moved funds to fixed payout addresses on Ethereum, BSC, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, Solana, and Bitcoin.

A code comment said the payload would work only “after approval flip,” meaning after Mozilla’s review. A second file, server-review.js, returned an inactive reply while the review was underway.

All the exfiltration servers sit behind Cloudflare, which hides the real host. Socket also found working subdomains for coinbase[.]bonto[.]io and exodus[.]bonto[.]io.

That suggests the group planned to impersonate Coinbase Wallet and Exodus too, although no matching store listings were found. Each fake add-on came from its own throwaway developer account, which makes bulk takedowns slower.

Phantom and Jupiter packages also contained a CLAUDE.md file, an AI jailbreak prompt that was never loaded. Socket says this points to AI-assisted malware writing and an attempt to fool AI-based review.

The campaign also faked its reputation. Over about two days, the Phantom listing’s reviews jumped from 275 to 546, and its rating rose from 2.9 to 3.9.

That pushed down one-star reviews from users who said they lost funds, though those claims are unverified. The listings had only one to three daily users, but the servers were active.

The group looks like a repeat offender, much like the earlier Offside Wallet Theft Factory campaign that Socket tied to 77 Firefox add-ons.

Wallet users should install extensions only through links on the wallet maker’s official website, not through store search. No real wallet will ask for a recovery phrase on a web page.

Anyone who typed a phrase or key into one of these add-ons should create a new wallet on a clean device and move their funds right away.

Deleting the extension does not make a leaked phrase safe. Security teams should block the bonto[.]io domain and its subdomains and look for extensions that fetch settings and then run the result as code.

Browser add-ons are not the only wallet risk. The Odyssey Stealer campaign shows that attackers also hunt wallet data on desktops.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.]) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM.

articles.description:
Attackers are sending fake court notices to organizations in Colombia and using them to install XWorm, a remote access tool that gives criminals full control of an infected PC. The emails look like real legal letters. The attached files are hidden Windows scripts that quietly start the infection. The lure works because few people ignore […]

The post Hackers Use Fake Court Notices to Deliver XWorm Malware Through Hidden Windows Scripts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are sending fake court notices to organizations in Colombia and using them to install XWorm, a remote access tool that gives criminals full control of an infected PC. The emails look like real legal letters.

The attached files are hidden Windows scripts that quietly start the infection. The lure works because few people ignore a message that says a court case needs urgent attention. The emails are written in Spanish and come from Colombian organizations.

The file names copy real administrative and legal papers, so a busy employee may open the file without a second thought. Behind that file sits a long chain of hidden steps, similar to the new XWorm infection chain seen last year.

Researchers at Arctic Wolf Labs published their findings on GitHub on October 26, 2026. They noted that the campaign targets Colombian organizations.

They also found that the final loader matches one used in a separate September 2026 XWorm case linked to the UK, which suggests the attackers are reusing their tools.

Hackers Use Fake Court Notices

The infection starts with an email that carries a VBScript or JavaScript file. Some files arrive inside ZIP archives, and the second-stage files are downloaded from public file-hosting services such as Filestack and ImageKit.

File names like “ACTA_NOTIFICA_TUTELA.js” and “PROCESO DISCIPLINARIO_ RAD_00470032.vbs” are meant to look like real legal papers.

Courts in Colombia are a common theme for local criminals, and the same trick appeared in Blind Eagle-linked phishing campaigns that also used fake judicial messages.

Once the victim opens the script, it does not show any warning. Instead, it unlocks a hidden PowerShell command. The script is heavily scrambled to avoid detection.

The VBScript version uses a custom Base93 decoder and several layers of encryption, while the JavaScript samples use other encryption methods and randomly generated function names. This makes it very hard for antivirus tools to spot the real purpose of the file.

The hidden PowerShell code then unpacks two files: a .NET DLL called RSG_UnityApp and the XWorm program itself. PowerShell loads the DLL and passes it the path to RegAsm.exe, a trusted Windows tool, along with the XWorm code.

The loader injects XWorm into RegAsm.exe, so the malware runs inside a program that looks normal. Security teams that only watch for unknown files can easily miss this step.

What XWorm Can Do and How to Defend Against It

After it starts, XWorm reads its hidden settings and contacts its command server. It sends back details about the PC, including the user name, system details, hardware, antivirus status, and whether a webcam is present.

Traffic is encrypted with AES-128-ECB, and every message begins with its length followed by a null byte. The researchers saw commands for running shell commands, capturing the screen, managing files, loading plugins, and starting DDoS traffic.

XWorm is sold as a service, so many criminals can buy it, and it often ranks high in weekly malware threat rankings. The researchers found three command servers, and the same servers appear in public sandbox records under different sample hashes and mutexes.

This points to several separate builds that share the same infrastructure. Arctic Wolf also saw the same loader deliver DCRat in another sample.

Defenders should watch for wscript.exe or cscript.exe starting PowerShell, especially with hidden or encoded commands. They should also flag RegAsm.exe when it runs after PowerShell, creates suspended processes, or makes network connections.

Checking DNS and firewall logs for the domains and ports below is a quick way to find infected systems. Staff should confirm any court notice through an official channel and never open unexpected script files, which are among the common XWorm delivery methods.
