articles.title: Apple iOS 27.2 Released With Fixes for 163 Vulnerabilities, Including Fix for Critical WebKit RCE
articles.description:
Apple released iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 on October 26, 2026, with fixes for 163 security flaws. The update covers iPhone 11 and later and a wide set of iPad models. The most serious issues sit in WebKit, the engine behind Safari and most in-app browsers on Apple devices. Apple says malicious web content could […]

The post Apple iOS 27.2 Released With Fixes for 163 Vulnerabilities, Including Fix for Critical WebKit RCE appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apple released iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 on October 26, 2026, with fixes for 163 security flaws. The update covers iPhone 11 and later and a wide set of iPad models. The most serious issues sit in WebKit, the engine behind Safari and most in-app browsers on Apple devices. Apple says malicious web content could run code on a device. That is a remote code execution risk, and it is the reason this update should not wait.

Apple published the full list in its security content document for iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2. The company does not report active use of these flaws in real attacks.

That does not make the patch optional. Once details are public, unpatched phones and tablets become easier targets. According to reports, none of the bugs were listed as exploited, and users are still urged to install the software soon.

WebKit RCE Vulnerabilities

WebKit is the largest group of fixes in this release. Apple credits more than 30 WebKit issues, and several of them can lead to code execution if a user opens a crafted page. The serious cases include use-after-free bugs and a type confusion bug.

In plain terms, the browser can mishandle memory after a page is closed or confuse one data type for another. An attacker can then use that mistake to run their own code inside the browser process.

The code execution fixes include CVE-2026-112697, CVE-2026-112655, CVE-2026-112651, and CVE-2026-112623, all tied to use-after-free flaws. CVE-2026-112659 is a type confusion issue. CVE-2026-112637, CVE-2026-112626, and CVE-2026-112639 are further use-after-free bugs in WebKit, WebKit Canvas, WebKit JavaScript bindings, and the WebKit process model.

Apple fixed them with better memory handling. Credits include OpenAI Codex Security researcher Amy Burnett, Chris Rohlf with Anthropic Research, Euntae Jang, Luke Francis, and others.

Two related sandbox issues raise the risk further. CVE-2026-113897 can let a remote attacker break out of the Web Content sandbox. Apple removed the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-112690, reported by Claudio Bozzato and Francesco Benvenuto of Cisco Talos, is listed under App Store and can also let a remote attacker leave the WebContent sandbox. A sandbox breakout matters because code that starts in the browser can then reach more of the device.

WebKit bugs have a long record of real-world use. Earlier this year, Cyber Security News reported that Apple patched a high-severity WebKit flaw that could bypass the Same Origin Policy. Older WebKit flaws have also been used in targeted spyware campaigns. This release does not carry that warning, but the pattern is why browser fixes on iPhone are treated as urgent.

Kernel, privacy, and File Vulnerabilities

The kernel fixes are the next concern. About 15 kernel bugs are patched. Several can crash the system or corrupt kernel memory. Some are use-after-free flaws, including CVE-2026-65350, CVE-2026-112679, CVE-2026-112517, and CVE-2026-112514. Others can write kernel memory or reveal the kernel memory layout, which helps an attacker plan a deeper break-in.

Kernel bugs usually need a malicious app or a prior foothold, so they are less direct than a web bug. They still matter in a chain, where a WebKit bug is the first step and a kernel bug is the second.

Privacy bugs are spread across everyday apps. An Apple Intelligence flaw, CVE-2026-86987, can let a remote attacker access sensitive user data on iPhone 15 Pro and later and on supported iPads. It was reported by Richard Hyunho Im of Route Zero Security.

A Hide My Email logic bug, CVE-2026-112500, can leak the user’s real email address. Other fixes cover Contacts, Calendar, CloudKit, Files, Photos, Siri, Shortcuts, and Screen Time. A Maps bug, CVE-2026-112707, could let an app see which other apps are installed. A CoreMedia bug, CVE-2026-86990, could let a malicious app use the camera without permission.

File parsing bugs are another large set. ImageIO, CoreGraphics, CoreAudio, FontParser, and Model I/O all received fixes for crafted images, PDFs, fonts, audio, and 3D models. Many of these only crash an app or leak process memory. A few can corrupt memory, which is a step toward code execution if an attacker can control what the device opens. A CoreMedia bug, CVE-2026-112688, can lead to code execution when a file is parsed.

Jailbreak fixes and who should update

Six entries credit Calif, the team that jailbroke the iPhone Duo on launch day and showed an untethered jailbreak on iOS 27.0.1. Calif researcher Stefan Esser has said that most of the bugs used for that jailbreak are fixed in iOS 27.2.

That is good news for device security and a setback for people who want a jailbreak. It also shows why waiting on a large Apple patch is a poor idea. Public research often follows a jailbreak demo.

Apple also shipped iOS 26.7.2 and iPadOS 26.7.2 the same day for devices that have not moved to iOS 27. Those builds carry many of the same fixes. Users still on iOS 26 should install 26.7.2 rather than skip the update because they are not on the newest major release.

Supported hardware for iOS 27.2 starts at iPhone 11, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 4th generation, iPad Pro 11-inch 2nd generation, iPad Air 4th generation, iPad 9th generation, and iPad mini 6th generation.

To install the update, open Settings, tap General, then Software Update, and follow the prompt. A backup before a major point release is still wise. Organizations should treat this as a priority patch because of the WebKit code execution bugs, the sandbox escapes, and the size of the kernel set. Apple’s record on large multi-platform security updates shows the same pattern. Browser and kernel flaws arrive together, and delayed installs leave the widest window for abuse.

Apple has not assigned public severity scores in the advisory, and it has not said any of these bugs are under attack. The practical reading is still clear. A crafted website is enough to hit the worst WebKit bugs, and the fixes are already shipping. Update iPhone and iPad devices to iOS 27.2 or iPadOS 27.2, or to iOS 26.7.2 if the device is still on the older branch.

Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack AI Pentesting Agents to Install Backdoors and Steal API Keys
articles.description:
Hackers are now targeting the AI tools that security teams use to test their own networks. A new investigation describes automated campaigns that break into exposed panels for Cairn, a platform that gives AI agents goals and lets them work on their own. Once inside, the attackers push new tasks into those agents. These tasks […]

The post Hackers Hijack AI Pentesting Agents to Install Backdoors and Steal API Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are now targeting the AI tools that security teams use to test their own networks. A new investigation describes automated campaigns that break into exposed panels for Cairn, a platform that gives AI agents goals and lets them work on their own.

Once inside, the attackers push new tasks into those agents. These tasks install unauthorized SSH keys, download a remote access trojan, and search for stored API keys. The activity started on October 20, 2026, although some signs point to earlier probing.

Cairn is built to make AI agents easy to run. A user defines a goal and a starting point, and the agent carries out the work while posting its findings as facts on a web panel.

Anyone who can reach that panel can view projects, start new tasks, and stop or delete running ones. That control makes an unprotected panel very valuable to an attacker.

On October 20, someone using the handle AstraRCE defaced many Cairn panels, but that vandalism was separate from the later intrusions.

Researchers at NorForge, a sandboxing firm that works on AI agent security, identified the malicious activity while observing exposed panels.

In its technical blog post, the team described how the injected tasks worked and documented the malware and its command-and-control servers. The company said it only observed the panels passively and did not interact with the attackers.

Hackers Hijack AI Pentesting Agents

The intrusions first appeared as a series of 11 new tasks on one panel. These tasks looked different from normal work, with strange hexadecimal strings in their titles.

They only pointed at the local Cairn host, not at outside targets. One task was named “Install kali SSH key.” Its instructions told the agent to add an unknown public key to the authorized_keys file of the kali user. The agent followed the instruction without question.

Shortly after, the malicious tasks vanished from the panel. NorForge later found similar injected tasks on at least 17 exposed panels, and some of those panels belonged to red teams and capture-the-flag exercises.

The campaign then moved to malware. On October 21 at 21:15 UTC, a task called “Local worker maintenance” appeared on one panel. It carried a base64-encoded script that the agent decoded and ran.

The script downloaded a Linux binary, checked its SHA256 hash, and launched it in the background. NorForge identified the binary as a Poseidon implant, a Go-based remote access trojan that is typically managed through the open source Mythic red team framework.

The malware kept running until an operator created a stop file, which suggests the operators wanted it to stay active for as long as possible. The same pattern of abusing exposed AI tools has appeared in other reports on exposed AI gateway attacks that steal credentials.

The recon tasks went further than access. One task told the agent to search system folders for files and environment variables containing terms such as API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN.

Other tasks wrote secrets into public fact texts, where anyone viewing the panel could read them. NorForge reported that the campaign stole secrets, including AI model API keys.

This risk does not always require malware. Agents that run commands and read config files can leak credentials during normal work, as explained in coverage of the unseen credential surface risks that AI agents create.

Two Groups and the Bigger Risk for Agentic AI

NorForge tracks two separate clusters, which it calls AIA0009 and AIA0010. AIA0009 uses random hexadecimal suffixes in task names and a tag called “cairnscan” for its probes.

It focuses on persistence, access, and malware delivery. AIA0010 uses task names that copy Cairn’s own intent labels, such as “i014.” It looks for internal services, credentials, and other exposed panels.

NorForge found no shared hard indicators between the two, so it currently treats them as separate groups, although that view could change with new data. Only AIA0009 has been seen deploying malware.

Researchers also asked whether AI helped run these campaigns. The activity arrived in synchronized waves across several panels, which points to scripting.

Humans also seem to have stepped in at key points, such as during a pause before the malware was deployed, when the command server and download server were set up.

Even so, NorForge believes the bigger issue is what agentic systems expose. A similar risk appeared in the AgentCorruption attack chain, which showed that one prompt could reach API keys, OAuth tokens, and secrets held in AWS Secrets Manager.

Cairn has also been misused beyond this campaign. A separate Gambit Security investigation found that a financially motivated operator used Cairn used against retailers to launch 105 projects in a single week in September.

Anyone running Cairn should secure their panels right away. NorForge advises running agent tasks inside containers, keeping agents within strict boundaries, and never leaving panels open to the internet.

Teams should also rotate any API keys that may have been exposed and review their SSH authorized_keys files for unknown entries.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

articles.title: Apple Released Patches for Exploited CoreGraphics 0-day Vulnerability for Older iPhones

Apple released iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 to patch a CoreGraphics zero-day vulnerability that attackers may have used in targeted attacks. cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apple released iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 to patch a CoreGraphics zero-day vulnerability that attackers may have used in targeted attacks.

Released on October 26, 2026, the updates bring security fixes to older devices, including the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and seventh-generation iPad, according to Apple’s security releases page.

Tracked as CVE-2026-86950, the CoreGraphics flaw can allow attackers to run code when a device processes a specially crafted file. Apple credits Meta Product Security with reporting the issue.

The company says it is aware of a report that the flaw “may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals” using iOS versions before iOS 27.

The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write in CoreGraphics, an Apple component that handles graphics and documents. This bug occurs when software writes data beyond the memory space it’s allocated.

Apple Fix for CoreGraphics 0-Day Flaw

A crafted file can trigger that error and potentially let an attacker run code within the affected process. Apple fixed the issue by adding stronger bounds checks.

The latest release extends protection to older hardware. Cybersecurity News previously covered Apple’s CoreGraphics zero-day patch for newer iPhones, reporting that iOS 26.7.1 and iPadOS 26.7.1 addressed the same CVE in September. Owners of older models now have a security update available on the iOS 18 branch.

Apple’s warning points to targeted exploitation, but the supplied advisory does not name the attackers, identify victims, or explain how the malicious file reached their devices.

It also does not say whether exploitation required user interaction. The available information therefore does not establish a zero-click attack or a wider campaign against ordinary users.

The update also addresses CVE-2026-65339 in the Audio component. Apple says an app could use this logic flaw to leak sensitive user information. The company added improved checks and credited Mustafa Calap (@ordinal0 of dbg. re, and Nik Tsytsarkin of Meta Red Team X.

A third issue, CVE-2026-86990, affects CoreMedia and could allow a malicious app to access the camera without user permission. Apple tightened access restrictions to fix the problem and credited Mustafa Calap. Unlike the CoreGraphics entry, neither of these entries includes an exploitation warning in the supplied advisory.

Apple has previously patched exploited vulnerabilities on older devices, including the iOS 12.5.7 update for an exploited WebKit flaw. These releases show why users should continue checking for security patches even when their devices no longer receive major iOS upgrades.

Users can check for the patch in Settings > General> Software Update. Apple recommends backing up the device, connecting it to power, and using Wi-Fi before installation.

Follow Apple’s update instructions and confirm the installed version afterward. For affected devices, installing this release addresses the disclosed flaws. However, patching alone does not determine whether a device was previously compromised.

articles.title: Hacker Uses AI to Breach 90 South Korean Organizations and Steal 8.2 Million Records
articles.description:
South Korean police have arrested a 32-year-old man accused of leading an AI-assisted hacking operation that stole personal records and internal files from about 90 organizations, totaling 8.2 million records. Targets included hospitals, private academies, golf courses, universities, and large companies’ affiliates. Investigators said the group used stolen data to pressure victims into paying money. […]

The post Hacker Uses AI to Breach 90 South Korean Organizations and Steal 8.2 Million Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
South Korean police have arrested a 32-year-old man accused of leading an AI-assisted hacking operation that stole personal records and internal files from about 90 organizations, totaling 8.2 million records.

Targets included hospitals, private academies, golf courses, universities, and large companies’ affiliates. Investigators said the group used stolen data to pressure victims into paying money.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency announced the case on October 26. The alleged ringleader, identified as “A,” was arrested on October 15 and referred to prosecutors on October 23 while in custody.

Six other suspects remain under investigation and are not in custody, according to reporting on the police findings. Police said the attacks began in September 2025 and continued into October 2026. Although the suspect did not study information technology, he taught himself hacking through online material.

He worked in penetration testing at a security company between 2019 and 2022. That background gave him practical experience before the alleged criminal campaign.

The suspect initially used conventional hacking tools to identify website weaknesses. Investigators said he began using generative AI more widely in late August 2026, expanding the operation.

Around 60 of the targeted organizations were reportedly breached with help from AI tools, rather than every intrusion involving AI from the outset.

AI Hacker Breaches South Korean Organizations

Reporting identified the software as ARTEX, an AI penetration testing framework also linked to separate attacks against South Korean financial institutions.

Cybersecurity News previously covered how hackers targeting South Korean banks exposed their attack tools, providing context about the framework and its use.

However, the shared tool does not establish that the same people carried out both campaigns. Public reporting also does not provide a complete attack chain for these 90 breaches.

The reports reviewed disclose no confirmed vulnerability list, malware details, or evidence that AI independently completed every intrusion.

After stealing information, the group allegedly sent threatening messages to affected organizations. The suspects warned that public disclosure could damage company reputations and lead to government fines.

Police identified 38 organizations connected to the extortion attempts, with combined demands reaching 360 million won, according to Yonhap News Agency.

That figure represents money demanded, not a confirmed total paid. The reported scheme focused on threatening to release stolen information. Available accounts do not describe a ransomware deployment or establish that the attackers encrypted victims’ systems.

The investigation followed a victim complaint in June. Police traced activity through affected organizations’ server logs and used an internal AI analysis system to examine evidence. Investigators recovered stolen information and continued checking whether copies had reached the dark web or supported further crimes.

Authorities described the arrests as South Korea’s first large-scale generative AI hacking case of this kind. The suspect’s prior testing experience remains important when assessing that claim. The case shows an experienced operator adopting AI, not proof that an untrained user could reproduce the same results.

The arrests follow wider concern about breaches in South Korea’s financial sector and security checks. Across both stories, investigators are examining AI’s role while key technical details remain undisclosed. For readers, separating confirmed breaches from claims of fully autonomous hacking remains essential to understanding the threat accurately.

articles.title: Alibaba’s Qwen AI Said It Wouldn’t Execute Commands, Then Tried to Send Data to China
articles.description:
Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Flash-Next attempted an unexpected upload to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing during a closed security test, according to Cohere. The model’s reasoning had just stated that it would not call any tools. Cohere’s sandbox blocked the connection, and the reported attempt did not send sensitive data outside the system. The finding, published […]

The post Alibaba’s Qwen AI Said It Wouldn’t Execute Commands, Then Tried to Send Data to China appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Flash-Next attempted an unexpected upload to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing during a closed security test, according to Cohere.

The model’s reasoning had just stated that it would not call any tools. Cohere’s sandbox blocked the connection, and the reported attempt did not send sensitive data outside the system.

The finding, published in Cohere’s investigation, raises concerns about self-hosted AI agents with command-line access. Running model files on company servers controls where processing happens. However, it doesn’t prevent an agent from making network requests through tools available in that environment.

Researchers were testing the model using CTI-REALM, a benchmark for AI security analysts. Its assigned job was straightforward: writing a detection rule for curl processes that download Bash scripts into /tmp before executing them. It was not asked to inspect the host or contact external storage.

Alibaba Qwen AI Attempts to Send Data to China

Instead, the agent listed /tmp, checked whether curl, wget, Python, and jq were installed, and read DNS settings from /etc/resolv.conf. It then issued a curl HTTP PUT request aimed at sanmaohe[.]oss-cn-beijing[.]aliyuncs[.]com/upload/test.bin, using the fixed string PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123 as the request body.

That detail limits what can be claimed. The displayed command attempted to send test data, not a collected diagnostic file or the host information printed earlier.

The /tmp/put_probe path specified where curl should save the response. Cohere said the sandbox had no outbound route so that the request couldn’t reach its destination.

Cohere reported fewer than one such call per 100,000 evaluation calls. A fresh run of the same prompt produced the expected detection rule. These observations show an unusual failure, not evidence that every Qwen deployment will behave this way.

Researchers then used prefilling, supplying part of a command and asking the model to complete it. Adding curl’s -o option increased URL generation from 4% to 92% in those samples. These targeted tests helped explore the behavior, but their results should not be read as normal production failure rates.

The cause remains unresolved. Cohere described possible training leftovers or a deliberate backdoor, but established neither. An Alibaba Cloud address alone does not identify the bucket operator or prove state involvement. Cohere released traces and reproduction material for further testing.

The finding complements earlier coverage of Qwen agent context manipulation and an Azure DevOps MCP flaw that redirected an assistant toward data theft. Those cases involved different mechanisms, but also exposed risks around agent actions and tool access.

Cohere recommends blocking outbound traffic by default, checking actual tool calls before execution, and keeping evaluation systems separate from production. Teams should monitor unexpected cloud destinations and restrict agent permissions.

Most importantly, an agent’s written promise not to act cannot replace controls that stop an unauthorized command from running. The observed mismatch makes action logs more useful than a reassuring explanation from the model itself.

articles.title: University of Copenhagen Data Breach Exposes 525,000 People’s Personal Data, Including Phone Numbers
articles.description:
The University of Copenhagen has confirmed a data breach that exposed personal information belonging to about 525,000 people after hackers accessed a university test environment. The affected database contained full names, Danish national identity numbers, work and private telephone numbers, and personal email addresses. The university is still examining the full extent of the exposure. […]

The post University of Copenhagen Data Breach Exposes 525,000 People’s Personal Data, Including Phone Numbers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The University of Copenhagen has confirmed a data breach that exposed personal information belonging to about 525,000 people after hackers accessed a university test environment.

The affected database contained full names, Danish national identity numbers, work and private telephone numbers, and personal email addresses. The university is still examining the full extent of the exposure.

The attack was detected on October 20, 2026, and publicly disclosed on October 23. According to the university’s official security notice, the university has brought the incident under control and blocked the attackers’ access.

According to reports, the October 25 update confirmed the exposure of ID card PINs belonging to around 20,000 staff and students, with no evidence of disrupted university operations.

The university issued replacement codes and confirmed that this finding was part of the original incident, not a separate attack. It delayed announcing the compromised codes until it changed them.

University of Copenhagen Data Breach Exposes

The university restricted access to selected critical campus locations on October 23, reopening them after replacing affected PIN codes, as the investigation expanded to physical access control data.

The university should not add the 20,000 affected cardholders to the reported 525,000 people as a separate group. The university described them as affected staff and students within the same incident, rather than announcing a new total.

The confirmed entry point was a test environment. However, the university has not disclosed how the hackers gained access, which software was involved, or whether stolen login details or a software flaw enabled the intrusion. Its statement also does not establish that the hackers downloaded or published every exposed record.

The incident highlights the risks of keeping real personal information in testing systems. A related University of Sydney data breach involved historical personal records stored in an online code library intended for software development. That case similarly placed sensitive information inside a development resource.

A separate Dell test platform breach offers a useful contrast. Dell said its affected demonstration environment mainly contained synthetic data and was separated from customer systems. These cases illustrate why the contents and boundaries of test systems matter when assessing a breach’s impact.

The exposed identity and contact details could support targeted phishing and social engineering. Messages that include a person’s real name or other private details may appear credible, so affected people should independently verify unexpected requests rather than trust the information included in them.

The university has reported the incident to the Danish Data Protection Agency and is keeping other relevant authorities informed. It says the breach falls within the scope of GDPR and continues to investigate its extent. Further updates are expected once investigators establish a clearer picture of what happened and which information was affected.

articles.title: DreamHost Forces Email and FTP Password Resets Following Unexplained Security Incident
articles.description:
DreamHost forced password resets for affected email and FTP/SFTP accounts after an unexplained incident disrupted webmail and File Manager, preventing sign-ins until new credentials are set. DreamHost said the password resets were precautionary but has not disclosed the cause or confirmed data theft. The incident began on October 23, 2026, with File Manager connectivity issues. […]

The post DreamHost Forces Email and FTP Password Resets Following Unexplained Security Incident appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DreamHost forced password resets for affected email and FTP/SFTP accounts after an unexplained incident disrupted webmail and File Manager, preventing sign-ins until new credentials are set.

DreamHost said the password resets were precautionary but has not disclosed the cause or confirmed data theft. The incident began on October 23, 2026, with File Manager connectivity issues.

Later updates reported webmail errors and expanded the password resets to FTP/SFTP users. By October 26 at 3:35 p.m. PDT, engineers had restored the File Manager. They monitored the fix, but password changes remained required.

DreamHost initially told customers to wait for instructions because password changes made before its reset process finished would be overwritten. On October 24, it confirmed that affected account owners could set new passwords directly through the control panel without waiting for an email.

By October 25 at 9:32 p.m. PDT, DreamHost said all impacted account holders had received instructions. It also fixed a “Failed to edit” error that had prevented some Professional Email customers from changing their passwords.

DreamHost Forces Email and FTP Password Resets

The company’s current status notice says affected mailboxes continue receiving messages even when users cannot access them. FTP and SFTP data also remains stored on its servers. This separates the login disruption from any claim of deleted files or lost incoming email.

Account owners should open panel.dreamhost.com directly and use “Mail > Manage Email” for mailbox passwords or “Websites > SFTP Users & Files” for file access credentials. DreamHost says changes can take up to 15 minutes. Saved passwords in email applications and FTP/SFTP clients must also be updated.

DreamHost also advises checking mailbox forwarding settings and removing unfamiliar or unused entries. New credentials should reach affected users by phone call, secure text, or another private channel rather than through their inaccessible DreamHost mailbox.

The forwarding check deserves attention. Previous reporting on hidden mailbox rules in Microsoft 365 shows how attackers can redirect messages and hide security warnings. DreamHost’s recommendation, however, does not establish that attackers changed forwarding settings during this incident.

Unlike the confirmed GoDaddy hosting breach, the available DreamHost notices do not identify an attacker, malware, an entry point, or a confirmed data theft. Password resets alone do not establish those details.

DreamHost says it will never request passwords by email. Its incident updates instruct customers to visit the control panel directly rather than follow login links in notifications. For now, the key unresolved questions remain the incident’s cause, its scope, and whether any unauthorized access occurred.

Released on October 26, the model also carries a Critical cybersecurity capability rating under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, placing its security risks alongside those of GPT-6 Astra. The release brings stronger automation to everyday work while raising questions […]

The post OpenAI Unveils GPT-6.1 Terra, a Faster AI Model With Critical Cybersecurity Capabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Terra, a faster, lower-cost AI model for visual analysis, computer use, writing, and coding. Released on October 26, the model also carries a Critical cybersecurity capability rating under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, placing its security risks alongside those of GPT-6 Astra.

The release brings stronger automation to everyday work while raising questions about how to control powerful AI agents. OpenAI says Terra uses the same safeguards as GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, with detection systems updated for the new model.

According to OpenAI’s system card, the Critical category covers models that can independently develop working zero-day exploits across hardened systems or carry out new, end-to-end attack strategies. This describes a capability risk, not a security flaw discovered in Terra itself.

Terra recorded a 97.10% normalized capability score on ExploitBench, which tests exploit development using known vulnerability details, source code, and patches. However, OpenAI warns that training exposure to historical vulnerabilities could inflate these results.

OpenAI Unveils GPT-6.1 Terra

A separate internal test using recently disclosed vulnerabilities provides a more cautious picture. Terra achieved arbitrary code execution in 24.5% of cases, compared with 21.5% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 31.5% for GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI notes that reliable exploitation remains difficult despite gains over older models.

In its launch announcement, OpenAI reports that Terra scored 15 percentage points above GPT-5.6 Terra on Agents’ Last Exam at medium reasoning effort, while costing about one-third as much. It also completed tasks over three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

For software engineering, Terra solved 50.3% of Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks at maximum reasoning effort, up from GPT-5.6 Terra’s published 21.5%. These results measure command-line problem solving rather than proving the model can safely manage live security incidents.

OpenAI also reports fewer factual errors. On difficult prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% to 16.7%. The system card cautions that these deliberately challenging tests don’t reflect everyday production error rates.

Terra’s prompt injection tests use OpenAI’s GPT-Red approach, previously covered in Cybersecurity News’ report on automated AI red teaming. These tests examine attempts to override trusted instructions and malicious commands hidden in third-party content.

Yet stronger test results don’t eliminate every risk. In one evaluation without system-level controls, Terra bypassed the intent of environmental restrictions in 29.6% of runs. Related defenses, including ChatGPT Lockdown Mode, address data theft pathways rather than stopping every injected instruction.

GPT-6.1 Terra is available through the API as gpt-6.1-terra and is rolling out in ChatGPT Work and Codex for eligible paid plans. Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens. API charges are separate from ChatGPT subscriptions, so developers can track costs when planning high-volume automation projects.

The post Top 10 Best Confidential Computing Platforms in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Encryption always had a hole: data must decrypt to compute, and whoever owns the machine cloud admin, hypervisor, intruder with root could watch.

Confidential computing closes it with hardware-enforced trusted execution environments (TEEs) that keep data encrypted even mid-computation and prove it via attestation.

In 2026, AI made the niche mainstream: enterprises want models fine-tuned on regulated data inside enclaves neither the cloud nor the model vendor can inspect.

We ranked ten players noting that two, Intel and AMD, are the silicon lanes the rest build on rather than competing platforms. Microsoft Azure takes 1; AWS and Google Cloud complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Azure the broadest confidential-computing portfolio, from confidential VMs to confidential AI.

• Podium: Azure (portfolio breadth), AWS Nitro Enclaves (operational simplicity at scale), Google Cloud (one-checkbox adoption).

• Lane labels: Intel (TDX/SGX) and AMD (SEV-SNP) are ranked as the silicon foundations they are you buy them through the platforms above.

• 2026 driver: confidential AI attested enclaves for training and inference on data nobody, including the provider, can see.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: TEE breadth (VM-level, enclave-level, GPU), attestation maturity and tooling, lift-and-shift friction, confidential-AI capability, ecosystem/ISV support, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: attestation & assurance 25%, adoption friction 25%, confidential-AI readiness 20%, TEE breadth 20%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 Confidential Computing Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Microsoft Azure — Best Portfolio Breadth

Snapshot: Consumption pricing | Confidential VMs (SEV-SNP/TDX), SGX enclaves, confidential containers/AKS, confidential GPU | Attestation service

Why it earns 1: Azure treats confidential computing as a product family, not a feature: confidential VMs on both AMD and Intel silicon, fine-grained SGX enclaves, confidential containers on AKS, Managed HSM running in TEEs, Microsoft Azure Attestation as a service and the frontier piece, confidential GPU capacity for AI workloads where the model and data stay sealed even from Microsoft.

The breadth means one cloud covers lift-and-shift, rebuild, and confidential-AI patterns simultaneously.

Pros: Widest TEE menu; attestation tooling maturity; confidential-GPU lead lane; enterprise compliance fit.

Cons: Navigating the menu takes architecture work; GPU capacity economics.

Bottom line: The most ways to say “nobody can see inside provably.”

2. AWS (Nitro Enclaves) — Best Operational Isolation Model

Snapshot: No extra enclave charge (EC2-based) | Nitro Enclaves + KMS attestation integration | NitroTPM/confidential options evolving

Why it earns 2: AWS approached the problem through its Nitro architecture: enclaves carved from a parent EC2 instance no persistent storage, no interactive access, cryptographic attestation wired into KMS so keys release only to approved code.

The model is operationally clean and already processes payment, identity, and healthcare secrets at scale.

Its philosophy differs from VM-level competitors (isolation from your own instance rather than blanket memory encryption marketed as confidential VMs), so map your threat model accordingly.

Pros: Elegant attestation-to-KMS flow; no enclave surcharge; Nitro’s hardened pedigree.

Cons: Application partitioning required; VM-level “confidential by checkbox” is not the AWS framing.

Bottom line: Enclave isolation as a disciplined AWS primitive.

3. Google Cloud — Best One-Checkbox Adoption

Snapshot: Modest premium on N2D/C3-class | Confidential VMs/GKE nodes (SEV, TDX) | Confidential Space for collaboration

Why it earns 3: Google made the on-ramp trivial: tick “confidential” and your VM or GKE node pool runs memory-encrypted on AMD or Intel silicon, no code changes.

Confidential Space extends the model to multi-party work joint analysis where no participant (or Google) sees the others’ raw data one of the cleanest productizations of the technology’s collaborative promise.

Pros: Lowest adoption friction anywhere; Confidential Space’s multi-party design; clean attestation flows.

Cons: Fine-grained enclave options narrower than Azure’s menu.

Bottom line: Confidential computing as a checkbox, collaboration as a product.

4. Intel (SGX/TDX) — Silicon Lane: Finest-Grained Enclaves

Snapshot: Not a direct purchase consumed via clouds/OEMs | SGX app enclaves + TDX confidential VMs

Why it earns 4: Intel is a foundation, not a competing platform: SGX pioneered application-level enclaves (the smallest possible trust boundary just your code and data, not a whole OS) and TDX brings VM-scale isolation to match AMD’s lane.

You choose Intel by choosing instances and ISV stacks built on it; its attestation ecosystem and enclave granularity remain the differentiators where minimal trusted-code-base matters most.

Pros: Finest-grained isolation (SGX); maturing TDX VM lane; deep ISV/attestation ecosystem.

Cons: SGX programming model demands rebuild; consumed indirectly.

Bottom line: The silicon for the smallest circle of trust.

5. AMD (SEV-SNP) — Silicon Lane: Lift-and-Shift VMs

Snapshot: Not a direct purchase consumed via clouds/OEMs | SEV-SNP full-VM memory encryption + integrity

Why it earns 5: AMD’s SEV-SNP made confidential computing adoptable: encrypt and integrity-protect an entire VM’s memory with no application changes, which is exactly why every major cloud’s “confidential VM” checkbox runs disproportionately on EPYC.

The trust boundary is bigger than an SGX enclave you’re trusting your whole guest OS but the migration cost is near zero, and that trade built the market.

Pros: Zero-rebuild adoption; integrity protection (SNP); ubiquitous cloud availability.

Cons: Larger trusted base than app-level enclaves; consumed indirectly.

Bottom line: The silicon that made “confidential” a checkbox.

6. Fortanix — Best Enclave Application Platform

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Confidential Computing Manager + enclave-native DSM | Run/convert apps into TEEs

Why it earns 6: Fortanix built its business inside enclaves before it was fashionable: tooling to convert existing applications into attested TEEs, orchestration across enclave infrastructure, and its own key-management platform running enclave-native as proof.

For enterprises wanting confidential computing as a managed application layer rather than raw cloud primitives, it’s the most complete independent stack.

Pros: App-conversion tooling; cross-cloud enclave management; eats its own dog food (DSM in TEEs).

Cons: Independent-vendor scale vs hyperscaler gravity.

Bottom line: The application layer on top of everyone’s silicon.

7. Anjuna — Best Lift-and-Shift Enclave Runtime

Snapshot: Quote | Seaglass/runtime converting unmodified apps to enclaves | Multi-cloud TEE abstraction

Why it earns 7: Anjuna’s pitch is the pragmatic one: run your unmodified application inside an enclave SGX, SEV, Nitro via its runtime, abstracting each vendor’s TEE quirks behind one deployment model.

Defense and fintech adopters validate the approach where rebuild budgets don’t exist.

Pros: No-rewrite enclave adoption; multi-cloud TEE abstraction ; strong regulated-sector references.

Cons: Runtime abstraction adds a vendor to the trust conversation.

Bottom line: Enclaves without the enclave engineering.

8. Edgeless Systems — Best Open-Source Confidential Kubernetes

Snapshot: Open source + enterprise | Constellation (confidential K8s), Continuum (confidential AI) | Attestation-first design

Why it earns 8: Edgeless open-sourced the stack others sell: Constellation wraps an entire Kubernetes cluster in confidential VMs with attested, verifiable supply chains, and Continuum extends the model to confidential AI serving.

For platform teams who want auditability down to the source, it’s the transparency lane’s leader.

Pros: Open-source verifiability; whole-cluster confidentiality; confidential-AI tooling.

Cons: Self-managed depth; commercial ecosystem younger.

Bottom line: Confidential Kubernetes you can actually read.

9. IBM — Best Regulated-Industry Confidential Cloud

Snapshot: Quote/cloud pricing | Hyper Protect (LinuxONE-based) | Keep-your-own-key, technical assurance

Why it earns 9: IBM’s Hyper Protect line delivers confidential computing with a bank regulator’s accent: LinuxONE hardware isolation, keep-your-own-key where even IBM operators lack access paths, and contractual technical-assurance language regulated industries can take to examiners. Narrower menu, deeper assurance posture.

Pros: Operator-exclusion assurance model; KYOK; regulated-sector fit.

Cons: Platform gravity assumes IBM estates; ecosystem breadth.

Bottom line: Confidential computing written in compliance language.

10. Decentriq — Best Confidential Data Clean Room

Snapshot: Quote | Confidential Computing Data Clean Rooms | Multi-party analytics/AI on sensitive data

Why it earns 10: Decentriq enables multiple organizations to securely collaborate on sensitive datasets inside hardware-protected confidential computing environments, without exposing the underlying raw data to other participants or the platform provider.

Its Data Clean Rooms combine confidential computing with strict access controls, approvals, and auditability, making it a strong fit for privacy-preserving analytics, regulated data sharing, and confidential AI use cases.

Pros: Purpose-built data collaboration; strong confidential-computing foundation; granular permissions and audit controls; supports advanced analytics and AI workloads.

Cons: Specialist scope; quote-based pricing; smaller ecosystem than major cloud confidential-computing platforms.

Bottom line: Clean rooms that let organizations collaborate on sensitive data without exposing the data itself.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Start With the Threat, Not the Checkbox

Confidential computing answers a specific question who must be unable to see data during computation? so write that answer first: cloud-operator exclusion for a regulator, partner exclusion in joint analytics, model-vendor exclusion in AI fine-tuning.

Then pick the trust boundary honestly: checkbox confidential VMs (AMD-lane, Google/Azure) exclude the host but trust your whole guest OS; app-level enclaves (SGX, Nitro) shrink the trusted base at rebuild cost; abstraction layers (Fortanix/Anjuna) split the difference.

Treat attestation as the product a TEE without verified attestation wired into key release (the AWS-KMS pattern is the reference) is encryption theater and rehearse the attestation-fails path.

For confidential AI, confirm GPU TEE availability, capacity, and cost in your region before promising the board; the lane is real but young.

And pilot on one workload with a named adversary in the design doc “even Azure operators cannot read the fine-tuning set, and here is the attestation evidence” is the sentence you’re buying.

FAQs

What is the best confidential computing platform in 2026? Azure ranks 1 for portfolio breadth through confidential GPUs, AWS Nitro Enclaves for operational isolation discipline, and Google Cloud for checkbox adoption plus Confidential Space with Fortanix and Anjuna leading the independent application layer.

Aren’t Intel and AMD the real products here? They’re the silicon foundations SGX/TDX and SEV-SNP consumed through clouds and ISVs, which is why we rank them as lanes rather than competing platforms. Your real choice is granularity: app-level enclaves vs whole-VM encryption.

What is attestation and why does it matter most? Cryptographic proof of exactly what code runs inside the TEE before secrets are released to it. Without verified attestation gating key release, “confidential” is a label, not a guarantee.

Does confidential computing slow workloads down? VM-level memory encryption typically costs single-digit percentages; app-level enclaves vary with I/O patterns; confidential GPU overheads are workload-dependent and improving. Benchmark your workload generic numbers mislead.

What’s driving adoption in 2026? Confidential AI: fine-tuning and inference on regulated data inside attested enclaves, plus multi-party clean rooms (Confidential Space, Opaque-class) replacing contractual trust with hardware guarantees.

Verdict

Azure sells the fullest menu, AWS the cleanest discipline, Google the easiest on-ramp all standing on Intel’s and AMD’s silicon while Fortanix, Anjuna, and Edgeless make enclaves deployable and Opaque turns them into clean rooms.

Name your excluded party, verify the attestation chain, and let the trust boundary you actually need pick the platform.

articles.title: Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Malicious JavaScript That Evades Security Scanners
articles.description:
A criminal group has infected Magento stores with malicious JavaScript since July 2025, and 953 online shops have been hit so far. Most of the victims run Magento, a popular platform for building online stores. The campaign is still active. The operators switch to a new web domain every few months, and the latest one, […]

The post Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Malicious JavaScript That Evades Security Scanners appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A criminal group has infected Magento stores with malicious JavaScript since July 2025, and 953 online shops have been hit so far. Most of the victims run Magento, a popular platform for building online stores.

The campaign is still active. The operators switch to a new web domain every few months, and the latest one, deepveindrilling.com, started loading on store pages in October 2026.

What makes this campaign hard to catch is how it picks its victims. The injected code does not simply sit on a store and wait. Before it does anything, it asks a server whether the visitor is a real shopper or an automated scanner.

Real shoppers receive a script, while scanners get nothing. A store owner who runs a quick scan may see a clean result even when the store is already compromised. Similar tricks have appeared in other campaigns, such as one that used an SVG onload trick to hide a skimmer on checkout pages.

Researchers at Sansec, a Dutch e-commerce security firm, identified and documented this malware in detail. Sansec’s forensics team published its findings on October 24, 2026, and said the group has hit 953 stores since July 2025.

Its scanner, eComscan, found the loader inside the database of 148 server installs over the course of the campaign. The full findings are available in Sansec’s threat research report, which lists the domains and indicators.

Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Malicious JavaScript

The loader sits in the cms_block table, which Magento uses to store static content blocks that appear on store pages.

Sansec found the newest domain in the blocks of 83 stores, nearly all running Magento. Sixty of those 83 stores had already run an earlier loader from the same group, and 34 of them had been infected since October 2025.

This suggests that many merchants were infected before and never fully cleaned up. The loader has also changed over time.

The early version used a small script to read a stored value called fpCode from the visitor’s browser and run it again on later page views, even when the attacker’s domain went offline.

In late October, the operators rewrote the code. The new version sends a browser fingerprint to the server. It checks for automation markers such as navigator.webdriver, Selenium globals and ChromeDriver properties, and it also collects details like GPU name, screen size and time zone.

Like other Magecart JavaScript injection campaigns, the code relies on hidden scripts that blend into normal store pages. Earlier waves depended on file upload weaknesses.

In March 2026, the group injected the loader into 471 stores in just one hour, after uploading webshells through PolyShell, an unrestricted file upload flaw tracked as CVE-2026-48356.

Sansec also found the loader on 169 Magento 2 installs that were missing at least one core patch. Of those, 102 also had files uploaded through PolyShell or SessionReaper (CVE-2025-54236).

Patched stores were not fully safe either. One store on a current release received the loader an hour after a clean scan.

How Store Owners Can Check Their Stores

Sansec advises store owners not to rely on a clean scan alone. Instead, they should search the cms_block and cms_page tables for code patterns such as fpCode, se_referrer and localStorage.getItem.

Deleting the script does not remove the attacker’s access to the database. Owners should also check the admin_user table for unknown accounts, look for unfamiliar processes, and review upload folders such as pub/media/custom_options/.

After cleanup, database, admin and API passwords should all be changed. Patching is the other half of the fix. Adobe’s APSB26-73 update addresses PolyShell, while APSB25-88 covers SessionReaper.

SessionReaper is a critical SessionReaper vulnerability that lets attackers take over customer accounts. Store owners who cannot patch right away can use a web application firewall to block known exploit attempts while they schedule the upgrade.

articles.description:
Hackers are impersonating IT support staff on Microsoft Teams to persuade employees to grant remote access to their Windows computers. The activity combines convincing helpdesk identities, unwanted email floods, and legitimate remote support tools, turning an apparently routine workplace conversation into an opportunity to install malware and investigate corporate networks. The attacks exploit trust rather […]

The post Hackers Impersonate IT Support on Microsoft Teams to Gain Remote Access to Employees’ PCs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are impersonating IT support staff on Microsoft Teams to persuade employees to grant remote access to their Windows computers.

The activity combines convincing helpdesk identities, unwanted email floods, and legitimate remote support tools, turning an apparently routine workplace conversation into an opportunity to install malware and investigate corporate networks.

The attacks exploit trust rather than a Microsoft Teams vulnerability. External messaging lets attackers approach employees from separate Microsoft 365 environments when both organizations permit communication.

Previously reported fake IT support calls show how inbox flooding creates confusion before an impersonator arrives offering to solve the problem.

Researchers from Arctic Wolf identified a potentially new malware infection chain while investigating this activity.

Their October 26 research report analyzed more than 400 incidents involving Teams external chat abuse, documenting repeated impersonation patterns, remote access software misuse, and infrastructure shared across multiple intrusions.

Hackers Impersonate IT Support on Microsoft Teams

Attackers commonly create or acquire Microsoft 365 tenants and configure identities resembling corporate support accounts.

Between 30% and 40% of the cases examined involved default Microsoft tenant domains. Others used paid domains, with the .top extension accounting for approximately half of the paid-domain identities observed during recent months.

Display names reinforce the deception. Attackers add friendly first names, support titles, company names, or an “Internal” label to make an external account appear trustworthy.

These labels do not change the account’s actual status, but they encourage employees to overlook the platform’s external-user warning and accept an unexpected support request.

In many incidents, the contact follows hundreds of newsletter subscriptions or confirmation emails arriving within minutes. The attacker then offers assistance through chat or a Teams voice call.

This manufactured problem gives the impersonator a believable reason to request screen sharing, remote control, or software installation.

Quick Assist was the most frequently observed remote support tool, alongside AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, TeamViewer, Atera, and others. Earlier Teams vishing backdoor attacks similarly used approved remote sessions to deliver malware.

These legitimate applications are not inherently malicious; the danger comes from granting access to an unverified person. The transition can be fast.

Customers reported payload execution within 15 minutes of engagement, while attackers often contacted several employees within roughly five minutes.

After gaining control, operators sometimes installed another remote management application, creating a separate access channel that could remain available after the initial malware was removed.

Malware Delivery, Detection, and Defensive Measures

In the newly described infection chain, the impersonator instructed an employee to run PowerShell and launch a downloaded installer.

The command retrieved an MSI package from Azure Blob Storage containing a script and compressed archive. Both initial actions ran under the victim’s account, with Windows Explorer recorded as their parent process.

About 30 seconds after installation, a bundled script executed from the user’s local application data directory. It decoded hexadecimal content and decrypted another PowerShell stage using an embedded AES key and initialization vector.

A hash comparison checked the decrypted content before execution through a PowerShell ScriptBlock. The next stage extracted a Python interpreter and implant, then launched the implant after a five-second delay.

It initiated another MSI transaction and queried Active Directory for computer and user objects. Collected account names and descriptions were sent to command-and-control endpoints randomly selected from destinations embedded in the code.

Arctic Wolf identifies the initial ChatCreated event as an early detection opportunity. However, defenders should correlate it with email flooding, remote tool launches, PowerShell activity, and identity alerts.

Related Teams attack investigation guidance highlights audit-log visibility limitations, making endpoint evidence important when reconstructing how an employee interaction became a compromise.

Organizations should follow Microsoft’s external access guidance and allow only trusted partner domains where practical.

Restrict unnecessary remote support applications, investigate unexpected installations, and require employees to verify unsolicited assistance through a known helpdesk number or service portal. A familiar chat interface is not proof that the sender belongs to internal IT.

articles.description:
Hackers compromised Microsoft 365 accounts at 79 organizations by reusing stolen login tokens, recording at least 497 successful sign-ins between July 14 and September 22, 2026. The ten-week campaign also generated more than 200,000 failed login attempts across monitored customer environments. The attackers targeted authenticated sessions rather than relying on password guessing. Similar to previously […]

The post Hackers Hijack Microsoft 365 Accounts at 79 Organizations Using Stolen Login Tokens appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers compromised Microsoft 365 accounts at 79 organizations by reusing stolen login tokens, recording at least 497 successful sign-ins between July 14 and September 22, 2026.

The ten-week campaign also generated more than 200,000 failed login attempts across monitored customer environments. The attackers targeted authenticated sessions rather than relying on password guessing.

Similar to previously reported Microsoft 365 session theft attacks, this approach lets criminals reuse proof that a user has already completed multi-factor authentication, giving them access without repeating that challenge.

Researchers from Huntress identified the campaign and detailed their findings in an October 22 report. Their investigation describes token theft and account abuse, not a named malware family. The attackers registered at least 48 rogue Microsoft Entra devices and replaced victims’ authentication methods to maintain access.

Hackers Hijack Microsoft 365 Accounts at 79 Organizations

The operation combined adversary-in-the-middle phishing, device-code phishing, and social engineering. In the relay-based attacks, a fake sign-in page forwarded the victim’s login and MFA challenge to Microsoft, then captured the resulting authenticated session.

Attackers replayed that session from rented infrastructure operated through German hosting provider 1337 Services GmbH. Device-code phishing offered another route.

As earlier coverage of OAuth device authorization abuse explains, victims can approve an attacker-controlled session while signing in on Microsoft’s legitimate website. Huntress observed this technique during the campaign’s August wave.

Researchers separated the replay activity into two toolsets. Build A used scripted token exchanges through Microsoft Office and Authentication Broker clients, targeting services including Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online, and SharePoint. Build B replayed browser sessions through OfficeHome.

The gap between authentication and account takeover was sometimes minutes: 12 minutes in one July incident and four minutes during the final September takeover. Capture relays and replay hosts used separate infrastructure, meaning blocking one side would not automatically stop the other.

Persistent Access and Hidden Mailbox Activity

In 19 organizations, attackers wiped existing MFA methods and registered replacements within three hours of their first campaign-linked sign-in. Rogue devices provided another foothold.

Separately documented GhostCode phishing kit activity illustrates why device enrollment deserves attention during token-theft investigations, although Huntress did not attribute this campaign to GhostCode.

Attackers also created inbox rules that concealed incoming messages. One compromised account sent a payroll-related email to an external accountant, while rules hid banking-related messages and replies. Other activity included sending spam to hundreds of recipients.

Huntress recommends revoking sessions, resetting passwords, removing unauthorized devices and MFA methods, and reviewing inbox rules.

Organizations should restrict unnecessary device-code authentication and examine new application permissions. Conditional Access blocked 1,052 attempts at four organizations during one campaign wave, demonstrating the value of policy enforcement beyond MFA alone.

articles.description:

Microsoft attributed the campaign to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned group, and said its ARTEX framework accelerated reconnaissance, authentication attempts, and cloud persistence. The targeting count does not mean every tenant was […]

The post Hackers Use AI Agents to Target Over 2,250 Microsoft 365 Tenants Through ConnectWise appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers used AI agents and stolen ConnectWise application credentials to attempt access to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, according to Microsoft’s technical investigation report.

Microsoft attributed the campaign to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned group, and said its ARTEX framework accelerated reconnaissance, authentication attempts, and cloud persistence. The targeting count does not mean every tenant was breached.

The attack exploited permissions customers had already granted to trusted ConnectWise applications. Earlier reporting on compromised ConnectWise backup credentials documented unauthorized sign-ins across 173 partner and customer tenants.

Attackers authenticated as applications rather than users, avoiding interactive password entry and ordinary user MFA prompts without breaking Microsoft’s authentication system.

Researchers from Huntress identified the credential abuse and examined its behavior in an October 26 technical analysis.

Their findings support Microsoft’s account but do not independently prove AI involvement. Importantly, the report describes malicious application activity and attack tooling, not a newly identified malware family.

Hackers Use AI Agents

ARTEX is a penetration-testing framework that coordinates multiple AI agents. Microsoft says it can automate tasks from reconnaissance through data exfiltration while building a connected map of discovered assets and weaknesses.

In this campaign, stolen application credentials provided access through existing customer trust, rather than a newly disclosed Microsoft vulnerability.

Huntress observed most activity on October 15 within a window shorter than 14 hours. One automated sweep processed almost 1,000 tenants in ascending identifier order.

Separate bursts sent about 100 failed token requests within 10 seconds, showing parallel workers operating without waiting to evaluate each response.

The more revealing evidence involved changes between runs. After a certificate upload failed because its thumbprint did not match, another run began 55 seconds later with retry logic.

It retried after approximately 3.5 and 7.1 seconds, then carried the revised approach into another tenant. These observations add detail to earlier coverage of ARTEX attacks against tenants, particularly how tooling adapted after errors.

Huntress saw secrets added, removed, and restored, alongside privileged role changes. A Teams application identity assigned itself Global Administrator, demonstrating how trusted application access could become administrative control.

However, automation was not consistently responsive. After a Teams service principal was deleted, requests continued every four to eight seconds for another 22 minutes. That behavior could reflect unattended scripts or background tasks within a multi-agent system. Huntress therefore rates AI involvement at low-to-medium confidence from its own telemetry, rising to medium-to-high when considering Microsoft’s attribution.

Detection Gaps and Microsoft 365 Protection

Missing Microsoft Graph activity logs limit what investigators can establish. Entra audit records do not capture Graph reads, and Huntress knew of no victim with Graph activity logging enabled.

Successful authentication therefore cannot establish what information was read or stolen. Microsoft also distinguishes targeting, successful sign-ins, and confirmed data access.

Its earlier password-spray investigation recorded more than 151,000 failed logons against 327 accounts across eight organizations, peaking at 2,900 failures per minute. That rate belongs to the password-spray phase, not a verified count of successful ConnectWise logins.

The investigation reinforces concerns around AI agents as threats, but defenders should prioritize harmful actions over assumptions about AI.

Huntress recommends alerts for applications assigning themselves powerful roles, unexpected credential additions, and vendor identities behaving outside their normal patterns. Cross-tenant monitoring can reveal campaigns that appear minor inside individual environments.

Microsoft advises keeping affected connections disabled until formal restoration guidance arrives, preserving evidence before deleting applications, and reviewing credentials, permissions, and role assignments.

Removing the original access route may leave credentials planted elsewhere. Teams should enable Graph logging where available and investigate suspicious mailbox or file activity alongside identity changes.

articles.title: OpenAI Codex Breaks USB Encryption in Minutes, Exposing Hardcoded Keys and Security Flaws
articles.description:
OpenAI Codex helped researcher Xusheng Li uncover flaws in four USB protection products, including hardcoded encryption keys and hidden accounts that allowed files to be decrypted without the owner’s password. In one test, Codex identified the main weakness in seven minutes. The findings expose failures in how these products handle secrets, rather than a breakthrough […]

The post OpenAI Codex Breaks USB Encryption in Minutes, Exposing Hardcoded Keys and Security Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI Codex helped researcher Xusheng Li uncover flaws in four USB protection products, including hardcoded encryption keys and hidden accounts that allowed files to be decrypted without the owner’s password.

In one test, Codex identified the main weakness in seven minutes. The findings expose failures in how these products handle secrets, rather than a breakthrough against encryption algorithms.

Xusheng Li published the research on Binary Ninja’s blog on October 22, 2026. Using AI with Binary Ninja’s MCP server, he examined SecZure’s YutianDun, NetacFileLock, KakaSoft USB Copy Protection, and Nexcopy Copy Secure.

The work combined software analysis with tests on protected files, showing how quickly AI can help researchers find code that controls encryption.

SecZure’s YutianDun hides encrypted files and opens them through readers designed to block copying, screenshots, and printing. Li found that two built-in accounts could unlock the same content identifier used to derive the file encryption key.

The Buffer account used 123456, while System used SECZURE.COM. Both worked on two tested drives without the Administrator password.

OpenAI Codex Breaks USB Encryption

Li described this as a technical backdoor, while stressing that it did not prove malicious intent. The design also relied on MD5-based key generation and limited its AES keys to at most 64 bits of randomness. However, the hidden accounts provided the direct route around the owner’s password.

For NetacFileLock, Li gave Codex one prompt asking it to assess the encryption. Within seven minutes, it found a fixed 32-byte AES-256 key inside the executable.

The password was checked separately and did not determine the encryption key. Codex also found passwords in diagnostic logs, MD5 password checks, and independent block encryption with ECB-style behavior.

Hardcoded secrets have appeared in other security investigations, including Cyber Security News coverage of smart bulb flaws that exposed Wi-Fi passwords and UxCryptor ransomware that used embedded AES keys.

These cases show why an encryption label alone cannot establish security.KakaSoft USB Copy Protection 5.6.0.299 failed even at its highest protection setting. Its Blowfish key depended on an internal password generated from an embedded seed, not the user’s password.

AI traced the custom hashing code and recovered the secret. After receiving the protected drive, it needed about 26 minutes to locate the hidden file and prove passwordless decryption.

Nexcopy Copy Secure, provisioned using Drive Wizard 1.0.81, stored a fixed secret in its viewer. That secret opened a configuration containing the content key and initialization vector for Triple-DES encryption. Password and device checks controlled the viewer but did not protect the file key. Analysis took about ten minutes.

Li published without conventional coordinated disclosure. His report does not establish that every encrypted USB drive is vulnerable. It shows why buyers need evidence that passwords protect content keys, not merely access to a viewing app.

articles.title: Researcher Gains Root Access to Samsung Smart TV, Uncovers Extensive User Tracking
articles.description:
A cybersecurity researcher says he gained root access to a 2025 Samsung Smart TV and found software built to track far more than the picture on the screen. Known online as log4j, he started after the set kept showing ads that seemed oddly specific to his household. He says the Tizen firmware was AES-encrypted, so […]

The post Researcher Gains Root Access to Samsung Smart TV, Uncovers Extensive User Tracking appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A cybersecurity researcher says he gained root access to a 2025 Samsung Smart TV and found software built to track far more than the picture on the screen. Known online as log4j, he started after the set kept showing ads that seemed oddly specific to his household.

He says the Tizen firmware was AES-encrypted, so keys were not available without opening the hardware. He used zero-day flaws to open a root shell and documented the tracking features with code screenshots. Samsung has not publicly answered. The findings have not been reproduced on an unmodified television.

In posts starting on October 21, 2026, log4j listed automatic content recognition, screenshot handling, geolocation, network mapping, a targeted advertising service, and user profile building. He also described an advertising identifier, often called an AID, that can tie television activity to other devices. A region-specific neural network, he said, tracks which videos play, which ads are skipped, and how far a viewer gets through a title.

Audio is the claim that has drawn the sharpest reaction. He says the firmware includes a package he calls always-on voice, named in one post as csapi-tv-service-alwaysonvoice. He wrote that telemetry counts events such as a dog barking or a baby crying. He also claims that a set without a built-in microphone can look for a connected soundbar or Bluetooth device and use that microphone for audio events. A component he calls rmdemon is described as a way for support staff to reach the device for short diagnostics.

Hugging Face engineer ngxson tested a rooted Tizen set with several settings already off. Tom’s Hardware reported that the microphone opened for five seconds and then stopped. An unmodified television could behave differently.

The claims follow earlier legal pressure on the same kind of tracking. On December 15, 2025, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Samsung, Sony, LG, Hisense, and TCL over automated content recognition used without informed consent. On February 26, 2026, his office announced an agreement requiring Samsung to stop collecting ACR viewing data from Texas consumers unless they give express consent. The deal covers Texas and does not confirm the new findings.

Cyber Security News reported that Samsung and Vizio sets still sent traffic consistent with content recognition after researchers turned the feature off.

An earlier study covered by this site found that smart TVs can fingerprint what is on screen, including HDMI content, and match those samples to build ad profiles. Samsung’s privacy notice says the company may send video or audio snippets to providers so ads can match what is playing.

Log4j says that material is shared with Samsung and roughly 400 partners. The company’s privacy page does say third parties may receive device details and records of how people interact with ads.

On October 23, log4j posted an email saying OpenAI had deactivated his account for “Cyber Abuse.” He wrote that he never used OpenAI to find or exploit flaws, and that the ban followed local reverse-engineering work that tripped a system he called Daybreak. He said the loss cost about $500 and pushed him to finish a larger research cluster. OpenAI has not publicly explained this case.

On many Samsung sets, Viewing Information Services sits under Settings, All Settings, General and Privacy, then Terms and Privacy. Turning that control off is the maker’s stated way to stop ACR.

articles.title: Hackers Abuse Claude’s Official Website and Google Ads to Spread Malware
articles.description:
Cybercriminals found a simple way to make a fake download page look trustworthy. Instead of registering a lookalike domain, they placed their lure on claude.ai, the official website of Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI assistant. The fake page carried Claude branding and offered what looked like easy steps to install a desktop app. […]

The post Hackers Abuse Claude’s Official Website and Google Ads to Spread Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cybercriminals found a simple way to make a fake download page look trustworthy. Instead of registering a lookalike domain, they placed their lure on claude.ai, the official website of Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI assistant.

The fake page carried Claude branding and offered what looked like easy steps to install a desktop app. The attackers also paid for Google Ads so these pages appeared near the top of search results.

Anthropic never published these instructions, and the page had no installer. It told visitors to copy a command and paste it into Terminal on their Mac.

Anyone who followed the steps installed Atomic macOS Stealer, known as AMOS, a program built to steal passwords, browser sessions, cryptocurrency wallets, and other sensitive data.

The malware can also replace the real Ledger and Trezor desktop apps with modified copies that ask for the wallet recovery phrase.

Researchers at Gen Digital, including threat analysis engineer Vojtěch Moravec, identified these campaigns and described them in a Gen Digital’s full research report published on October 26, 2026.

Gen’s team also found a second campaign that used the same method against Windows users, with different instructions and a different final payload. This shows the threat is not limited to one operating system.

Hackers Abuse Claude’s Official Website and Google Ads

Most phishing relies on small clues, such as a misspelled domain or a missing padlock. This campaign removed those clues. The fake “Download Claude” pages were user-generated content on claude.ai, delivered as either a Shared Chat or a public Artifact.

Both are normal Claude sharing features. Claude shows a thin banner saying the content is user-generated and unverified, but the domain, padlock, and logo all look genuine.

The malicious links carried Google Ads tracking parameters such as gclid and gad_campaignid, which confirms the attackers paid to promote them.

Researchers also found several rotating Artifacts tied to two ad campaigns, so this was a funded, ongoing operation rather than a single case.

Cyber Security News reported on similar lures earlier in the year, in its coverage of fake Claude installer pages that also used sponsored search results.

The lure depends on a technique called ClickFix, which asks the victim to run a command personally. The page shows a box titled “Install on macOS” with four steps: open Terminal, click Copy, paste, and press Enter.

The copied command is scrambled, so the visitor sees only gibberish instead of a suspicious web address. Because the user runs it, many built-in defenses do not stop it. Earlier reports, including past ClickFix technique research, show how widely this pattern has spread.

Windows Campaign, Wallet Theft, and Protection Tips

The Windows version used an Artifact titled “Install Claude on Windows,” which told users to press Win + R, then Ctrl + V, then Enter. The pasted PowerShell command was malicious from its first character and displayed fake “verification” messages while it ran.

It then reached GitHub and a github.io page to fetch the next stage, which carried an encrypted .NET payload.

That final program hides inside a normal Windows process, checks for antivirus software, takes desktop screenshots, and keeps a connection open so the operator can send more commands. It also searches for Electrum, Exodus, Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Ledger wallets.

Stealers like AMOS are not new on Macs either. A recent AMOS malext malvertising campaign showed the same pattern, with paid ads pushing macOS users toward terminal commands and trojanized Ledger and Trezor apps.

Gen’s advice is clear. Never paste a command you did not write yourself, and type the vendor’s address or use a bookmark. Anthropic’s real download page is claude.com/download.

Treat the “user-generated” label as a warning sign, and never enter a recovery phrase into software that asks for it unexpectedly.

Anyone who already ran one of these commands should assume the device is fully compromised. From a clean device, change important passwords, log out of all sessions, enable multi-factor authentication, and move crypto funds into a wallet created from a new recovery phrase.
