Hackers are using malicious Instagram advertisements to infect vulnerable iPhones with spyware while users scroll through their feeds. A documented attack used a World Cup advertisement to deliver the P7 variant of DarkSword, exposing sensitive information without requiring the victim to tap the ad, download a file, or install an application. The findings show how […]

The post Hackers Use Malicious Instagram Ads to Infect iPhones With Spyware Without a Click appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using malicious Instagram advertisements to infect vulnerable iPhones with spyware while users scroll through their feeds.

A documented attack used a World Cup advertisement to deliver the P7 variant of DarkSword, exposing sensitive information without requiring the victim to tap the ad, download a file, or install an application.

The findings show how online advertising can become a delivery channel for mobile attacks. Unlike phishing, these infections do not depend on persuading someone to open a suspicious link.

Earlier reporting on spyware delivered through advertisements documented a separate campaign, highlighting how advertising infrastructure can help attackers reach devices during ordinary browsing.

Researchers from iVerify identified the DarkSword P7 infection while investigating an employee’s mobile device at a customer organization.

Hackers Use Malicious Instagram Ads

Their joint investigation with Report URI, published October 21, 2026, describes criminal groups abusing advertisements and abandoned website integrations to distribute DarkSword and Coruna, two iOS exploit kits capable of stealing private data.

In the Instagram case, the employee was simply scrolling when the malicious advertisement loaded. The same person later faced another attack after clicking a malicious link distributed by a different group using another DarkSword variant.

Near-real-time alerts allowed the organization’s security team to rotate credentials before stolen login details could be sold and used against corporate systems.

The researchers describe these as “half-click” attacks: users must visit a webpage or social platform, but no further interaction with the malicious content is necessary.

This distinction matters. The report does not describe an attack that reaches an idle phone without browsing activity, nor does it establish that fully updated iPhones are vulnerable.

Investigators have not established how the Instagram advertisement passed Meta’s checks. They discuss several possibilities, including concealed malicious content, abuse of advertising resellers, or a compromised vendor.

None is confirmed. The observed infection demonstrates an advertising delivery route, not proof of a vulnerability in Instagram itself.

The underlying compromise depends on vulnerable iOS software. Previous analysis of Coruna and DarkSword exploits explains how linked browser and system flaws can move an attacker beyond the browser’s safety boundaries.

In this investigation, both kits target older iOS versions; placeholders for newer releases do not demonstrate working exploits against them.

DeadTag Expands Spyware Delivery Through Forgotten Website Tags

Report URI also uncovered DeadTag, an operation that buys expired domains previously used for analytics and advertising services. Thousands of websites still load scripts from those domains through forgotten tags.

Once attackers control a domain, those existing connections give them a way to redirect visitors without first compromising each website directly.

The researchers identified hundreds of re-registered domains and estimated 135 million monthly visits to sites capable of serving the spyware when visitors meet targeting conditions.

That figure measures potential traffic exposure, not confirmed infections. Much of the redirected traffic leads to scams, while selected iPhone visitors receive Coruna or DarkSword.

The exploit crew also planted DarkSword loaders on hundreds of PrestaShop stores, hiding them in folders resembling analytics components. Some paths led to a fake Polymarket page.

The identified variants targeted keychain passwords, device information, and wallets including Binance, Coinbase Wallet, OKX, Bitget, Trust Wallet, Exodus, TronLink, and Bitpie.

The potential damage extends beyond cryptocurrency. Both exploit kits can collect messages, contacts, location information, and passwords.

For employers, a compromised personal phone can therefore become a source of corporate credentials, even when the employee never opens a suspicious attachment or knowingly approves an installation.

Financial theft appears to be the main motive. Chinese-language code comments and related infrastructure suggest Chinese-speaking operators, but do not establish nationality or state involvement.

DeadTag’s operators remain unidentified. Separately, previous reporting on malicious website theme packages shows how browser-side dependencies can expose iPhone visitors to spyware and wallet theft through trusted-looking websites.

Users should install available iOS security updates promptly. People facing elevated risk should consider Lockdown Mode, acknowledging its restrictions.

Website owners should remove unused third-party tags, monitor external scripts, and enforce a Content Security Policy.

Following suspected compromise, the researchers recommend preserving logs before restarting, changing exposed credentials, and replacing affected cryptocurrency wallets with new recovery phrases.

articles.title: Palo Alto Confirms Brotli Vulnerability Impact on PAN-OS and Releases Workarounds
articles.description:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that a critical Brotli vulnerability affects some PAN-OS firewall deployments and its Prisma Cloud Application Security Transporter Client. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the flaw could let an attacker corrupt memory, expose sensitive data, crash a service, or potentially run code without authentication. The company published its advisory on October 26, 2026. […]

The post Palo Alto Confirms Brotli Vulnerability Impact on PAN-OS and Releases Workarounds appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that a critical Brotli vulnerability affects some PAN-OS firewall deployments and its Prisma Cloud Application Security Transporter Client.

Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the flaw could let an attacker corrupt memory, expose sensitive data, crash a service, or potentially run code without authentication. The company published its advisory on October 26, 2026.

The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 9.2, although Palo Alto assigns it moderate response urgency. The company says it is not aware of malicious exploitation. Its investigation across products and cloud services remains ongoing, so customers should check the official security advisory for changes to affected versions and patch schedules.

Brotli Vulnerability Affects PAN-OS

The flaw sits in c/dec/decode.cpart of Google’s Brotli decoder. A specially crafted compressed stream can trigger an out-of-bounds write, meaning the decoder writes beyond its intended memory area. Fixed Brotli releases include 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1 for their respective release branches.

The same vulnerability also affects other software that uses Brotli. Cybersecurity News previously covered Node.js security updates addressing the decoder flaw and HTTP2Shell research showing its impact beyond web traffic. Those reports show why updating one application may not remove vulnerable copies elsewhere in an organization.

For PAN-OS, exposure depends on configuration. PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls must have both Brotli traffic inspection and TLS/SSL decryption enabled on the dataplane, which processes network traffic. The management web interface and API are not affected. Brotli inspection is disabled by default and is unsupported before PAN-OS 11.2.4.

PAN-OS 11.1 and 10.2 are unaffected, as are Panorama virtual appliances and M-Series appliances. Administrators running PAN-OS 11.2.4 or later can check the setting with show system setting brotli. An Enabled: yes result confirms Brotli inspection is active, but TLS/SSL decryption must also be enabled for the stated exposure conditions.

Workarounds Administrators Can Apply

Palo Alto recommends disabling Brotli inspection while awaiting fixes. Through the command-line interface, administrators can run set system setting brotli-encoding disable, then use show system setting brotli to confirm Enabled: no. On PAN-OS 12.1.2 and later, they can instead open Device > Setup > Content-ID, clear Allow Brotli Encoding, and commit the configuration.

Threat Prevention subscribers also receive partial coverage through Threat ID 97686 in Applications and Threats content version 9165 or later. This protection is conditional, not a complete fix. The advisory specifies traffic routing, decryption, certificate, and policy requirements for the signature, so customers should not assume installing the content update alone provides protection.

The planned PAN-OS fixes span October 27–30. They include 12.2.4-h1, 12.1.4-h13, 12.1.7-h11, 12.1.10-h3, 11.2.4-h23, 11.2.7-h23, 11.2.10-h17, 11.2.13-h4, and 11.2.16-h1. These dates are estimates, not confirmation that every build is available. Notably, 11.2.10-h16 fixes PHP issues only, while 11.2.10-h17 addresses both PHP and Brotli.

Prisma Cloud Application Security Transporter Client users should upgrade to version 0.2.9 or later. Palo Alto says listed cloud services, including ADEM, Cloud Identity Engine, Hub, and Prisma AIRS Gateway, have been remediated without customer action. For exposed firewalls, the immediate priority is to disable Brotli inspection, verify the setting, and track the appropriate hotfix for deployment once available.

articles.title: New Aokigahara Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, and Cursor Login Credentials
articles.description:
A newly observed Windows infostealer called Aokigahara is targeting login credentials and session data associated with ChatGPT Desktop, Claude, Codex, and Cursor. The malware searches infected computers for authentication files and application storage, extending familiar password theft into the AI tools developers increasingly use for everyday work. The threat is not evidence that these AI […]

The post New Aokigahara Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, and Cursor Login Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A newly observed Windows infostealer called Aokigahara is targeting login credentials and session data associated with ChatGPT Desktop, Claude, Codex, and Cursor.

The malware searches infected computers for authentication files and application storage, extending familiar password theft into the AI tools developers increasingly use for everyday work.

The threat is not evidence that these AI services have been breached. Instead, attackers collect locally stored information that may help them access accounts.

Similar AI coding agent theft has shown why tokens, saved connections, and project records deserve the same protection as browser passwords and cloud keys.

Researchers from Check Point identified Aokigahara in the wild and detailed its capabilities in an October 23 research report.

New Aokigahara Malware

They noted that an earlier version may have been known as Kamidere or Stygian, while stressing that the operators’ methods for making money from stolen information remain unconfirmed.

A dedicated collection module named aisessions searches for data linked to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, ChatGPT Desktop, and Cursor.

Its scope also covers Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, JetBrains AI Assistant, Amazon Q, and Kiro. The module additionally queries Windows Credential Manager for stored credential information.

For Claude, collection targets include credential files and desktop application folders. Codex targets include authentication, configuration, and environment files.

Cursor’s local storage databases are also selected, while ChatGPT Desktop’s application cache is searched. These locations may contain useful secrets, but not every targeted file necessarily holds a password or token.

Earlier reporting on Aoki credential stealing described similar interest in AI application data. The practical risk depends on whether collected secrets remain valid and reusable: working session tokens could give attackers account access without requiring them to enter the victim’s password again.

That access could expose private conversations, uploaded material, or development information. Attackers might also consume paid services or resell compromised accounts.

Check Point described these as potential outcomes, not confirmed activity by Aokigahara’s operators, and raised possible data extortion where stolen access reveals sensitive business content.

A separate ide module widens collection to Git credentials, SSH files that may contain private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud configuration data.

Alongside its AI focus, Aokigahara steals browser credentials and cookies, captures screenshots and clipboard contents, and collects wallet, messaging, VPN, and email application data.

Evasion, Encrypted Uploads, and Incident Response

Aokigahara includes optional checks designed to frustrate malware analysis. Depending on configuration, it examines debugger indicators, virtual machine traces, hardware resources, process counts, and mouse movement.

It can also stop running when keyboard or Windows interface language settings match an excluded group, including Russian, Ukrainian, and several regional languages.

Its configuration is encrypted with AES-256-CBC and controls which built-in collection modules execute. It also stores server details, communication settings, and fallback destinations.

Importantly, disabled collection modules remain embedded in the executable, so the capabilities present in a sample may exceed those enabled during a particular run.

The malware packages collected information into ZIP archives, then encrypts uploads using AES-256-GCM. An X25519 key exchange helps establish the encryption key.

Separate requests open an upload session, transfer each collection category, and mark completion. The latest analyzed samples use a Windows-looking User-Agent string, although that string alone cannot prove infection.

Upload headers identify the collection category and sequence number, allowing the server to separate browser data from AI sessions and other stolen material.

The final completion message signals that the upload phase ended; it does not independently confirm that every stolen archive reached the server.

The wider trend is already visible in incidents involving a fake Gemini npm package that targeted local data from several AI tools.

That separate campaign does not establish Aokigahara’s delivery method; it shows how developer workflows have become attractive places to collect reusable access credentials.

For defenders, the collection pattern supports monitoring unexpected processes that read AI authentication stores, editor databases, cloud credentials, and SSH material.

Network findings should be checked alongside endpoint evidence rather than treated as standalone proof. Check Point also published a YARA rule to support identification of the malware.

After a suspected infection, responders should isolate the device and use a clean system to revoke AI sessions, rotate exposed keys, and review connected cloud and repository accounts.

Resetting passwords alone may leave stolen sessions usable. Teams should also review AI account activity and determine whether sensitive conversations or uploaded files were accessible.

The findings concern theft from compromised endpoints, not a demonstrated vulnerability in ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, or Cursor.

Organizations should therefore include AI application sessions in their existing infostealer response plans rather than treating them as ordinary application settings.

The following table reproduces all 150 Aokigahara sample SHA-1 hashes. Each cell represents a separate sample; columns do not indicate relationships between samples.

Additional source-reported network and file artifacts can support behavioral hunting. Unlike the listed sample hashes and command-and-control destinations, these artifacts are not necessarily malicious in isolation.

articles.title: Hackers Sell ICMacOS Remote Access Trojan for $699 a Week to Target Mac Users
articles.description:
Cybercriminals are selling a Mac malware kit that can do far more than steal passwords. The tool, called ICMacOS or Icarus macOS, is offered for $699 a week on Russian-speaking dark web forums. It began as a basic data stealer, but its newer version can stay hidden on a Mac, survive restarts, and run commands […]

The post Hackers Sell ICMacOS Remote Access Trojan for $699 a Week to Target Mac Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cybercriminals are selling a Mac malware kit that can do far more than steal passwords. The tool, called ICMacOS or Icarus macOS, is offered for $699 a week on Russian-speaking dark web forums.

It began as a basic data stealer, but its newer version can stay hidden on a Mac, survive restarts, and run commands sent by its operators.

SOCRadar’s Threat Research Unit first identified the malware in September 2026 and published a detailed report on October 12.

The seller uses the name GlowComa, a financially motivated actor active since January 2026, who promotes the tool under the banner of the MADHASH crypto-draining affiliate group.

For more background on how the threat grew, read our detailed ICMacOS evolution report, which explains each change in order.

Researchers at Moonlock Lab also noted that ICMacOS is the most affordable macOS stealer sold on the dark web. Moonlock’s write-up, which quotes SOCRadar, compares the price with other Mac threats.

AMOS reportedly sells for $3,000 a month, Banshee for $1,500 to $3,000 a month, and MacSync for $1,000 to $1,500 a month.

These figures are based on historical reported prices. The seller also has a mixed reputation in the underground market, with several disputes on Exploit.in over poor results and slow service.

Hackers Sell ICMacOS Remote Access Trojan

The infection starts with fake web pages that trick victims into copying a command and pasting it into Terminal. The command downloads a dropper script that hides the Terminal window and shows a fake System Preferences prompt asking for the login password.

The dropper checks that password against the login Keychain and allows up to five tries. It then checks whether the Mac uses Apple Silicon or Intel and downloads the matching payload.

This lure style is similar to the fake disk cleanup campaign that Microsoft researchers have tracked since January. The biggest change is in Version 2. It keeps the theft modules but adds a live WebSocket connection to the attacker’s server.

Operators can then send commands that run through /bin/sh, and the output returns in real time. The malware also installs a LaunchAgent named com.apple.systemupdater.plist, a name chosen to look like a normal Apple process.

It restarts automatically if it stops and runs again every 60 minutes as a backup. Similar tricks have helped other threats get past Apple’s checks, as described in our signed app Gatekeeper bypass coverage.

The malware is also built to avoid certain victims. It checks the system language and the victim’s public IP location, and it stops running on systems in Russia and other CIS countries.

Its main goal stays the same, which is to steal money and data, but the remote access feature lets criminals stay inside longer.

Why Developer Secrets Are at Risk

ICMacOS collects a wide range of data. It targets browser passwords and cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, 29 browser extensions, Keychain data, and messaging apps such as Telegram, WhatsApp, and Discord.

Developers face the greatest risk because the malware searches for SSH keys, AWS and Kubernetes settings, Git credentials, and .env files.

Picus Security’s Umut Bayram warned that one compromised laptop can open a path into a company’s code, cloud systems, and customers.

Kevin M. Coles of Coles Technical Group added that developers and executives use Macs often, and those machines hold SSH keys, cloud logins, and crypto wallets.

Mac users can lower their risk with a few simple habits. They should never paste commands from a website into Terminal, and they should download software only from verified sources.

Apple has added a warning for some risky pasted commands, but it may not catch every case. Anyone who wants to recognize these lures can review our ClickFix Terminal command tricks before running any command.

Moonlock sells a Mac security app, so its advice should be read with that in mind, but its tips on checking app privacy policies still apply.

articles.title: Claude Code Reportedly Finds 214,856 Deleted Photos and Videos Hidden on Android Phone
articles.description:
Anthropic’s Claude Code reportedly found 214,856 files linked to deleted photos and videos on a Google Pixel, raising privacy concerns about Android photos. The user, known as Cooler (@coolerwave), said files remained in a hidden thumbnail folder even after the original images were permanently deleted. This claim is unverified and cannot be confirmed as an […]

The post Claude Code Reportedly Finds 214,856 Deleted Photos and Videos Hidden on Android Phone appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic’s Claude Code reportedly found 214,856 files linked to deleted photos and videos on a Google Pixel, raising privacy concerns about Android photos.

The user, known as Cooler (@coolerwave), said files remained in a hidden thumbnail folder even after the original images were permanently deleted. This claim is unverified and cannot be confirmed as an Android security flaw.

According to a post Cooler (@coolerwave) shared on X, the user connected the Pixel to a MacBook and asked Claude Code to search for leftover media. The tool reportedly identified DCIM/.thumbnails, a hidden folder containing image previews.

Claude Code Finds Deleted Photos

Most files were described as compressed copies, while several dozen were said to be close to their original size. The user claimed the files included passport images, bank screenshots, private photographs, and a cryptocurrency seed phrase. The account also said many items were absent from the gallery trash and MediaStore, Android’s media index.

However, the material reviewed does not establish that every counted file represented a unique, previously deleted photo or video. The distinction between a cached preview and an original file matters. Android supports loading thumbnails so apps can display smaller previews instead of full media files.

Finding a preview would not, by itself, show that Claude Code recovered the original photograph or a playable deleted video.

A count of 214,856 files also needs context. A reliable review would need to separate unique images, repeated previews, database files, and other cached content. Without that breakdown, the headline figure should be treated as the user’s reported result, not a verified recovery total.

The story follows another reported AI discovery covered by Cyber Security News, in which Claude identified a suspected hidden cryptocurrency miner on a Mac. Such reports show interest in AI-assisted checks, but individual findings still need independent validation.

The post’s claim that any app with storage access can read every deleted image is too broad. Android’s scoped storage rules limit file access, with scoped storage required for apps targeting Android 11 or higher.

Actual access depends on the Android version, app permissions, and file location. Android 14 also introduced selected photo access, allowing users to share specific images rather than their entire library.

Separately, the special MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE permission grants broad access to shared storage, but does not unlock other apps’ protected directories. Ordinary photo permission and “All files access” are therefore not interchangeable.

That distinction matters because excessive permissions can create real risks. Cyber Security News previously covered Android spyware posing as WhatsApp and Google Photos, which used granted privileges to support surveillance and data theft.

Users should review photo permissions and special all-files access, removing access that does not match an app’s purpose. Selected-photo sharing offers a narrower option where supported. Cloud copies need separate attention. Google explains that its “Free up space” feature removes local copies while keeping backed-up images available in Google Photos.

articles.description:
Apache Camel has released fixes for multiple security flaws, including high-severity XML External Entity vulnerabilities that could expose local files or reach internal systems. The issues affect several components, with risks ranging from unsafe XML processing to remote code execution, stolen credentials, and failed access checks. Apache’s security advisories list patched releases for each affected […]

The post Apache Camel Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities Including High-Severity XXE One’s appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apache Camel has released fixes for multiple security flaws, including high-severity XML External Entity vulnerabilities that could expose local files or reach internal systems.

The issues affect several components, with risks ranging from unsafe XML processing to remote code execution, stolen credentials, and failed access checks.

Apache’s security advisories list patched releases for each affected branch. The fixes cover different parts of Camel, so exposure depends on the components and settings an application uses.

Teams should check their deployed versions against the individual advisories rather than assume every Camel application faces the same risk. Several flaws require attacker-controlled messages to reach a specific processing path.

One significant issue, CVE-2026-90885, affects Camel-Saxon. Its XQueryBuilder processed message bodies already represented as javax.xml.transform.Source objects using Saxon’s default parser settings. This allowed an external entity declared inside the XML body to be resolved, creating an XXE weakness in that processing path.

According to Apache’s Camel-Saxon advisory, this issue is separate from CVE-2026-85250 in Camel-XPath. The XPath flaw appears when documentType=InputSource passes the payload to an engine that builds its own parser using JDK defaults. XML declarations blocked by the default document type could therefore be accepted through this alternative path.

Apache Camel Fixes Multiple Vulnerabilities

A third high-severity issue, CVE-2026-88901, affects Camel-Smooks. Its default XML reader resolved external general and parameter entities and loaded external document type definitions.

An attacker-controlled XML message could consequently read local files or contact internal hosts. Camel-FOP also received a medium-severity XXE fix for unsafe handling when certain third-party XML transformer implementations were present.

The broader update includes CVE-2026-88900, a high-severity unsafe Java deserialization flaw in Camel-JGroups that can lead to remote code execution.

Another high-severity issue, CVE-2026-78165, affects Camel-Spring-Redis. An attacker who can publish to a subscribed channel could exploit its default deserializer, which lacks an object input filter.

Camel-HTTP also contains a high-severity credential disclosure issue tracked as CVE-2026-85251. When followRedirects was enabled, the component attached the Authorization header to the destination named by a redirect, allowing a remote server to choose where those credentials were sent. Other fixes address OAuth authentication bypass and Keycloak token validation weaknesses.

These findings follow earlier coverage of Apache Camel header injection and attacks targeting Tomcat and Camel vulnerabilities. Those reports concern older flaws and should not be treated as evidence that the newly listed issues are being exploited.

For the Saxon flaw, Apache lists fixes in versions 4.18.5, 4.22.2, and 4.23.0. Apache fixed the XPath and Smooks issues in 4.18.5, 4.22.1, and 4.23.0.

Organizations choosing an upgrade should account for the later Saxon fix rather than stop at 4.22.1. Review deployed XML components, message entry points, and redirect settings during patch planning.

Use Apache’s component-specific version ranges to confirm coverage, especially where multiple Camel libraries are packaged within one application.

articles.title: New DarkCore RAT Targets Gmail and WhatsApp Sessions While Hiding Behind Victims’ IP Addresses
articles.description:
A newly uncovered remote access trojan called DarkCore is being marketed with a browser designed to reuse stolen Gmail, WhatsApp, and other account sessions while routing traffic through victims’ IP addresses. The approach could make unauthorized account access look like normal activity from an already trusted connection. The Windows malware combines advertised credential theft, file […]

The post New DarkCore RAT Targets Gmail and WhatsApp Sessions While Hiding Behind Victims’ IP Addresses appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A newly uncovered remote access trojan called DarkCore is being marketed with a browser designed to reuse stolen Gmail, WhatsApp, and other account sessions while routing traffic through victims’ IP addresses.

The approach could make unauthorized account access look like normal activity from an already trusted connection. The Windows malware combines advertised credential theft, file transfers, a reverse proxy, and hidden desktop access.

However, researchers drew an important line between the seller’s claims and confirmed code behavior: their analysis established the client’s configuration and module loading, but did not independently verify every advertised browser feature.

Researchers from BlackFog identified DarkCore during routine threat hunting and examined a marketplace listing dated August 11, 2026.

Their published technical malware analysis compared promotional screenshots with a supplied Windows executable and an accompanying malicious shortcut. A screenshot contained 118 credential rows, but that figure does not establish how many victims were compromised.

New DarkCore RAT Targets Gmail and WhatsApp Sessions

Session cookies represent a login that has already succeeded. Instead of entering a password and completing another authentication challenge, an attacker may reuse a valid stolen session.

Earlier reporting on Cookie-Bite session theft attacks explains the same broader risk: stealing authenticated cookies can undermine protections applied during login.

DarkCore’s seller showed Gmail, WhatsApp, YouTube, and MediaFire inside its dedicated browser. According to the advertised changelog, operators can inject stolen cookies and send browser traffic through the infected device’s IP address.

The proxy reportedly stops when the last browser window associated with that session closes. These remain seller-described functions rather than fully validated findings.

The distinction matters because a familiar IP address does not prove that the legitimate user controls an account. Victim-IP routing is intended to disguise unauthorized access as ordinary browsing.

Investigators therefore need to connect account activity with endpoint evidence rather than treating a recognized network address as sufficient reassurance.

DarkCore also advertises hidden virtual network computing, or HVNC, which lets an operator control a browser on a Windows desktop the victim cannot see.

Similar MedusaHVNC hidden desktop capabilities illustrate how attackers can work inside existing browser sessions without changing the visible desktop. DarkCore’s promotional interface showed Chrome open on Gmail.

PDF Shortcut Delivery and Technical Findings

The accompanying shortcut uses a PDF icon and presents itself as a report launcher. Opening it starts a minimized command window that downloads a genuine World Bank report as a decoy and separately retrieves an executable.

String slicing, character removal, and CALL expansion conceal the underlying download and launch commands. Before opening either download, the commands attempt to remove its Zone.Identifier stream, the Windows marker associated with internet downloads.

This can reduce warnings. The executable download is attempted even if the decoy PDF fails, and its launch command does not check whether retrieval succeeded. How attackers originally distributed the shortcut remains unknown.

This resembles PDF decoy delivery techniques reported in another RAT campaign, where a document distracts the user while malicious code runs.

BlackFog could not hash the remotely hosted executable, so it could not confirm that the download matched the supplied sample it examined.

That sample was an unsigned, 64-bit Windows executable. Researchers recovered its settings by reproducing a decoder that rotates bytes from a 32-byte key and XORs them against 758 encoded bytes.

The configuration selected direct TCP communication, disabled Tor and WebSocket options, and left installation and startup persistence flags unset.

Additional modules can load directly into memory or through temporary DLL files written to disk. For detection, BlackFog recommends examining command-shell downloads, process ancestry, file signatures, and network connections together.

If theft is suspected, responders should isolate the endpoint, preserve evidence, stop unauthorized transfers, revoke active sessions, and reset affected credentials.

articles.title: Hackers Can Abuse Logged-In WordPress Admin Sessions to Secretly Install PHP Backdoors
articles.description:
WordPress administrators often keep their dashboard open in the same browser they use for everyday browsing. A new attack chain shows why that habit is risky. Researchers have documented a JavaScript loader that waits for a signed-in administrator to visit a compromised page, then uses that browser’s trusted session to install a hidden PHP backdoor […]

The post Hackers Can Abuse Logged-In WordPress Admin Sessions to Secretly Install PHP Backdoors appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WordPress administrators often keep their dashboard open in the same browser they use for everyday browsing. A new attack chain shows why that habit is risky.

Researchers have documented a JavaScript loader that waits for a signed-in administrator to visit a compromised page, then uses that browser’s trusted session to install a hidden PHP backdoor on the website.

The attacker never needs the admin password, because the administrator’s own browser does the work. Recent cases point to the same pattern.

One example is an admin-triggered WordPress malware campaign that exposed more than 1.2 million websites to potential compromise.

Malware that activates only during logged-in sessions is hard to spot during routine scans, which makes it a growing concern for site owners.

Security researchers at Securonix Threat Research, Akshay Gaikwad and Aaron Beardslee, identified the malware and named the chain TRUST#GRAFT.

Their analysis shows that the JavaScript does not break the WordPress login. Instead, it checks whether the visitor is already signed in as an administrator, then reuses that session to add new code to the site. Securonix also notes that it has not confirmed how the first script reached the compromised page.

Hackers Can Abuse Logged-In WordPress Admin Sessions

The infection begins with a fake security check. The script places a full-screen frame over the page that looks like a Cloudflare “Just a moment” verification screen.

While the visitor waits, the script collects details such as screen size, graphics data, timezone, and installed plugin count. It also checks for signs of automated analysis tools.

After solving a small puzzle, the browser sends this data to a controller server, which decides whether to send the next stage. The key step follows.

The script requests the WordPress plugin upload page using the browser’s existing login cookies, then reads a WordPress security token, called a nonce, from that page.

It downloads a ZIP file named wm.zip from a staging server and uploads it through the standard plugin installation endpoint.

If the upload works, the script opens the plugins page and activates the new plugin. WordPress accepts each request because the browser is already signed in with plugin rights.

Securonix stresses that this is not a standalone login bypass. The account must already be an administrator with permission to install plugins.

Even so, the risk is serious for anyone who browses public websites while signed in to wp-admin, or who uses one browser profile for both daily browsing and site management.

Persistent PHP Backdoor Hides in Must-Use Plugins

The ZIP file contains a PHP plugin named Web Media Optimizer, version 2.1. The name suggests a harmless image or media tool, but Securonix describes it as a backdoor.

It injects remote JavaScript into public pages, turns off TLS certificate checks when it fetches its controller script, and can set an administrator login cookie for the first admin account through a hardcoded token.

The plugin also protects its own presence. On activation, it copies itself to wp-content/mu-plugins/wmedia-recovery.php.

WordPress loads every file in that folder automatically, and those files do not appear on the normal Plugins page. Similar hidden must-use plugin malware has been reported before, and it shows why removing only the visible plugin is not enough.

Site owners should also take cleanup seriously. Removing the visible plugin, the mu-plugins copy, and any leftover remote script source is necessary to stop reinfection.

Admins should also review recent WordPress self-restoring backdoor malware cases, which show how deleted files can return.

Securonix recommends using a separate browser profile for wp-admin, signing out after suspicious activity, rotating administrator credentials, limiting plugin upload rights, and watching for new PHP files in mu-plugins.

articles.title: Hackers Revive BlackLotus Techniques to Bypass Windows Secure Boot and Deploy Malware
articles.description:
Hackers have revived techniques associated with the BlackLotus bootkit to bypass Windows Secure Boot and deploy espionage malware against diplomatic organizations in Central Asia. The new bootkit, named BlackX, appeared in attacks targeting agencies in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan in early 2026. Investigators linked the campaign to APT41 with medium confidence, leaving attribution short of […]

The post Hackers Revive BlackLotus Techniques to Bypass Windows Secure Boot and Deploy Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers have revived techniques associated with the BlackLotus bootkit to bypass Windows Secure Boot and deploy espionage malware against diplomatic organizations in Central Asia.

The new bootkit, named BlackX, appeared in attacks targeting agencies in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan in early 2026.

Investigators linked the campaign to APT41 with medium confidence, leaving attribution short of confirmation. The finding was not simply another case of missing security updates.

Investigators found that affected computers were fully patched, but vulnerable boot components remained trusted because additional certificate revocation steps had not been completed.

Earlier reporting on Windows boot manager downgrades explains how older, signed components can undermine protections on otherwise updated systems.

Researchers from Securelist identified BlackX during their investigation and detailed its operation in an October 22 technical report.

Hackers Revive BlackLotus Techniques

Kaspersky researchers Georgy Kucherin, Vladimir Nestor, and Vasily Berdnikov found that its exploitation chain closely resembles BlackLotus, although its implementation and later payloads differ.

BlackX exploits Baton Drop, tracked as CVE-2022-21894, to manipulate the startup trust chain. Attackers deploy it after compromising a network and obtaining administrator privileges.

It is therefore a tool for extending an existing compromise, rather than the initial route into a victim’s environment. The report does not establish how those networks were first breached.

Installation separates the executable from an encrypted package containing the required components and strings. This arrangement leaves the installer without embedded malicious payloads, making recovery and analysis harder when responders cannot retrieve its companion file.

The package writes components to system and UEFI partitions, then exploits Baton Drop to install custom Machine Owner Keys. These keys enable attacker-controlled EFI files to load.

The bootkit subsequently injects a signed malicious driver into the Windows kernel. Its signing certificate has since been revoked. The driver attempts to disable security callbacks and interfere with Event Tracing for Windows providers, reducing visibility into malicious activity.

However, researchers found that its Kaspersky-specific interference routines failed during testing. It also redirects requests for protected bootkit files toward a harmless Windows executable.

Espionage Payloads and the Secure Boot Protection Gap

BlackX delivers two observed user-mode payloads. One is a remote-access Trojan capable of loading additional .NET code and exchanging instructions through Google Drive, OneDrive, or Yandex.Disk.

Similar Google Drive command channels have appeared in separate APT41-linked reporting, illustrating how trusted cloud platforms can carry attacker instructions alongside ordinary business traffic. This similarity alone does not prove attribution.

The second payload, OxiDLLRunner, uses an obfuscated DLL loaded through a legitimate executable. It decrypts a nearby data file containing shellcode and a Rust executable.

That payload contacts command infrastructure and receives additional DLL plugins, which execute in separate threads. The design gives operators a way to extend functionality after establishing access.

Researchers based their APT41 assessment on shared development identifiers, overlaps with previously reported FishMonger activity, DLL sideloading patterns, and OLLVM obfuscation.

These clues support their medium-confidence judgment, but do not establish who wrote BlackX. They suggested its developers might have reverse-engineered BlackLotus or purchased its source code; neither explanation was confirmed.

The protection gap involved continued trust in vulnerable components signed under Windows Production PCA 2011. Securelist reported that installing updates did not automatically activate the required revocation on affected systems.

Certificate expiration on October 19 also did not independently block existing binaries. Microsoft’s certificate expiration advisory likewise explains that existing devices continue starting normally after expiration.

Administrators should verify boot-trust revocations rather than relying only on update status. Previous UEFI Secure Boot vulnerabilities demonstrate why forbidden-signature databases matter.

Revocation changes require compatibility planning because older recovery media and boot configurations may depend on certificates being removed.

articles.title: Hackers Use VLC Media Player and VMware Tools to Load Malware Through DLL Side-Loading
articles.description:
Hackers are using legitimate VLC Media Player and VMware components to load malware onto Windows systems, hiding harmful code behind familiar software. The activity forms part of three malware campaigns targeting users in Brazil and Portugal through fake legal notices, financial documents, and invoice download pages. The attacks combine phishing, hidden scripts, and trusted programs […]

The post Hackers Use VLC Media Player and VMware Tools to Load Malware Through DLL Side-Loading appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using legitimate VLC Media Player and VMware components to load malware onto Windows systems, hiding harmful code behind familiar software.

The activity forms part of three malware campaigns targeting users in Brazil and Portugal through fake legal notices, financial documents, and invoice download pages. The attacks combine phishing, hidden scripts, and trusted programs to make infections harder to spot.

The main technique, side-loading, tricks a genuine application into loading an attacker’s DLL, a file that supplies supporting code. Instead of changing the trusted executable, attackers place a harmful library beside it.

When the application starts, it loads the malicious file, giving defenders a reason to examine both the program and its nearby libraries.

WatchGuard Red Cell researcher Euler Neto identified the activity in an investigation of three campaigns published on October 22, 2026.

The research covers Overlord RAT, the Lampion banking malware, and a separate infection involving a malicious driver management library. Although the cases share delivery methods, the findings do not establish that one group controls all three operations.

Hackers Use VLC Media Player and VMware Tools

In the Overlord RAT campaign, phishing emails impersonate Brazilian notary offices and direct recipients toward supposed legal documents. The links deliver VBScript files that download executables or Windows Installer packages.

Some scripts hide their instructions by building text from character codes, while others join strings together to make their purpose less clear during inspection.

Two installer packages examined by WatchGuard used DLL side-loading. One paired a malicious library with a legitimate Microsoft .NET Framework utility; the other used VLC Media Player.

Both placed their files inside a temporary folder named Adobe. Similar DLL side-loading malware attacks show why checking only the main executable can miss the harmful library responsible for execution.

Other Overlord delivery paths use Dropbox or Google Cloud Storage to retrieve additional files. Batch scripts attempt to add Microsoft Defender exclusions, while downloaded programs create scheduled tasks or startup entries.

One loader uses the Windows Error Reporting name to blend into normal activity. Researchers also found encrypted content that decoded into Donut shellcode, allowing another payload to run in memory.

The VMware-related case starts with a Portuguese invoice page titled “Download Seguro – Factura.” A fake CAPTCHA leads visitors to download an ISO disk image.

Inside are an obscured VBScript, a genuine VMware network installation utility, a malicious DLL, and a module-definition file. The trusted VMware executable serves as the loading vehicle rather than the final malware itself.

That packaging resembles earlier ISO-based malware delivery chains that placed genuine software alongside harmful libraries. Here, the malicious DLL decrypts embedded data with XOR, revealing a second, 64-bit DLL written in Pascal.

Its main function checks whether another copy is running, prepares screen capture, creates a bot identifier, and sets a user-level registry entry for persistence.

Remote Access Capabilities and Detection Priorities

The Pascal payload gives attackers control over the infected computer. Its commands support remote mouse and keyboard activity, command execution through PowerShell or CMD, file writing, screen streaming, and hidden interactive shells.

It can also uninstall itself and remove associated evidence. Failed connections to its command server are retried every three seconds, providing another behavior defenders can investigate.

WatchGuard also reviewed Lampion, which uses finance-themed phishing messages and heavily padded scripts. In one example, a script measured roughly 5 MB, but its working code was only about 5 KB.

Lampion mainly targeted Portugal, while the Overlord case targeted Brazil. Repeated references to the number seven appeared across the cases, but those references alone do not prove a shared operator.

For security teams, the clearest warning signs are unexpected script downloads, new Defender exclusions, unfamiliar scheduled tasks, and trusted applications loading libraries from unusual folders.

Previous fake Claude installer attacks also combined security exclusions with side-loading, showing how several ordinary Windows actions can form one infection chain. Investigators should connect those events rather than assess each alert in isolation.

WatchGuard recommends reviewing process chains, persistence settings, and outbound connections, then isolating compromised endpoints where needed.

The practical lesson is to verify what trusted software loads, not simply whether its executable looks legitimate.

Phishing protection, behavior monitoring, and endpoint visibility remain important because these campaigns spread harmful activity across scripts, cloud downloads, libraries, and Windows features.

articles.title: Hackers Weaponize Public PHP2Shell Exploit Code to Target Universities and Business Websites
articles.description:
Hackers are now using public exploit code to break into websites that run PHP, and universities and business sites are among the main targets. The bugs behind this wave are two critical flaws in the PHP engine, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and nicknamed PHP2Shell. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and can […]

The post Hackers Weaponize Public PHP2Shell Exploit Code to Target Universities and Business Websites appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are now using public exploit code to break into websites that run PHP, and universities and business sites are among the main targets.

The bugs behind this wave are two critical flaws in the PHP engine, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and nicknamed PHP2Shell. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and can let an outside user run commands on a server without logging in.

PHP released fixed versions on October 21, 2026, but many servers had not been updated when working exploit scripts spread online almost immediately after the release.

The PHP team says the bugs sit inside the PHP engine itself, so clean website code does not protect a server. The PHP project rates the risk highest for Apache servers that run PHP as a module, known as mod_php, because the bug can be triggered before any site code runs.

Firewalls and web application filters may never see the bad request, which makes patching the main defense. Our earlier report on the public PHP2Shell testing tool explains the research repository that first appeared and what it claimed to test.

Researchers from Akatsuki Legion, an independent adversary research group, identified the malware activity and documented it in a detailed public report.

Their analysis credits the exploit chain to a researcher known as 9bie, and says AI-generated proof-of-concept scripts appeared on GitHub right after the October 21 release.

The group also captured telemetry from its own honeynet and published the tools it found in use, which you can review in the group’s research archive.

Hackers Weaponize Public PHP2Shell Exploit Code

The fastest fix is an upgrade to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Linux vendors received the patches early, so their package channels may already carry them, and the emergency PHP security update details list every affected branch.

Older releases such as PHP 8.1 and earlier no longer get official updates from the PHP project, so those sites need a vendor backport or a move to a supported version.

The public code shows how the bugs chain together. The first flaw, CVE-2026-109618, appears when PHP runs out of memory during an upload, and the cleanup step then works with partly built data.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-109619, leaves old request data in a shared worker, so a later request can reuse it. The public scripts use two memory leaks to learn addresses, then place a fake structure in memory so PHP calls its system function and runs a chosen command.

Activity started before the public release. Amazon Threat Intelligence observed exploit probing starting October 17 and said it came four days before the fixes, while the flaws were still under coordinated disclosure.

That timing matters because some servers may have been probed before their administrators knew the bugs existed. Researchers tracked the spread from several sides.

Hunt.io telemetry recorded three distinct exploit toolkits on October 21, including a mass-exploitation script hosted on one IP address.

Botnet link

Akatsuki Legion also described an open directory that hosts listener scripts logging exploit traffic on ports 80 and 8888. Taken together, the findings show that several groups were sharing and testing the code at the same time.

The botnet link is now clear. Sophos studied a blocked Potassium botnet payload sample that appeared to be a likely Mirai variant.

Its customer data showed scanning and a few failed tries, and Sophos found no proof of a successful compromise. Even so, the sample checks for a Linux program before it runs, which points to a plan to turn exposed servers into DDoS bots.

Patching remains the only complete fix. PHP’s official security advisory says temporary steps, such as setting session.upload_progress.enabled to 0 and restarting workers, only lower the risk and do not replace an upgrade.

Administrators should also check that PHP-FPM, Apache modules, containers and bundled appliances run the new build, because updating the command-line package alone may leave a live service exposed.

For universities and companies, the lesson is direct. Public exploit code lowers the skill needed to reach a vulnerable server, and the same PHP setup often runs school portals, course sites and small business pages.

Security teams should inventory every PHP runtime, patch it, restart the services, and check logs for POST requests that contain PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS.

articles.description:
Microsoft has restored Microsoft Teams service after investigating an issue affecting some users in the United States on October 26, 2026. The company tracked the disruption under incident TM1526111 and said automatic scaling efforts had returned the service to healthy levels. The recovery update changes the picture from Microsoft’s initial notice, which described a potential […]

The post Microsoft Investigation Teams Issue Affecting Users in the United States appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has restored Microsoft Teams service after investigating an issue affecting some users in the United States on October 26, 2026. The company tracked the disruption under incident TM1526111 and said automatic scaling efforts had returned the service to healthy levels.

The recovery update changes the picture from Microsoft’s initial notice, which described a potential issue and confirmed that an investigation was underway. Microsoft has not identified the number of affected users or named the Teams features involved.

Microsoft first alerted customers through its Microsoft 365 Status account, directing administrators to the Microsoft 365 admin center for incident details. Its initial statement limited the reported impact to some users in the United States, rather than describing a global outage.

In a follow-up update, Microsoft said automated recovery actions were taking effect and that engineers were beginning to observe restoration. The company continued monitoring recovery while investigating what caused the disruption.

Its latest status update said telemetry, the data used to track service performance, confirmed that automatic scaling had successfully increased processing throughput. In simple terms, the recovery process increased the service’s ability to handle work. Microsoft said service health had returned to normal, but the update did not explain the original trigger.

The public statements do not establish a cyberattack, data breach, or account compromise. They also do not specify whether users experienced failed calls, delayed messages, meeting problems, or sign-in errors. Those details should not be inferred from the general incident notice.

The incident follows Teams disruptions covered by Cybersecuritynews.com, including a September calling issue and an August outage affecting multiple features. These reports provide background on service availability, not evidence that the incidents share a cause.

Administrators can check Health, then Service health, in the Microsoft 365 admin center and look for TM1526111. Microsoft’s service health guidance explains how this dashboard presents active incidents, investigation updates, and resolution notices.

For organizations reviewing the disruption, the key distinction is between restored availability and a confirmed root cause. Microsoft’s latest update confirms recovery, while its public statements leave the initial cause unexplained. The incident record remains the reference for details.

articles.title: Hackers Can Hijack OpenAI Codex and Claude Code Using Malicious Files in Downloads Folder
articles.description:
A plain text file placed in the Downloads folder can trick AI coding agents into changing their settings, installing malware, or exposing login tokens. Forever Security discovered the risk after stopping an agent on a real customer’s computer from installing a known malicious npm package. The company later reproduced separate attack paths against OpenAI Codex […]

The post Hackers Can Hijack OpenAI Codex and Claude Code Using Malicious Files in Downloads Folder appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A plain text file placed in the Downloads folder can trick AI coding agents into changing their settings, installing malware, or exposing login tokens.

Forever Security discovered the risk after stopping an agent on a real customer’s computer from installing a known malicious npm package. The company later reproduced separate attack paths against OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code in controlled tests.

The incident began when Forever Security blocked an AI coding agent from installing a package named function-color. Investigators traced the order back to an AGENTS.md file stored in the customer’s ~/Downloads folder.

The file looked like a normal set of engineering notes, but it contained carefully written instructions telling the agent to change its own setup and install the package.

The source of the file remains unknown. Researchers did not prove that a malicious website placed it on the customer’s machine. Instead, they later showed that a website could deliver a file with the same name through normal browser download behavior, creating a possible path for the attack.

An AGENTS.md file is similar to a README written for AI tools. OpenAI’s documentation says Codex reads these files before starting work and uses them to learn project rules, commands, and other instructions. Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md for a similar purpose and reads it at the start of a conversation.

The danger comes from combining trusted agent instructions with a folder where web downloads normally arrive. A Markdown file cannot run by itself, so operating system checks designed for downloaded programs may not treat it as dangerous. The risk appears when an AI agent reads the text as trusted instructions and uses its own tools to carry them out.

The attack is not fully automatic. The victim must run the coding agent from Downloads or otherwise allow it to process the planted instruction file. The agent must also have enough access to edit files, run commands, connect to the internet, or install packages. Approval prompts and sandbox controls can therefore reduce the chance of success.

Codex Attack Creates Persistence

In Forever Security’s controlled tests, Codex followed the malicious file in more than 90% of attempts. The instructions persuaded Codex to add an MCP server entry to ~/.codex/config.toml, its machine-wide configuration file, and start a second Codex session with approval and sandbox checks disabled.

This change made the attack persistent. Once the rogue server was written into the global configuration, later Codex sessions could load it even when the user moved to another folder or project. Most tests used a harmless program, while the real malicious package was run once inside an isolated virtual machine.

The package belonged to MALFEX, a long-running npm malware campaign targeting Windows developers. Checkmarx found that function-color pulled in function-flag, which could download and quietly run a Windows program.

The wider campaign also used packages able to deliver remote-access malware and steal browser, Discord, Telegram, and cryptocurrency wallet data. More technical details are available in Cyber Security News’ report on the MALFEX npm malware campaign.

Claude Code Exposed Tokens

Claude Code required a different method. Researchers created a malicious CLAUDE.md that asked Claude to write an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL value into .claude/settings.json. This redirected Claude’s API traffic to a server controlled by the researchers and exposed the OAuth token carried with the requests.

Forever reported that Claude made the change in about half of its tests. The team replayed a captured token against Anthropic’s service and gained access as the victim. In some tests, the fake server also returned tool commands that led to code execution. Same-session execution through a helper agent worked about one-fifth of the time.

The research adds to growing evidence that instruction files and add-ons can become a software supply-chain risk. Earlier research found that malicious agent skills targeting Claude Code and Codex could hide harmful actions from automated scanners.

Developers should never start Codex, Claude Code, or another coding agent inside Downloads. Unknown AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files should be reviewed before an agent opens the folder. Users should also keep approval checks and sandboxes enabled, limit agent network access, and avoid instructions that request unsafe bypass options.

Security teams should inspect ~/.codex/config.toml for unknown MCP servers and review .claude/settings.json for an unfamiliar ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or proxy.

Finding function-color, unexpected agent settings, or redirected API traffic should be treated as a possible compromise. Affected tokens and connected credentials should be revoked from a clean device, while the system should be isolated and checked for malware.

articles.title: OpenBSD 8.0 Released With Major Security Hardening and Post-Quantum SSH Support
articles.description:
OpenBSD 8.0 has been released with security fixes across its kernel, network services, firewall, and update tools, alongside experimental post-quantum SSH signature support. Released on October 20, 2026, the project’s 61st release includes OpenSSH 10.6 and LibreSSL 4.4.0, bringing stronger checks for untrusted data and changes to secure connection handling. The official release notes detail […]

The post OpenBSD 8.0 Released With Major Security Hardening and Post-Quantum SSH Support appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenBSD 8.0 has been released with security fixes across its kernel, network services, firewall, and update tools, alongside experimental post-quantum SSH signature support.

Released on October 20, 2026, the project’s 61st release includes OpenSSH 10.6 and LibreSSL 4.4.0, bringing stronger checks for untrusted data and changes to secure connection handling.

The official release notes detail changes that address memory errors, unsafe file handling, and gaps in process isolation. For administrators, the update reaches beyond remote login security, covering web servers, mail delivery, DHCP services, virtual machines, and firmware installation.

OpenSSH 10.6 includes experimental support for the composite mldsa44-ed25519 signature scheme, which combines ML-DSA 44 with Ed25519.

The release also switches the scheme’s identifier from its OpenSSH-specific name to an IANA-allocated codepoint, a change that administrators testing earlier implementations should review.

OpenBSD 8.0 Released

This work concerns digital signatures rather than the initial introduction of post-quantum key exchange. As covered in OpenSSH 10.0’s security changes, that earlier release made hybrid ML-KEM and X25519 key agreement the default.

OpenBSD 8.0 therefore builds on existing quantum-resistant connection protection rather than introducing it.mSSH hardening also includes turning off the LZ77 dictionary coder to avoid a potential side-channel leak.

Developers corrected enforcement of ChannelTimeout and RekeyLimit settings and ensured the authorized_keys “restrict” option applies to tunnel forwarding. DisableForwarding now overrides PermitTunnel, tightening control over remote access features.

Additional fixes address client memory errors, excessive expansion of compressed data, and validation of state passed between SSH server processes before and after authentication. Some key parsing and verification paths were also removed from the code exposed before login.

On amd64 systems, OpenBSD now places the kernel’s direct memory map at a random location. The release also fixes kernel stack information leaks and removes an unprivileged kernel memory read and write vulnerability affecting the m88k 88100 data pipeline.

These changes extend the security focus described in OpenBSD 7.7’s release coverage. Version 8.0 adds tighter pledge socket checks and limits file access for manual-page tools through unveil.

The PF firewall receives fixes for out-of-bounds reads, connection counter races, and crafted reset packets that could incorrectly remove TCP state. Meanwhile, httpd rejects ambiguous request framing and obsolete folded headers.

Relayd rejects duplicate Content-Length headers and removes Content-Length from chunked messages, reducing differences in how HTTP requests are handled.

Firmware updates now verify signatures on local SHA256.sig files, restrict download sizes, and skip archive entries outside expected locations. Package installation no longer searches the current directory by default. At the same time, pax blocks malicious archives from extracting files outside the working directory.

LibreSSL 4.4.0 makes X25519MLKEM768 the preferred TLS 1.3 group in libtls. It also fixes certificate checks, an OCSP responder authorization bypass, and excessive DTLS handshake buffering.

Administrators should review compatibility changes, consult the linked upgrade documentation, and check release errata before deploying the update across production systems.

The claim was discovered on October 25, 2026, at 03:22 UTC. The tracker lists the same day as the estimated attack date, but that […]

The post Emperador Ransomware Group Claims to Have Stolen 3.9GB of Data from the Maker of Budweiser and Corona appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Emperador ransomware group claims to have stolen 3.9GB of data from AB InBev and demands $1 million in Bitcoin, but the alleged breach remains unverified, with no company confirmation reported.

The claim was discovered on October 25, 2026, at 03:22 UTC. The tracker lists the same day as the estimated attack date, but that does not establish when any unauthorized access began.

Emperador says its collection includes 329,244 social-listening alerts, 2,510 corporate emails across AB InBev subsidiaries, around 19,000 access logs, and GBS portal records.

The group also claims to hold internal public key infrastructure certificates and 3.2GB of Azure Blob assets. These figures describe the attackers’ account, not independently verified findings.

“We hold 329,244 AB InBev social-listening alerts,” the group states in its posting, before listing the other records and its payment demand.

The Azure assets account for most of the claimed data volume, but the listing does not explain their contents or how the group obtained them.

Emperador Ransomware Claims AB InBev Data Theft

According to Ransomware.live’s victim listing, the claims about corporate emails and access logs remain unclear, as the posting does not specify the type of email data involved or prove that attackers retained active access to company systems.

The claimed certificate exposure needs careful interpretation. Microsoft’s X.509 certificate documentation explains that certificates contain public keys, not private keys.

Therefore, possessing certificates alone does not prove an attacker can impersonate an internal service or decrypt protected information. The listing does not say whether private keys were obtained.

The Azure claim lacks evidence of a compromised storage account, exposed token or key, or specific software flaw, and naming Azure files does not prove a Microsoft platform breach or explain how attackers accessed AB InBev’s environment.

Separate Cyber Security News coverage of the Storm-3168 cloud attack documented compromised service identities and storage-key collection. Those findings illustrate why cloud identity evidence matters, but they should not be attributed to this alleged incident.

The available claim does not establish that Emperador encrypted AB InBev systems, disrupted brewing operations, or affected product distribution. It also provides no verified count of affected people. Describing the event as a confirmed operational ransomware attack would go beyond the evidence currently available.

That distinction also appears in Cyber Security News reporting on the PwC data-theft claim, which explains why a leak-site entry should not automatically be treated as proof of ransomware deployment.

For now, the supported development is an extortion claim naming AB InBev. Confirmation requires evidence establishing the records’ authenticity, ownership, age, and source, alongside a clearer account of any unauthorized access and its impact.

The post PHP Releases New Windows Build Security Updates to Fix Critical HTTP2Shell Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The PHP team has released updated Windows builds to fix a serious flaw known as HTTP2Shell. The new packages are PHP 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1, and 8.2.35-1, and PHP announced them on October 26, 2026.

Each build now includes Brotli 1.2.1, which fixes CVE-2026-111497. Windows users who run PHP should install these packages without delay.

The flaw sits in Google’s Brotli library, a compression tool that many programs use to unpack data. It is an out-of-bounds write, which means the code writes data past the memory area it was meant to use. Node.js disclosed the bug in its security release on October 21, and researchers first called it Node2Shell.

PHP HTTP2Shell Vulnerability

As more software turned out to be affected, the name changed to HTTP2Shell. Google rates the issue with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. Depending on the setup, it can crash a program, expose memory contents, or let code run remotely without a login.

PHP’s own advisory explains how the flaw reaches PHP on Windows. The vulnerable decoder can be reached through the cURL extension when automatic HTTP response decompression is turned on. This setting is off by default in cURL, according to the libcurl documentation. However, applications and HTTP client libraries can enable it.

A PHP setup is therefore most at risk when it decodes Brotli data from sources it does not trust. The “-1” suffix in the new version numbers marks a Windows rebuild with updated dependencies, and the PHP runtime versions themselves do not change.

Administrators should also check for a separate security release that PHP published on October 21. That release fixed two other critical flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which can allow remote code execution without a login. PHP 8.2 will reach end of life on December 31, 2026, so teams still on that branch should plan an upgrade to a supported version.

The bug is not limited to PHP. Researchers have found it in Node.js, Python packages, .NET, FFmpeg, ClickHouse, and Apache Arrow. Microsoft and the maintainers of two Python packages have also shipped patches.

Because so many products reuse Brotli, a version number alone may not show the full picture. Some vendors backport the fix into older releases, so a build can be safe even when its version number looks old.

Security teams should start by confirming that every Windows PHP host runs one of the new -1 packages. They should also check any bundled Brotli libraries, since the fixed upstream versions are 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1.

Teams that cannot patch right away should keep untrusted Brotli input away from production systems. The official PHP security advisory page and the Brotli 1.2.1 release notes on GitHub list the details, and the PHP Windows downloads page hosts the updated packages.

For a wider view of the issue, read our earlier report on how HTTP2Shell reaches beyond web traffic into other software. Our coverage of the Node.js security updates also explains which release lines received fixes.

articles.title: Researchers Use AI Agents to Breach Anthropic’s Internal Systems in Just 12 Hours
articles.description:
Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its AI agents found routes into Anthropic’s internal business systems in less than 12 hours, exposing how fast automated security tools can find and chain flaws across connected services. The work took place through Anthropic’s program for outside researchers, making this an authorized security test rather than a criminal attack, according […]

The post Researchers Use AI Agents to Breach Anthropic’s Internal Systems in Just 12 Hours appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its AI agents found routes into Anthropic’s internal business systems in less than 12 hours, exposing how fast automated security tools can find and chain flaws across connected services.

The work took place through Anthropic’s program for outside researchers, making this an authorized security test rather than a criminal attack, according to The Washington Post.

Anthropic Internal System Breach

According to reporting from The Washington Post, the agents did not break Anthropic’s core AI models or exploit the company’s own code. Instead, Cathedral said they used weaknesses in unnamed third-party software used for administrative and sales work.

Once inside, researchers reached meeting transcripts, salary and job-offer details, and internal Slack talks about Anthropic’s advanced AI models.

Anthropic confirmed in a statement to The Washington Post that Cathedral accessed a limited group of sales, human resources, and IT systems. Those systems held business contact information for some customers and partners, along with basic user account records.

However, customer prompts, Claude responses, source code, and model weights were not accessed. This limit matters because model weights and source code are among an AI company’s most sensitive assets.

Anthropic also said its monitoring tools flagged some of Cathedral’s actions before the startup reported them. The company ended the access on the same day, disabled the affected business software, and restored it only after the vendors confirmed that fixes were ready.

Anthropic said it found no evidence that anyone outside Cathedral had used the weaknesses. The two sides disagree on parts of the test. Anthropic said Cathedral did not fully follow its bug bounty rules because it failed to disclose all activity within the company’s systems.

Cathedral said it kept data access to the minimum needed for responsible research. The vendors behind the affected software were also notified, but their names and the exact flaws were withheld to reduce the risk of misuse.

The case shows why third-party application security is now a major concern for AI labs. A company may protect model infrastructure while connected HR, sales, identity, and collaboration tools create other paths into sensitive business data.

Security teams should map every software connection, limit application permissions, review OAuth tokens, monitor unusual account behavior, and quickly remove access that is no longer needed.

It also shows how AI agents can compress security testing. Agents can scan systems, test paths, run tools, and review results with less waiting between steps.

Cyber Security News has previously reported how AI agents can automate the cyber kill chain and how Claude exploited software flaws during controlled evaluations. These cases do not mean humans are removed. Researchers still set the scope, judge findings, and control disclosure.

Cathedral is only months old, but it has gained attention. The company was co-founded by Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, Marko Elez, and Jack Stein, all former DOGE staffers. Kliger served as the Pentagon’s chief data officer.

Reuters reported in July that Cathedral raised $160 million at a $1.4 billion valuation, with Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital leading the round. A senior Trump administration official told The Washington Post that three federal agencies had contracted with Cathedral and that the government was working with the startup on hostile AI scenarios.
